docs.title: The improvement loop
docs.text:
An improvement loop tries revisions of something you want to improve and measures their results. You supply a starting value, a proposer that revises it, and an independent evaluator. Search decides what to try next. Meta-Evolve records the attempts, measurements, and relationships between versions.

The duration-parser walkthrough makes this concrete. Its starting parser reads seconds correctly but ignores minutes and hours. One handwritten revision adds the missing behavior. Python evaluates both versions against the same six checks: 2/6 → 6/6 checks passed.

An improvement procedure, or method, combines proposal and search decisions to try changes under the declared evaluation and work allowance. Here it uses a handwritten revision and Greedy search. Other methods can use different proposal rules, feedback, or several stages of search.

docs.title: Follow one run
docs.text:
1. Evaluate seed record outcome
  2. Search parent or stop
  3. Propose and validate
  4. Evaluate valid proposals
  5. Record outcome

repeat from Search until it stops

Invalid or failed proposals skip Evaluate and go straight to Record outcome.

Optional, explicit feedback: authorized prior observations reach the proposer.

Evaluation and limits belong to the experiment. A proposed revision cannot rewrite its checks, award itself a score, or grant itself more work. A failed attempt has a typed outcome even when it produces no measurement or valid version; it is not assigned a low score.

Search can branch from different parents or retain weaker stepping stones. It can stop with the seed still selected, or with no successful evaluation. The parser's improving chain is one measured trajectory through this loop.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
These names describe the pieces of a run. Follow a term for more detail.

Term Plain meaning Artifact The thing you want to improve—a prompt, skill document, program, or agent setup. Seed The starting version, such as the parser that ignores minutes and hours. Version One recorded form of the artifact. Revisions keep their links to the versions they came from. Proposer The function that suggests a revision, using handwritten rules or your model SDK. Evaluator The independent function that measures a version against your checks. Score An evaluation measurement, such as checks passed. Your objective says whether higher or lower is better. Trial One attempt and its recorded outcome. The trials= allowance counts proposal attempts after the seed evaluation. Search The rule for choosing which version to revise next and when to stop. Run / history One execution and its recorded versions, measurements, failures, and work used. History stays in memory unless you configure saving. Feedback Prior observations explicitly supplied to help the proposer, such as failed checks. Recording them alone does not supply them. Harness The setup around an agent: its instructions, tools, and rules for working. Only declared parts can be revised. Meta-evolution Improving how improvements are made—for example, revising repair instructions and measuring the repairs they produce.

The first run uses improve() to assemble these pieces. To configure them yourself, follow the parser from Task to Experiment, Session, and Run. That example shows what each object needs and which operation you use next. Constructing a task or experiment declares the setup; run() or Session.start() begins execution, and the returned run lets you inspect what happened.

docs.title: A compact notation (optional)
docs.text:
For discussing an improvement procedure, these symbols name the roles above:

Symbol Meaning A₀ The seed artifact I The improvement procedure E Independent evaluation and the objectives used to interpret its measurements B The externally supplied work allowance R Retained execution results 
R = Execute(I, A₀; E, B)
A_selected = Selected(R)

Selection applies only when an eligible result exists. These are conceptual labels. In Python, use improve() or run(experiment) to execute a single experiment and receive a Run. I names the procedure; an Experiment declares the task, seed, proposer, and search configuration used to execute it. A composed method may retain several runs or its own documented result type, so R does not imply a new common result class.

If experience needs a symbol, use H for the prior observations authorized for the proposer. It is distinct from both evaluation E and the full history in R. The notation also does not promise identical future model responses. See runs and history for result inspection and replay.

docs.title: Read the concepts
docs.text:
Artifacts and versions explains what changes. In the parser, the source is the artifact; the returned numbers help evaluate it. History preserves versions and their parent relationships.

Proposals and search separates creating a revision from choosing its parent. Building on a successful revision and retrying from the original allocate the same allowance differently.

Evaluation and evidence explains what a score measures and which observations support it. Passing the development checks establishes a result on those checks, not correctness for every possible input.

Feedback and experience explains how prior observations reach the proposer. Recording failed checks does not automatically send them to the next attempt.

Runs and history explains how to inspect attempts, preserve their results, and distinguish reopening from resuming unfinished work. Budgets and failures explain how work stops and why an unsuccessful measurement has no score.

Meta-evolution applies the same pattern to an improvement procedure: its instructions, permitted harness settings, or search settings become the candidate, evaluated through their effects on other tasks.

docs.title: What stays under your control
docs.text:
The experiment owns evaluation and budgets; governance owns permissions and promotion. These controls stay outside candidate authority. Selecting a version does not deploy it. The authority boundary explains how these roles relate to the configured execution environment.

For deeper explanations, read identity and lineage, authority and promotion, artifact domains, and extension conformance. The architecture owns the domain rules; the programming model owns the shipped API contract. Project status separates shipped capabilities from future proposals.

docs.title: Artifacts and versions
docs.text: An artifact is the value you want to improve. A seed is its starting version. In the duration-parser walkthrough, that value is a string containing Python source. The proposer returns revised source, and the evaluator measures what each version does.

docs.title: Choose what changes
docs.text:
The starting parser returns 2 for "2m"; a revision makes it return 120. The source string is the candidate being searched. The returned number is an observation used to evaluate that candidate. The expected answer belongs to the evaluator and stays fixed while the source changes.

The same distinction applies to other tasks:

Task Artifact being revised Behavior being measured Parse durations Python source Numbers returned for test inputs Route messages Routing instructions Categories returned for messages Configure an assistant Permitted harness settings Answers on task cases Improve a search procedure Declared search-policy settings Outcomes of bounded inner searches

You choose this boundary when defining the experiment. A response could itself be an artifact in a task that searches over responses. In the routing example, the instructions are the artifact and the responses are observations used to evaluate it. Recording those observations as evidence is an explicit choice.

When part of the improvement procedure becomes the artifact, this is meta-evolution. The enclosing evaluator and controls remain outside that candidate's permitted changes.

docs.title: Keep versions and their parents
docs.text:
A valid revision creates a new artifact occurrence. Its parent is the version it was proposed from; changing the candidate does not overwrite that parent. The parser walkthrough builds this chain:

Seed: seconds
      ↓
Revision: seconds, minutes, and hours

These parent relationships form the version's lineage. Search determines which version gets another attempt, so a different policy can produce branches from the seed instead of one chain. Keeping these relationships lets you associate measurements with the revision tested and reconstruct the path to a selected artifact or procedure.

Two attempts can return exactly the same source and still have different parents, observations, and work counts. Their content can match while their places in history remain distinct. Identity and lineage explains how Meta-Evolve preserves both facts.

docs.title: A valid version may still perform poorly
docs.text:
Validity asks whether a proposed value satisfies the artifact's representation and mutation rules. Evaluation asks how well it performs the task. A source string can be an acceptable artifact yet contain code that fails to load or returns wrong answers. Those outcomes are distinguished by evaluation and failure handling.

result.best().value gives the selected value when at least one evaluation succeeded. The seed can remain selected if no revision beats it. result.lineage() follows the selected version's ancestry, while result.trials() includes all attempts, including regressions and failures. An attempt can fail before producing a valid artifact, so attempts and versions need not have the same count. See runs and history for inspection and saving results across Python restarts. Selection grants no deployment authority.

docs.title: When an artifact domain matters
docs.text:
Ordinary supported Python values use the default artifact contract. The first parser needs no custom codec or source-tree declaration. An explicit artifact domain becomes useful when representation or mutation rules matter, such as applying exact patches to a tree of files.

Try it: Improve a duration parser or improve a routing prompt. Reference: Artifact values and run queries and the identity rules.

docs.title: Authority and promotion
docs.text:
What stops a proposed change from changing the test instead of improving the answer? A declared mutation boundary can reject an attempt to change what a candidate is allowed to edit. The evaluator still judges permitted revisions, including revisions that make the answers worse.

We'll reuse the help assistant: change its matching instruction, ask three questions, and check the answers. This time, a structured harness declares the editable fields. One revision improves the answers, one regresses, and one tries to redefine the planner surface as evaluation_checks. The last is refused before evaluation.

The worker and proposer are handwritten Python simulations. This lesson runs in-process with no model, keys, or earlier notebook state. Its validation is not a security sandbox for arbitrary Python.

Download the notebook · Download the complete Python example

Or copy the five Python blocks into a fresh Jupyter notebook.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

docs.title: 2. Keep the worker and expected answers fixed
docs.text:
Exact matching answers “reset password” but misses “please reset password.” Topic matching allows extra words around the same topic. The worker recognizes these two instructions; it does not interpret arbitrary prompts.

HELP_NOTES supplies its replies. HELP_CASES defines the fixed questions and expected answers. Neither belongs to the configuration being revised.

from dataclasses import replace

import meta_evolve as meta
from meta_evolve import harness
from meta_evolve.domain import ComponentRef

HELP_NOTES = (
    ("reset password", "Open Settings > Password."),
    ("download invoice", "Open Billing > Invoices."),
)
HELP_CASES = (
    ("reset password", "Open Settings > Password."),
    ("please reset password", "Open Settings > Password."),
    ("download invoice", "Open Billing > Invoices."),
)


def answer(question, configuration):
    instruction = configuration.planner.value
    if instruction not in ("Match exact questions.", "Match topic words."):
        raise ValueError("Unsupported matching instruction")
    question = question.lower()
    for topic, reply in HELP_NOTES:
        if instruction == "Match exact questions.":
            matches = question == topic
        else:
            matches = set(topic.split()) <= set(question.split())
        if matches:
            return reply
    return "I don't have a matching help note."

docs.title: 3. Declare the editable values and evaluate real answers
docs.text:
HarnessArtifact has two mutable values: planner text and context-policy configuration. This example changes only the planner text. The parameter names, component references, and interfaces are fixed declarations; the context value is not used by this small worker.

The evaluator asks all three questions and retains the actual answer, expected answer, and pass/fail result. A missed question receives an ordinary poor score. The score does not depend on a revision's label.

HARNESS_SEED = harness.HarnessArtifact(
    planner=harness.TextParam(
        "planner", ComponentRef("planner", "help-matcher", "1"),
        "matching-instruction/v1", "Match exact questions.",
    ),
    context_policy=harness.PolicyParam(
        "context_policy", ComponentRef("context-policy", "fixed-notes", "1"),
        "help-context/v1", {"include": ("help-notes",)},
    ),
)


def evaluate_harness(configuration):
    checks = []
    for question, expected in HELP_CASES:
        actual = answer(question, configuration)
        checks.append({"question": question, "expected": expected,
                       "actual": actual, "passed": actual == expected})
    return meta.EvaluationResult(
        metrics={"score": sum(check["passed"] for check in checks) / len(checks)},
        evidence=(meta.EvidenceDraft(kind="help-checks", data={"checks": checks}),),
    )

docs.title: 4. Propose an improvement, a regression, and a forbidden edit
docs.text:
The first revision changes the planner's value to topic matching. The second restores exact matching, so the polite password question fails again.

The third uses replace to rename the planner's mutation surface to evaluation_checks and propose an always-pass rule. It bypasses the convenient mutation helper deliberately. It attempts to change the declaration of what may be edited; it never obtains or changes the actual evaluator or HELP_CASES.

def allowed_improvement(parent):
    return parent.apply(harness.HarnessMutation("planner", "Match topic words."))


def allowed_regression(parent):
    return parent.apply(harness.HarnessMutation("planner", "Match exact questions."))


def redefine_checks(parent):
    return replace(parent, planner=replace(
        parent.planner, name="evaluation_checks", value="accept every answer",
    ))


def propose_harness(parent):
    return next(proposal_steps)(parent)


def show_outcome(label, trial):
    work = f"attempts +{trial.usage.trials}, evaluations +{trial.usage.evaluations}"
    if trial.failure:
        print(f"{label}: {trial.failure.kind}; {work}")
        print("Refusal record: authority_result.trials()[-1]")
        print("Reason:", trial.failure.message, dict(trial.failure.details))
    else:
        checks = trial.evidence[0].data["checks"]
        print(f"{label}: {sum(c['passed'] for c in checks)}/{len(checks)} checks; {work}")
        check = checks[1]
        print(check["question"], "->", check["actual"], check["passed"])

docs.title: 5. Run and inspect the retained outcomes
docs.text:
The expanded Task declares the harness artifact type; improve() uses the default artifact type and cannot select this structured codec. The allowance covers three proposal attempts and up to four evaluations, including the seed. There is no score target that would stop the run at the first perfect result.

proposal_steps = iter((allowed_improvement, allowed_regression, redefine_checks))
authority_task = meta.Task(
    artifact=harness.HarnessArtifact, evaluator=evaluate_harness,
    objectives=(meta.Maximize("score"),), budget=meta.Budget(trials=3, evaluations=4),
)
authority_experiment = meta.Experiment(
    task=authority_task, seed=HARNESS_SEED, proposer=propose_harness,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=3),
)
authority_result = meta.run(authority_experiment)
for label, trial in zip(("Starting", "Improvement", "Regression", "Attempt 3"),
                        authority_result.trials()):
    show_outcome(label, trial)
selected_harness = authority_result.best().value
print("Original declaration:", HARNESS_SEED.planner.name)
print("Protected polite check:", HELP_CASES[1])
print("Selected instruction:", selected_harness.planner.value)
work = authority_result.usage()
print("Total:", work.trials, "attempts;", work.evaluations, "evaluations")
# Output:
# Starting: 2/3 checks; attempts +0, evaluations +1
# please reset password -> I don't have a matching help note. False
# Improvement: 3/3 checks; attempts +1, evaluations +1
# please reset password -> Open Settings > Password. True
# Regression: 2/3 checks; attempts +1, evaluations +1
# please reset password -> I don't have a matching help note. False
# Attempt 3: policy_violation; attempts +1, evaluations +0
# Refusal record: authority_result.trials()[-1]
# Reason: harness successor expands mutation authority {'changed_declarations': ('planner.name',)}
# Original declaration: planner
# Protected polite check: ('please reset password', 'Open Settings > Password.')
# Selected instruction: Match topic words.
# Total: 3 attempts; 3 evaluations

The starting instruction passes 2/3 checks, the improved instruction passes 3/3, and the permitted regression passes 2/3. Greedy keeps the better instruction as its parent for the remaining proposals and as the selected result. The regression is a distinct recorded version even though its content matches the seed.

The final attempt has a typed PolicyViolation, a refusal reason, and no score, successor artifact, or evaluation. Its record remains available through authority_result.trials()[-1]; its .id identifies that retained attempt. The output shows three attempts and three evaluations: seed, improvement, and regression. The refused attempt spends one proposal attempt and zero evaluations, leaving one evaluation unused. Each evaluation asks three questions; those are checks within one evaluation.

docs.title: What enforces the refusal?
docs.text:
The built-in harness codec's validate_successor checks the encoded proposal against its parent before a successor artifact is created or evaluated. It finds the changed declaration planner.name and records PolicyViolation. The experiment's checks, evaluator, objective, and budget remain unchanged. The public contract defines this boundary.

HarnessArtifact.apply also validates mutation requests, but that helper is only a convenience. Asking it directly for an undeclared evaluation_checks surface would return InvalidOutput. The demonstrated replace bypass shows that core admission independently rejects the changed declaration.

This protects the structured proposal path. Ordinary in-process Python can access notebook globals; declaring an independent evaluator does not isolate malicious callbacks. No process or filesystem confinement is used here. A path-valid SourceTree alone also does not enforce a file allowlist. For source execution controls and their limits, see the source execution guide.

Preventing this declared forbidden edit does not prevent every way to exploit an imperfect metric. Our three checks cannot establish general answer quality; see the broader specification-gaming research.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
In the final cell's proposal_steps, replace redefine_checks with allowed_regression, then rerun that cell. Predict four evaluations and a third revision with a real 2/3 score. The best instruction is still topic matching, so restoring exact matching is a change to that parent each time. Restore the forbidden edit to see the typed refusal again.

You can also change an expected answer as the experiment author and rerun. The score should change with the checks. That is a new evaluation setup, not authority a proposal receives within the original run.

docs.title: Three fields, three owners
docs.text:
Authority determines who may change a candidate, judge its results, or approve its use. The proposer supplies a revision, the evaluator measures it, search decides what to try or select, and governance controls promotion.

A trial's record splits into three kinds of fields:

  • Candidate-controlled — the proposed artifact content and its declared citations. Everything a proposer decides, and nothing else.
  • Experiment-controlled — the task, evaluator, hidden data, environment, seeds, and budgets. The evaluator scores independently; a proposer's claim about its own quality never moves a metric.
  • Governance-controlled — permissions, admission, visibility, and promotion. These live outside the run entirely.
candidate            experiment             governance
─────────            ──────────             ──────────
artifact content     evaluator + data       permissions
declared citations   budgets + seeds        visibility
                     environments           promotion

The experiment defines which fields a proposal may change. Evaluation rules, budgets, recorded failures, and permissions are outside that mutation boundary. The same rule applies when a procedure becomes the candidate: its permitted settings can change while the enclosing controls stay fixed.

Audited source inspection enforces grants on reads through the experience interface. Verification and presentation stay outside candidate authority. See audited pull for access checks and limits.

docs.title: Proposal is not promotion
docs.text:
Search may select a best measured artifact. That selection grants no production authority: promotion — actually deploying the selected artifact — is an external governance act that no candidate and no search policy can perform. This run leaves a selected instruction for the caller to review and use. The advanced harness repair study also makes the boundary explicit with promotion=external; selection and export do not deploy the result.

The authority invariants are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

Try it: Improve an agent's harness. Related: Evaluation and evidence and meta-evolution. Reference: Authority boundaries.

docs.title: Budgets and stopping
docs.text: A budget bounds the work an experiment may consume. A search limit bounds the attempts a policy chooses to make. A satisfaction threshold can stop search when a measured result is good enough. These controls act together and remain outside the candidate's authority.

docs.title: Count the seed as work
docs.text:
The parser walkthrough allows two proposal attempts with trials=2. Its seed is evaluated before either proposal:

Work Proposal attempts Evaluations Evaluate the seed 0 1 Propose and evaluate the minutes revision 1 1 Propose and evaluate the complete revision 1 1 Total for this run 2 3

An allowance is a ceiling, not a promise to perform all the work. A satisfaction threshold or a tighter evaluation budget can stop this run earlier. An invalid proposal still consumes an attempt but may never reach evaluation. A failure during evaluation consumes evaluation work without producing a score.

Use Set limits and stopping conditions to see how changing one control affects the selected parser and its recorded counts.

docs.title: Inspect recorded usage
docs.text:
The supplemental commands below run from the repository root after installing the project dependencies.

The inspection guide evaluates the seed and three proposed revisions. usage() counts four evaluations, including the attempt that failed while loading the source. There are no model calls. The supplemental minimal example below isolates the seed/attempt arithmetic.

uv run python examples/learn/checklist/_stories/search_story.py
Output
usage: Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, spend_micros=0, wall_seconds=0.0)

docs.title: Five dimensions, one ledger
docs.text: Usage counts five dimensions: evaluations (each independent scoring), trials (each attempted successor), tokens (model usage a component reports), spend_micros (charged monetary spend a component reports, in integer micro-USD), and wall_seconds (recorded elapsed work). The transcript's arithmetic is exact: the seed costs one evaluation and no trial; each of three successors costs one trial and, when valid, one evaluation — four evaluations, three trials.

docs.title: Nobody widens their own budget
docs.text:
Budget is checked before more work starts, and exhaustion is a recorded stop reason, not an error. That preflight covers counts, tokens, and wall time; monetary spend is knowable only after a call returns, so it is enforced post-hoc — the action that crosses the ceiling fails typed and the run then admits no further work at all, free work included, because the halt is recorded against the run rather than against the next action's price. A candidate or component never grants itself additional work; the run budget can narrow what a search preset would attempt, never expand it.

The five budget-inheriting presets make that direction explicit. Declaring max_trials=None on Greedy, BestOfN, Population, Specialists, or TreeSearch copies the effective finite Budget.trials into the policy limit once, at bind time; it is the preset deferring to external authority, not acquiring any. The reverse never holds: an explicit limit above the budget still stops at the budget, and records budget_exhausted rather than trial_limit_reached. See runs and results.

Unknown billed spend stays unknown; an estimate is evidence rather than a billed amount. A monetary ceiling stops further work when spend cannot be verified. It cannot guarantee that an in-flight provider request stays below its ceiling.

Spend is adjudicated at two scopes, and the second is not derivable from the first: the aggregate remainder, and each trial's own declared ceiling. A policy may submit per-trial ceilings while the task leaves spend unbounded, in which case the aggregate rule never arms and only the per-trial one stops paid work. Both are folds over committed facts, so live, resumed, and replayed runs reach the same verdict.

docs.title: Experience has its own meter
docs.text:
uv run python examples/learn/experience_reuse/learning_story.py
Output
pushed context: (10, 3)
audited pull: (10, 7, 20)

Memory reads are charged outside the task ledger, on their own separate bounds. The transcript pairs each score with its memory bill: pushed context reports (score, records pushed) and audited pull reports (score, operations, records returned). A proposer reading history spends experience budget, never evaluation budget, so memory can neither starve nor subsidize the search itself. run.experience_usage() exposes the meter on any result.

Exact-source inspection and its optional Git presentation use that same separate experience account. See the experience reference for operation and charging rules and the programming model for the API.

Accounting rules are canonical in the architecture and the evaluation and budgets guide, and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change max_trials=3 to max_trials=2 in the first transcript's Greedy run. Predict Usage(evaluations=3, trials=2, ...): one fewer attempted successor, one fewer independent scoring, and nothing else moves.

Try it: Set limits and stopping conditions. Related: Failures and measurements and feedback and experience. Reference: Exact accounting and monetary spend.

docs.title: Extension conformance
docs.text:
Conformance means that an extension follows the laws required by its component interface. It lets a custom component participate in the same loop as a built-in component. Start with artifact domains for one example of such an extension.

You wrote a custom evaluator, codec, or search program. How do you know it obeys the same rules the built-in components obey? You run the same published tests the library runs on itself.

docs.title: What a conformance suite is
docs.text:
meta_evolve.conformance publishes one pytest-native suite per extension component family. Each suite is a plain class of laws whose collaborators arrive as fixtures: subclass it, name the subclass Test... so pytest collects it, override the fixtures with your component, and the laws run against your implementation.

published suite               your test module
───────────────               ────────────────
ArtifactCodecTests      <--   class TestMyCodec(ArtifactCodecTests):
  law: decode(encode(v))          fixture: my codec
  law: decode is validation       fixture: rejected payloads
  law: no aliasing                fixture: mutable values

The suites install through an explicit extra, so using the library never pulls in a test runner:

uv sync --extra conformance

docs.title: What the library proves about itself
docs.text:
Every published suite is subclassed inside the repository's own tests, so the built-in codecs, evaluators, policies, and search programs pass exactly the laws an extension author receives. A suite also states what it does not check as carefully as what it does: EvaluatorTests skips its typed-failure law, visibly, when a subclass declares no rejected candidates, and ArtifactCodecTests does the same for its aliasing law. Silence is never counted as passing.

One law is easy to think redundant and is not: EvaluatorTests checks that scoring does not edit the candidate. With built-in codecs an evaluator only ever sees a frozen decoded value — but a custom codec that returns the instance it was handed gives the evaluator the real thing, so the law waits where the damage would land.

docs.title: When you reach for one
docs.text:
• You registered an artifact domain — run your codec through ArtifactCodecTests, as Add an artifact domain does in its final step.
  • You wrote an evaluator, context policy, workspace, sandbox, search program, or repository proposer — the extensions guide lists every family and its published suite.

Suite contents and deliberate limitations are canonical in the extensions guide and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Subclass ArtifactCodecTests around a codec whose decode returns the exact instance it was handed, and declare one mutable value. Predict a named aliasing-law failure, not a vague error: the suite tells you which contract your codec broke.

Try it: Add an artifact domain. Reference: Published conformance suites.

docs.title: Artifact domains
docs.text:
An artifact domain defines how a kind of value is represented and validated. Its codec translates between that value and its stored payload. Start with artifacts and versions when deciding what your experiment changes.

The first parser example uses an ordinary Python string through the default python-value artifact contract. You do not need to declare a new domain for it. Explicit text, source, and skill domains become useful when their distinct representation or mutation contracts matter.

The loop never inspects what it improves. A number, a prompt, a repository, a harness — every artifact travels as a typed payload that one registered codec translates, so no coordinator code branches on what you evolve.

docs.title: Six built-in kinds
docs.text:
Every artifact is stored under a (kind, representation) key. Six keys ship built in:

Kind Representation What it holds python-value canonical-json any canonically serializable value — the default text utf8-text-v1 one UTF-8 document: a prompt, a config, an essay source-tree utf8-tree-v1 an immutable directory of UTF-8 files skill-set utf8-tree-v1 named skill documents agent-harness harness-manifest-v1 a portable agent-harness bundle search-policy policy-manifest-v1 declarative search-policy values

Text optimization and context evolution run two of these through the identical meta.run call site; SQL migrations registers a seventh, custom domain and is the runnable tour of everything on this page.

docs.title: Kind versus representation
docs.text: The kind, never the bytes, decides which codec reads a committed payload. source-tree and skill-set share the same tree bytes (utf8-tree-v1) and still decode differently, because a payload's meaning is a declared contract rather than an inference from its shape.

docs.title: Persistence and custom domains
docs.text:
A registered custom codec is a live Python object with no verifiable manifest. A durable run must be reopenable by a reader who can decode every payload from the record alone — a payload another machine cannot decode is not shareable evidence. So durable-local mode accepts only the six built-in keys and rejects a custom codec before writing any event, with no silent fallback. A local run with a custom domain still works and may still write durable storage; reopening it later means rebuilding the same registry in Python, which grants decoding, not resumption.

To build a domain end to end, follow Add an artifact domain. Codec laws are canonical in the programming model and the published conformance suite, and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Seed a text task with a tuple instead of a string. Predict a typed refusal at ingress — utf8-text-v1 tasks require a str value — before any trial runs: decode and encode are validation, not best-effort coercion.

Try it: Add an artifact domain. Related: Extension conformance and runs and history. Reference: Extension contracts.

docs.title: Evaluation and evidence
docs.text:
An evaluator measures a candidate independently of the proposer that created it. Metrics report those measurements, and objectives say which results to prefer. Evidence records observations or claims alongside the measurements, with their authorship preserved.

A Task brings the evaluator and objectives together as a reusable evaluation contract. You supply the evaluator; the default objective prefers a higher score. Changing the proposer or search strategy can reuse that same task. The Task example shows the declaration and how an experiment uses it.

docs.title: Define what better means
docs.text:
In the parser walkthrough, the evaluator runs each source version on six fixed inputs and checks the returned numbers. Its metric is the fraction correct: the seed passes 2/6, and the proposed revision passes 6/6.

The default objective maximizes the scalar evaluator's score. You can instead return named measurements and declare their objectives, such as maximizing correctness or minimizing a measured error. The evaluation guide makes those choices explicit. An optional satisfaction threshold tells search when the results are good enough to stop; it is distinct from choosing which measured result is best.

The evaluator owns the cases and expected answers. A candidate changes its source; it cannot change those answers or award itself a better score.

docs.title: Understand what the measurement establishes
docs.text:
Passing all six development checks establishes behavior on those checks. It does not establish correctness for every duration string. Separate final checks help assess behavior beyond the cases used during search. If a check influences which candidate wins, it participates in selection even when the proposer cannot see its answer.

A parser that returns a wrong number can receive a low score. Source that cannot execute makes this evaluator fail with no score. The failure concept explains why a failed measurement cannot be substituted with a zero.

docs.title: Record observations beside scores
docs.text:
A 67% score does not identify which two checks still fail. The first parser walkthrough records only scores. The feedback guide uses staged revisions and adds evidence containing each failed check's input, expected answer, and actual answer. After its minutes-only revision, the remaining failed checks are:

Input Expected seconds Actual seconds "1h" 3600 1 "2h" 7200 2

You can inspect this evidence to understand the result. To supply it as feedback, explicitly select prior observations for the next proposal; recording them alone does not send them to the proposer.

Evidence can also contain the proposer's hypothesis about a change. Its authorship matters: a hypothesis is a candidate's claim, while a grader's transcript records the evaluator's observations. Neither replaces the independently measured metrics.

docs.title: Inspect evidence authorship and access
docs.text:
The following supplemental example uses two kinds of evidence and a later proposal that reads them. Run it from the repository root after installing the project dependencies; it is separate from the parser notebook.

uv run python examples/learn/experience_reuse/evidence_story.py
Output
seed evidence: ('grader-transcript',)
successor evidence: ('hypothesis-note', 'grader-transcript')
last proposal derived from: 3 prior records
audited pull: operations=6 records=8

docs.title: 1. Evidence on an evaluation
docs.text: The evaluator returns an EvaluationResult that carries an EvidenceDraft beside its metrics. The seed trial shows only grader-transcript: evaluator-authored evidence of what the grader observed. Evidence records what was observed; it is not a candidate-controlled score.

docs.title: 2. Evidence on a proposal
docs.text: The proposer returns a ProposalResult with a draft of its own. The successor trial adds hypothesis-note: candidate-authored evidence stating the claim behind the change. A proposer can write anything here, and its score does not move — the metrics stay with the independent evaluator.

docs.title: 3. Evidence a later candidate can read
docs.text: With PullAccess, a later proposal searches prior evidence records and opens the ones it uses. The last proposal cited three: the seed's grader transcript plus both records from the first successor. Every read is audited — six operations and eight returned records are charged and inspectable — and the citations land in the trial's derived_from edges.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Remove the hypothesis-note draft from the proposer. Predict the successor line shrinking to ('grader-transcript',) while derived_from still cites two prior records: the proposal's citations never depended on the proposal publishing evidence of its own.

Try it: Define what better means or give the proposer feedback. Reference: Evaluation, evidence, and objectives and evaluation independence.

docs.title: Feedback and experience
docs.text:
Experience is recorded prior work that a later proposal can use. Feedback is an observation supplied to help that proposal, such as a failed check from its parent's evaluation. Recording an observation and making it available to a proposer are separate choices.

Experience is explicit and off by default. Search can use recorded measurements to choose a parent while the proposer receives no prior run observations. An experiment can enable bounded feedback or inspection to inform revisions. The proposed change still needs independent evaluation.

docs.title: Turn a measurement into useful feedback
docs.text:
In the feedback guide, the starting parser returns 2 for "2m" instead of 120. The evaluator records the input, expected answer, and actual answer as evidence, alongside its score.

The proposer uses those records to choose a handwritten fix: repair minutes while minute checks fail, then repair hours. Evaluation measures the proposed source independently. The proposer uses the supplied observations without calling or changing the evaluator.

This guide deliberately gives the proposer no other way to choose a fix. With feedback disabled, it returns the seed unchanged. The evaluator still records the failures; they simply do not reach the proposer. The resulting score difference demonstrates that explicit connection, not a general promise about learning or model performance.

docs.title: Decide what reaches the proposer
docs.text:
Access Who selects the observations? What the proposer receives No experience Nobody Its artifact input, without prior run observations Pushed context An experiment-declared context policy A bounded bundle prepared before the proposal Audited pull The proposer requests records within an explicit access grant Authorized results, with reads recorded and charged

The feedback guide uses AncestorsOnly to supply history from the parent's lineage, including its evaluation. That excludes rejected siblings. A proposer should use the relevant recent observations rather than treating old failures as defects that must still exist in the current version.

Changing the context policy changes what the proposer can see. Changing search changes which parent it receives. These components can be varied independently.

docs.title: Keep the scope and cost explicit
docs.text:
Context selection and pull access have their own record and operation bounds. Experience accounting is separate from proposal and evaluation counts. A recorded observation may never be disclosed; a disclosed observation may go unused. Declared citations can refer only to authorized prior observations and record the proposer's attribution. They do not prove that the observation caused an improvement. The experience guide shows how to compare runs with and without that information.

Final evaluation cases must stay outside development feedback when they are intended to check generalization. Even a private score used to choose the winner participates in search. Calling it a final check does not make it independent if it repeatedly guides revisions.

docs.title: Supplying context and evolving its content
docs.text:
Giving a parser proposer failed checks is experience access. Revising a skill document or an agent's context settings changes an artifact. Those changes need their own independent evaluation, as explained in meta-evolution.

Try it: Give the proposer feedback. Reference: Experience access and experience provenance.

docs.title: Failures and measurements
docs.text:
A failure records why an attempt could not produce a valid outcome. Its type identifies what went wrong. A poor measurement and a failed measurement mean different things: one reports task performance, while the other has no valid score to compare.

In the inspection guide, a parser that returns wrong answers receives a measured score of 33%. Malformed Python source cannot execute, so its evaluation fails with no score. The supplemental example below isolates a malformed candidate proposal, which is also non-rankable.

Run the supplemental commands on this page from the repository root after installing the project dependencies.

uv run python examples/learn/checklist/_stories/search_story.py
Output
failure: ('trial_failed', 'InvalidOutput')

A proposer that returns an unusable object produces a failed trial with a named type. The run records what went wrong instead of inventing a number.

docs.title: The failure kinds
docs.text:
Parser outcome What evaluation establishes Returns the wrong number A measured incorrect answer, included in the score Returns correct answers A measured result on the cases that ran Contains source that this evaluator cannot execute An evaluator failure, with no score

Invalid candidate shape, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure all retain distinct types and details. The distinctions matter because the correct responses differ: retry a flaky environment, fix a broken proposer, and never penalize a candidate for the grader's crash.

docs.title: Rankable or non-rankable, never fake
docs.text: A trial with a valid independent evaluation is rankable: search may select it. A trial without one is non-rankable: it never becomes zero, negative infinity, or a fabricated metric, so no failure can outrank or sandbag an honestly measured candidate.

docs.title: Two failures that look alike but are not
docs.text:
uv run python examples/domains/python_function/learning_story.py
Output
invalid proposal: InvalidOutput
evaluator failure: EvaluatorFailure

Improve source runs three negative cases: a poor candidate is valid, evaluated, and rankable at 0.0; a patch whose expected bytes do not match is InvalidOutput with no successor; a broken grader is EvaluatorFailure with no score at all. The agent test-repair and adversarial-inputs examples push the same boundary further: three outcomes, not two.

Failure semantics are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Make the failing proposer in the first transcript return a well-formed tuple instead. Predict the trial_failed line becoming an evaluated trial: the type disappears because the cause disappeared, not because a score was substituted.

Try it: Inspect results and failures. Related: Evaluation and evidence and budgets and stopping. Reference: Typed failures.

docs.title: Runs and history
docs.text:
A run is one execution of an improvement experiment and the history it records. The experiment declares what to improve and how; the run tells you what happened, including unsuccessful attempts and work already consumed.

This is the retained result of one improvement loop. A composed method can retain several runs: in policy evolution, the outer run records procedure evaluations with evidence identifying distinct inner runs. Keeping those histories preserves which execution produced each outcome.

A Session controls an active execution. It needs an experiment to start; session.step() advances one search decision, and session.run provides the history recorded so far. run(experiment) handles that execution for you and returns the run after search stops. The paced parser example shows the same experiment executed both ways. Reading a run's methods does not execute further attempts.

docs.title: Read more than the selected version
docs.text:
The parser walkthrough records the seed and one revision. The inspection guide also includes a regression and malformed source. Both remain visible even when a different version wins.

Question Public query What value was selected? run.best().value What measurements selected it? run.best_trial() What attempts succeeded or failed? run.trials() Which versions led to the selection? run.lineage() How much work was recorded? run.usage() What is the overall state, including failures? run.inspect()

A result is rankable when a valid evaluation supplies measurements for selection. A run can contain failures without any rankable result. Inspect its state and outcomes before relying on a selected value. Finishing a run means that it stopped; it does not mean the candidate reached your desired quality.

docs.title: Preserve the history you need
docs.text:
By default, a local run records its history in memory. Passing durable storage writes committed facts to disk as the run executes. The saving guide reopens those facts after the original Python process exits, without redefining the proposer or evaluator.

Exporting the selected parser saves one value. Keeping the run's storage also preserves the versions, measurements, evidence, failures, and recorded relationships needed to understand that value. An exported source file alone does not contain its evaluation history.

docs.title: Reopen, replay, and resume
docs.text:
Operation What happens Does it execute more experiment work? Reopen Read a stored run for inspection No Replay Reconstruct state from committed records No Resume Continue compatible unfinished work from its recovery point Yes, when work remains

Saving a run that uses local Python callables preserves its recorded results; it does not make those callables reconstructible for resume. The durable-local execution mode requires registered, reconstructible components and compatible declarations. The durability reference owns those requirements.

Replay uses the recorded facts without rerunning a proposer, evaluator, or model. A new request to an external model can produce a different response. The record explains the earlier execution; it is not a guarantee of identical future responses.

docs.title: Use a selected version deliberately
docs.text:
Reading a saved artifact does not deploy it. Review or separately evaluate the selection for its intended use, then export or apply it through your own workflow. Authority and promotion explains that boundary.

Try it: Inspect results and failures or save and reopen a run. Reference: Run queries, durability, and the read-only history browser.

docs.title: Identity and lineage
docs.text:
An artifact has a content identity and an occurrence identity. Content identity describes its encoded value; occurrence identity describes one appearance in the run. Parent links connect those occurrences into its lineage. This keeps each attempt's evaluation and work attributable even when values repeat. The same distinction applies to a procedure artifact.

The search lesson follows recorded parent choices to explain the selected version's lineage. Even when two attempts produce identical values, each keeps its own measurements and usage. Read artifacts and versions for the basic model; the small example below isolates this identity rule. Run it from the repository root after installing the project dependencies.

A proposer can hand back a value byte-identical to one the run has already seen. Are they the same artifact? Meta-Evolve answers with two identities: one for the bytes, one for the causal event that produced them.

uv run python examples/learn/checklist/_stories/identity_story.py
Output
seed: id=f953e1f8 digest=6ae048f0 parents=()
successor: id=227a6a34 digest=6ae048f0 parents=('f953e1f8',)
successor: id=99877b49 digest=6ae048f0 parents=('f953e1f8',)
content digests equal: True
distinct occurrence ids: 3

The proposer restates its parent unchanged, twice, under BestOfN. Three artifacts hold the same five bytes. The run still records three distinct things.

docs.title: Content identity is the bytes
docs.text: The digest is a stable hash of the encoded artifact value. All three rows share 6ae048f0 because all three values are "draft". Equal bytes always produce an equal digest, so storage deduplicates payloads and a transcript of digests stays stable across reruns. The lineage: ('659bfe4a', '08abe248') line in Improve source prints exactly this: a digest prefix for each lineage step.

docs.title: Occurrence identity is the causal event
docs.text:
The occurrence id names one appearance of those bytes at one position in the run: proposed from which parents, at which logical step. The seed has no parents. Each successor names the seed as its parent and receives its own id. Equal artifact bytes in different causal positions remain different occurrences.

This distinction is also why audited source inspection authorizes an exact prior occurrence rather than matching content alone. See audited pull for source references and their validation.

docs.title: Why the run needs both
docs.text:
Two trials that produce byte-identical artifacts remain different causal events: they may have different parents, observations, usage, and failures. Collapsing them would erase which attempt actually earned its evaluation. Replay and audited experience address records by causal position, never by content, so history stays exact even when values repeat. The experience lesson shows the same rule inside the temporal graph.

Both identities are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change restate to return parent + "!". Predict digests that stop being equal while the parent links stay exactly the same: content identity follows the bytes; occurrence identity never depended on them.

Related: Artifacts and versions and runs and history. Reference: Identity and lineage rules.

docs.title: Meta-evolution
docs.text:
Meta-evolution applies the improvement loop to a declared part of an improvement procedure. The candidate might be an agent's instructions, permitted harness settings, or search settings. Its evaluator measures the outcomes produced when that candidate procedure is used on other tasks.

This is useful when the desired output is a reusable way to search, research, or revise artifacts. In AutoResearch, the editable artifact is a research recipe, and its evaluation runs bounded inner searches. The same experimental shape can be used when developing a discovery procedure: the author supplies the domain, observations, and independent evaluation. Scientific method mappings identify the additional methods still to implement.

  • Improve a parser

    Change the parser's source ↓ Run that parser in Python ↓ Count how many fixed checks pass Keep the best measured version

    The parser walkthrough tries one handwritten correction: 2/6 → 6/6 checks passed.

  • Improve how an agent repairs code

    Change the agent's repair instructions or context settings ↓ Run the same worker on fixed repository repair tasks ↓ Independently test the code it produces Keep the best measured settings

    The Meta-Harness example uses Claude SDK agents to propose settings and produce repairs. Independent checks measure those repairs before private selection and a held-out comparison. Its live capture is pending; the separate deterministic reference runs without model requests.

The second level measures the instructions through the repairs they produce. At both levels, the starting version can still win. Evaluation rules and limits stay fixed; proposed changes affect only the declared source or settings.

docs.title: Move the candidate boundary outward
docs.text:
In the parser walkthrough, source changes while the proposer, evaluator, and search policy stay fixed. Proposals and search shows that choosing different parents changes the result. To evaluate that choice systematically, search settings can themselves become candidates in an outer experiment.

The policy example makes that shift concrete. An inner run improves a number. The outer run tries revisions to the policy that chooses which number to build on and how many attempts to make:

Role Inner experiment Outer experiment Candidate A number Parent selection and a voluntary attempt limit Proposer Increment the selected number Revise a permitted policy field Evaluator Measure the resulting number Aggregate bounded inner outcomes on fixed tasks Search A trusted interpreter applies the candidate policy Fixed outer search compares policy measurements Retained results Each inner run's history and usage The outer run and evidence identifying its inner runs

The terms inner and outer describe relative roles. Both use the same experimental structure; nesting comes from the outer evaluator executing bounded inner work.

The outer evaluator owns the inner tasks and controls used for comparison. A candidate cannot choose easier grading or raise those controls to make itself appear better.

Schmidhuber's 1987 thesis, §2.2, pp. 9–11 describes a meta-evolution scheme in which programs that transform other programs can themselves be evolved. Higher-level candidates are assessed through the changes they produce at lower levels. Our connection is treating an improvement procedure as an evaluated candidate; Meta-Evolve expresses that boundary through its existing experiment contracts. The original page scans were inspected on 2026-09-17.

docs.title: Shipped examples
docs.text:
Example Candidate Independent evaluation Harness improvement Planner instructions and permitted context settings Answers from a small help assistant on fixed questions Policy improvement Parent selection and a voluntary proposal limit Results of bounded number-improvement runs AutoResearch A bounded research recipe Aggregated inner outcomes, followed by separate final checks

The harness guide uses a handwritten assistant to demonstrate how configuration affects behavior. Evaluating an assistant does not itself require another Meta-Evolve run; use a recorded inner loop when the task needs one.

The policy guide makes nesting explicit. Its inner proposer increments a number. One policy always starts from the seed; another can build on the best number so far. The outer evaluator compares the resulting inner outcomes. These deterministic examples demonstrate composition, not live-model gains.

docs.title: Keep evaluation and limits outside the candidate
docs.text:
The shipped policy artifact contains data: parent selection and a voluntary attempt limit. A trusted interpreter applies those values. It does not allow arbitrary executable policy code to become the candidate.

A candidate's voluntary limit can stop inner work early, but cannot enlarge the evaluator-owned budget. The outer evaluator, task cases, comparison rules, permissions, and promotion authority remain fixed. Harness changes are also limited to their declared mutable surfaces.

Each inner run has its own history and work counts. In shipped policy evaluation, inner proposal and evaluation counts stay inner; reported token usage, monetary spend, and elapsed work roll into the enclosing evaluation. A failed or incomplete required episode makes that outer evaluation non-rankable while preserving partial outcomes.

docs.title: Check the selected procedure on fresh tasks
docs.text: Development cases guide search. After selection, compare the baseline and selected procedure on separate held-out cases under equal external controls. Repeatedly using those checks to revise the procedure makes them development data too. A comparison reports evidence and eligibility; it grants no deployment authority.

docs.title: A compact notation (optional)
docs.text:
Using the loop's notation, let θ denote the procedure artifact and Iθ the procedure obtained by interpreting it under fixed controls. In the policy example, θ contains the two editable settings; the interpreter, task suite, and evaluation rules remain fixed.

R_j(θ) = bounded execution of Iθ
         on fixed inner task j

E_outer(θ) = aggregate of R_j(θ)

The same loop now applies outside: the seed is a procedure artifact θ₀, and the outer evaluator owns the aggregation in E_outer. Each R_j denotes one inner execution's results; the enclosing evaluator chooses what to capture and persist. The policy evaluator requires complete, rankable inner results and captures partial evidence on failure. AutoResearch retains score summaries without reopenable inner histories; compare their retention and accounting. These expressions describe the composition; they are not additional Python APIs.

docs.title: What would make improvement recursive?
docs.text:
A further step is to use an improved procedure to generate subsequent procedure candidates. To study whether that helps, retain which procedure produced each change and compare its ability to produce further improvements under comparable evaluation and resource controls.

The shipped policy example keeps its outer proposer fixed. It revises inner search settings, but does not feed the selected policy back into the procedure that proposes those policy revisions. Nested runs demonstrate bounded meta-evolution; they alone do not establish recursive self-improvement. The research survey discusses the additional evidence and its limits.

Try it: Improve an agent's harness or improve a search policy. Reference: Harness semantics and nested improvement loops. Further proposals are marked Design—not shipped in the design record.

docs.title: Proposals and search
docs.text:
A proposer creates a possible revision. A search policy chooses the version to revise next and when to stop. Keeping these roles separate lets you change how attempts are allocated while retaining the same proposer and independent evaluator.

An Experiment combines those components with a task and starting artifact. Supply the revision function as proposer and the policy as search. Calling run(experiment) executes that declaration. The Experiment example shows the fields together before execution starts.

docs.title: The proposer creates a candidate
docs.text:
In the parser walkthrough, propose(source) receives source and returns one handwritten replacement that adds minutes and hours support.

A real proposer can instead call your model SDK. In either case, the returned revision is a candidate. The evaluator measures its performance; a confident explanation from the proposer is not a passing result.

docs.title: Search chooses the parent
docs.text:
The parent is the version supplied to an attempt. The search guide compares a handwritten Greedy loop with recorded runs using Greedy and TreeSearch. Each run uses the same starting value, proposal rules, evaluator, and allowance.

Greedy builds on the best measured version so far. TreeSearch also allocates attempts to other branches. In the lesson, an initially weaker version leads to the best result. Its deliberately constructed score table illustrates parent selection; it is not a benchmark or a reason to expect TreeSearch to perform better on your task. The recorded attempts show which parent each policy chose and what happened next.

docs.title: An attempt need not improve the result
docs.text:
For these policies, a strictly better measured revision replaces the selected version. A tie keeps the earlier winner, and a regression stays in history without becoming the winner. A failed measurement contributes no score to compare. The seed can remain the best result throughout a run.

The first-run improve() call uses bounded Greedy search. trials=1 allows one proposal attempt after the seed evaluation. An explicit Experiment lets you choose a policy; its attempt allowance is still subject to the experiment's budgets and stopping conditions.

docs.title: Search and feedback answer different questions
docs.text:
Search chooses which version to revise. A context policy chooses which prior observations to supply with that version. Selecting a parent does not automatically provide its failed checks to the proposer. Configure feedback when the proposer should use those observations.

Other shipped presets include independent attempts from the seed with BestOfN, population search, and specialist retention. Their declarations and selection rules belong in the search reference.

Try it: Choose what to try next. Reference: Runs and search and experiment declarations.
