  --connect 127.0.0.1:9000 --key-file ./worker.key --worker-id shed-1

workers add may run before the store exists, so enrolling is not something to fit into the gap between starting a dispatcher and starting its workers. A worker nobody enrolled is refused at the handshake, told which command would fix it, and exits; the run it tried to join keeps every item ready and every attempt unspent.

--capability KEY=VALUE declares what the worker can do, once per key. VALUE is read as JSON when it is JSON (true, 16, null, ["x86_64","arm64"], {"kind":"gpu"}) and as text otherwise (arm64). Values nested too deeply to parse or record produce a usage error before storage opens. Every worker a listening dispatcher admits runs every item, so a worker is admitted only if its declaration satisfies the work_requirements of every component in the run, compared as recorded values, so 1 does not satisfy true. A worker that misses one is refused at the handshake and exits, again at no cost to the run. The refusal names the key and the value the run requires, and, when the worker declares that key at a different value, the value it declares too. A run whose components require one key at two values cannot be served by any worker, so it refuses to listen at all. Running add again may add capabilities; to drop one or change a value, revoke the worker and add it again.

What each option means:

  • --workers N spawns N children of this dispatcher. They exit with it: each one watches the pipe its parent holds, so even a SIGKILLed dispatcher leaves none behind. They are not replaced if they die, and a run whose workers have all died is refused by name so it can be resumed.
  • --listen ADDR --key-file PATH opens a port instead. The key file is created private (0600) if it is absent and REUSED if it is present, so restarting a dispatcher does not lock out the workers that hold it. A run that is listening WAITS when no worker is connected rather than failing. It needs storage that can hold an allow-list, so --storage and --mode distributed are what make it possible at all. Workers spawned with --workers N are the dispatcher's own and need no enrolment: their ids are in the reserved worker- namespace, and the way to stop them is to stop the dispatcher.
  • --lease-seconds S is how long a work lease lasts, at least 10. A worker's call is renewed while it runs; if a lease is lost anyway, that attempt is retried and at most one completion is ever accepted.
  • --worker-id ID names a worker. worker- is reserved for the ids a dispatcher mints for the children it spawns, and starting a second process with an id that is already connected is refused rather than taking the first one's place, including when both handshakes overlap.

Both ends authenticate with the key file before anything about the run crosses the connection, and a worker is admitted only if it is enrolled, runs the same build, and resolves the same components the run recorded. The key authenticates; it does not encrypt. Multi-host use is documented and untested: it needs TLS, which Meta-Evolve does not provide. Keep the address on a loopback or a trusted network.

Trust can be withdrawn while a run is live:

uv run meta-evolve workers list --storage ./store
uv run meta-evolve workers revoke shed-1 --storage ./store

A revoke belongs to the STORE, not to the run you were watching, so it reaches every run in that store at once. Whatever the revoked worker is holding is freed at that run's next broker transaction, with the withdrawal recorded as the attempt's cause, and another enrolled worker runs the item under the same trial -- the attempt the revoked worker started stays spent, because it did start it. The worker itself is told which refusal it met and exits rather than reconnecting into it, so nothing is left running against a store that has stopped trusting it.

workers list reports trusted and revoked rows alike: a revoke moves the generation on and marks the row rather than deleting it, and enrolling the same id again restores trust at the generation the revoke reached. The listing opens the store read-only, so it never migrates one and can be read while a dispatcher is driving.

Resuming is the same command with the same flags:

uv run meta-evolve resume RUN_ID --module examples/operations/command_line/best_of_n.py \
  --storage ./store --workers 4

A dispatcher that died mid-run leaves its work claimable again. An external worker retains a completed result even if its first write fails, reconnects, and resubmits it. A result already committed receives the recorded acknowledgment; an expired or superseded attempt receives a stale answer. If the listening address now serves a different run while the worker holds an unanswered result, the worker exits with a refusal naming both runs. It never submits one run's result to another.

A distributed run resumed in a changed environment — after a uv sync, say — is not refused. resume prints one line before the summary, environment changed since start: recorded ..., current ..., naming the two fingerprints and not the input that moved: the recorded value is one digest over the interpreter, platform, installed distributions and Meta-Evolve's own source, so it cannot say which. Every worker is still admitted only if it runs the resuming dispatcher's build. A resume that fails prints only its error; from Python, Run.environment_drift() answers the same question.

docs.title: Read-only local browser
docs.text:
ui is the one long-running lifecycle exception to the five deterministic report verbs. Install it explicitly and serve an existing durable store:

uv sync --extra browser
meta-evolve ui --storage ./store --port 8000

The host is fixed to 127.0.0.1, the worker count is fixed to one, and valid ports are 1..65535. There is no host or worker override. The command owns no domain query or HTML logic: it conditionally imports and delegates to the browser server. Uvicorn retains its operational logging. Missing browser dependencies give installation guidance and exit 2; store-open and schema failures remain typed CLI domain failures and exit 1 before a socket binds.

The browser is read-only, local, and unauthenticated. Loopback scope is not a remote-safety or authentication claim. See the browser guide for the replay, cache, polling, and rendering boundaries.

For a run using a custom artifact codec, ui --module MODULE loads the same side-effect-free experiment() convention and passes only its registry to the read-only browser. Browser dependencies are imported first. No proposer, evaluator, policy, session, execution, or mutation surface is invoked. Missing custom codecs remain actionable 422 capability states.

docs.title: Durability
docs.text:
For a complete notebook walkthrough, start with Save and reopen a run.

Storage composes artifact and event storage. In-memory storage is isolated to the process. Durable storage uses a verified filesystem artifact store plus an append-only SQLite event stream.

import meta_evolve as meta

storage = meta.Storage.durable(".meta-evolve/example")

docs.title: Store
docs.text: Pass durable storage to meta.run() to preserve committed artifacts, evidence, decisions, lineage, usage, and failures. mode="durable-local" additionally requires registered reconstructible components and their verified manifests. Validation happens before the first event is written.

docs.title: Reopen
docs.text:
open_run opens existing history for a with block:

with meta.open_run(".meta-evolve/example") as reopened:
    snapshot = reopened.summary()

print(snapshot)

Pass the directory used for Storage.durable(). Without run_id=, it opens the only recorded run. An empty store raises RunNotFound; several runs raise RunSelectionRequired with a run_ids tuple of available IDs. Choose explicitly with meta.open_run(path, run_id=saved_id), using a RunId or its saved string. IDs are listed lexically; their order does not establish which run is newest. An explicit missing ID never substitutes another run.

Calling open_run() creates a context manager. Entry validates the arguments, opens storage, and validates the selected history before yielding Run, including incomplete and unsuccessful runs. Storage closes on success or error. Capture summaries, inspections, usage, and selected values inside the block; those results remain usable afterward. A subsequent query on the live Run still requires open storage and surfaces a store error after close.

Reopen performs no proposal or evaluation and never resumes work. Local callable and SDK histories can be durable and inspectable even when their live components cannot be rebuilt. For custom artifacts, supply registry= with reconstructed codecs to decode values. Without the required codec, entry and usage() still work, while a decoded query such as best() raises CapabilityError naming the missing codec. Supplied codecs are trusted Python extensions invoked by decoded queries, not by opening the run.

For explicit storage ownership, keep using Run directly:

with meta.Storage.read_only(".meta-evolve/example") as storage:
    version = storage.run_version(run_id)
    inspection = meta.Run(run_id, storage).inspect()

is_durable and is_read_only answer different questions. The first says committed facts live on durable media; the second says this handle cannot commit. Storage.durable(...) reports True, False, while Storage.read_only(...) reports True, True. Artifact, blob, event, and unit-of-work writes all raise CapabilityError. Passing the handle to run(), improve(), or resume() is rejected before a codec, registry component, proposer, evaluator, provider, or subprocess runs.

run_version(run_id) is the maximum committed event sequence. It returns 0 for a well-formed id with no events and uses a new deferred transaction on each call, so a long-lived reader observes successive atomic commits from a WAL writer. It is deliberately a cheap polling query, not a full integrity check. An open_run() block also permits fresh reads: it selects the identity once, but does not freeze subsequent queries to the entry-time history. Run(run_id, storage).inspect() performs authoritative loading and still raises RunNotFound when that run is required but absent.

The optional local run browser owns one long-lived read-only handle on one dedicated thread. It calls runs() to discover additions, polls exact versions before replay, and never polls a cached completed run again. Its bounded caches are disposable observations; append-only storage and validated replay remain authoritative.

Read-only open requires an existing current store. It uses SQLite mode=ro plus query_only, and never creates a directory, changes journal settings, executes DDL, stamps a schema, or migrates. For an older or unstamped store, close readers and reopen it once with writable Storage.durable(...), then use Storage.read_only(...) again. Future schemas raise SchemaVersionRejected, malformed current schemas raise DurableCorruption, and missing or inaccessible database/filesystem/WAL state raises DurableStoreError with the underlying cause.

Read-only means no changes to committed history and no framework writes or migration. SQLite can create or maintain -wal and -shm sidecars even through a read-only connection; see its WAL documentation. The reader preserves live WAL visibility and does not use SQLite's immutable mode. It never creates a missing store directory or repairs an incomplete one.

docs.title: Resume
docs.text:
resume verifies manifests, declarations, store integrity, and the recovery frontier before doing missing work. It retains the same run ID and never re-executes a committed operation. A non-resumable local history raises CapabilityError.

Registered proposer verification includes the framework's invocation source. The explicit keyword-context cutover changes those manifests even for unchanged parent-only callbacks. Older histories remain readable; continuation requires their matching implementation. See the callback migration guide.

Use Session.resume to pace that same recovery:

with meta.Session.resume(run_id, storage=storage, registry=registry) as session:
    for decision in session:
        observe(decision)
result = session.run

A distributed run resumes through the same call and then drive(), because it is scheduled rather than stepped — iterating its decisions raises. resume() makes that choice for you; hold the session yourself and you make it:

with meta.Session.resume(run_id, storage=storage, registry=registry) as session:
    session.drive()

drive(lease_seconds=60) renews each call's lease while it runs; the duration must be at least 10 seconds. A failed renewal ends the drive, but Python cannot cancel the component's helper thread. Resume may execute that work again while the old call finishes. Leases and dispatcher epochs prevent accepting a stale result; this does not guarantee that external side effects happen only once.

Preparation validates and classifies the committed frontier but does not finish pending work. The first step() either completes the already committed trial or evaluation, or records and completes one new decision. Resuming an already stopped run iterates zero times; an explicit terminal step() returns the existing stop view without changing events or artifacts.

docs.title: Complete registered-resume example
docs.text:
Run this as a Python file with meta_evolve installed. It compares saving a local run with reconstructing registered components for resume. The temporary stores are for this demonstration only; retain a persistent directory for real work. Omitting session.step() leaves both revisions for resume to perform.

resume_checklist.py · complete example
"""Registered resume demonstration, moved from the beginner persistence lesson."""

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
import meta_evolve as meta


def add_item(items):
    return (*items, ("outline", "draft")[len(items)])


def score(items):
    return len(items)


def declaration():
    registry = meta.Registry()
    proposer = registry.register_proposer(
        "checklist:add", "1", add_item, deterministic=True, retry_safe=True,
    )
    evaluator = registry.register_evaluator(
        "checklist:score", "1", score, deterministic=True, retry_safe=True,
    )
    return meta.Experiment(
        seed=(), proposer=proposer, task=meta.Task(evaluator=evaluator),
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=2), registry=registry,
    )


with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    root = Path(directory)
    with meta.Storage.durable(root / "saved") as storage:
        result = meta.improve(seed=(), proposer=add_item, evaluator=score,
                              trials=2, storage=storage)
        saved_id = result.id
    with meta.Storage.read_only(root / "saved") as storage:
        reopened = meta.Run(saved_id, storage)
        print("Reopened:", reopened.best().value)

    with meta.Storage.durable(root / "continued") as storage:
        with meta.Session.start(declaration(), storage=storage, mode="durable-local") as session:
            session.step()  # Finish one revision, leaving one to perform.
            run_id = session.run.id
            print("Before resume:", session.run.usage().trials)
    with meta.Storage.durable(root / "continued") as storage:
        resumed = meta.resume(run_id, storage=storage, registry=declaration().registry)
        print("After resume:", resumed.usage().trials)
        print("Selected:", resumed.best().value)
# Output:
# Reopened: ('outline', 'draft')
# Before resume: 1
# After resume: 2
# Selected: ('outline', 'draft')

docs.title: Compare
docs.text: Reopened completed runs use the same comparison contract as live results. Declaration mismatches raise RunsNotComparable before ranking.

docs.title: Replay and reproducibility
docs.text:
Replay is a pure fold over immutable transitions and artifacts. It reconstructs logical decisions, projections, context selection, access audits, and usage without calling external systems. Named random streams reproduce deterministic local choices. Provider output is not promised to regenerate byte-for-byte; the durable guarantee is the exact committed transcript and declarations.

Usage records retain unknown billed spend as explicit null; omitted spend still means the historical default of zero. Existing zero and integer records keep their canonical bytes. Readers predating nullable spend cannot read these new unknown values. Inspection and replay reuse cost evidence without rerunning user callbacks; recovery may repeat external work whose outcome never committed.

Corrupt bytes, unknown schemas, gaps, mismatched IDs, and incomplete atomic batches fail explicitly rather than falling back to a partial interpretation.

docs.title: Open a store from an earlier version
docs.text:
The current durable store schema is 5. Schema 4 added the work and lease tables that distributed mode uses; schema 5 adds one more table, trusted_workers, which holds the worker identities an operator enrolled with meta-evolve workers add and is created empty. No recorded event byte changes at either step, and the upgrade is one-way: an earlier release refuses a migrated store as a future schema. A store an older release migrated from v1 has its events table rebuilt with the same rows, and one holding an event with no digest is refused as corrupt.

A schema-4 store still opens with Storage.read_only(...) and in the run browser: a reader validates it against the schema-4 shape and changes nothing. Its first writable Storage.durable(...) open migrates it to 5 and adds the table. A store written before schema 4 must be opened once with writable Storage.durable(...), which migrates it; until then Storage.read_only(...) and the run browser refuse it with SchemaVersionRejected.

Schema 5 also puts two triggers on the work_items table. They call a SQL function that Meta-Evolve registers on every writable connection it opens, so a connection that has not registered it cannot insert or update that table -- including the sqlite3 shell and any other external tool. Reads are unaffected. This is deliberate. A store's schema version is checked when it is opened, so a dispatcher that opened the store before an in-place upgrade would otherwise keep leasing work under the rules of the build it started with, unaware of anything the upgrade decided. The triggers stop its next work write instead, as a DurableStoreError, and the run continues under the new build. Both triggers are part of the validated schema: a schema-5 store missing one is DurableCorruption rather than something an open quietly repairs.

A trusted_workers row that cannot be read is DurableCorruption, never a row Meta-Evolve skips. While the worker it names holds a lease in a run, that run's next work write meets it -- whichever worker asked -- so the run stops until the row is repaired. Anything that looks the worker up by name meets it too: its own claims, meta-evolve workers list, which reports the refusal instead of a listing, and the door of any listening run the worker connects to, which stops that run, whether or not the worker holds anything in it. A run in the same store that the worker neither holds a lease in nor connects to keeps writing. Repair or replace the row -- a lease's authority cannot be read past.

A durable-local run that uses BestOfN and was recorded by an earlier release does not resume. Its RunStarted manifest records a digest of the policy's module source. The current release changes that module, and resume compares the digest exactly, so it refuses with CapabilityError. Finish such runs before upgrading. The run id and the stream's other bytes are unchanged.

Exact source matching also includes docstrings and other text in a hashed module. The reference refresh changes the source digests of Greedy, BestOfN, AncestorsOnly, and BestSibling, even though their execution logic is unchanged. Runs with those earlier manifests remain inspectable, but resume requires matching component source. Complete unfinished work with its matching package before upgrading; do not bypass the manifest check.

An artifact read that meets damaged durable state -- including a committed artifact the store no longer has -- now raises DurableCorruption with the original fault on local and durable-local runs. Earlier releases stopped the same run with InvalidDecision wrapping the cause, so code that catches InvalidDecision for this case no longer sees it.

The ordinary read failures that are still translated -- a KeyError, a timeout, anything the store answers with that is not damage -- now raise InputsUnavailable rather than InvalidDecision, so nothing reaching a caller from a parent load answers to that name any more. The two were one type and had come to mean two things: InvalidDecision is a verdict that a decision is malformed or exceeds its authority, and a distributed run ends a work item whose recorded cause names it WITHOUT retrying, because no second attempt makes an invalid decision valid. An input that could not be read is the case the retry bound exists for, and collapsing the two would have ended such an item on its first flaky read.

docs.title: Evaluation and budgets
docs.text:
For a complete notebook walkthrough, start with Define what better means or Set limits and stopping conditions. This reference covers detailed evaluation, accounting, and failure behavior.

A Task declares the evaluator, artifact representation, objectives, and optional budget ceiling. The evaluator—not the candidate—owns what better means.

import meta_evolve as meta

task = meta.Task(
    evaluator=lambda text: {"quality": len(set(text.split()))},
    objectives=(meta.Maximize("quality"),),
    budget=meta.Budget(evaluations=6, trials=5),
)

Maximize and Minimize identify ordered objectives. A run-level budget may narrow the task ceiling but cannot widen it. Omitted or None dimensions inherit task limits, so Budget(evaluations=2) retains the task's other ceilings. Budget() preserves them all; zero is a real limit. An explicitly wider finite value raises ValueError before work starts. See the budget override example and migration notes.

Task.environment is an immutable evaluator-owned declaration. Its empty default preserves ordinary runs; when supplied it contributes to task and run identity, so changing a nested episode environment invalidates its RunId.

docs.title: Exact accounting
docs.text:
Seed evaluation consumes one evaluation and no successor trial. Each attempted successor consumes one trial; a valid evaluated successor consumes one evaluation. Token, monetary-spend, and wall usage come from the component action that actually performed the work. Rich callbacks return Resources; the engine adds its own counts to durable Usage, aggregated in the run summary.

Run.summary().usage, Run.usage(), and inspection report the same committed costs even when nothing ranks or seed evaluation is pending. Prefer run.usage() when accumulating resources across nested runs: it reads the costs directly without constructing the rest of a report. Unknown spend remains unknown, and failed work remains charged.

Rolling a nested run's usage into an outer one also means dropping its counts, since trials and evaluations belong to the run that minted them. Project the inner resources and add the outer evaluator's own work exactly once:

total = own_resources + inner.usage().resources

run.inspect().overview.task_usage reports the same figure and remains available, but it builds a whole aggregate to reach one field; prefer the accessor.

Search checks the effective budget before starting more work — for counts, tokens, and wall time. Monetary spend is knowable only once a call returns, so it is enforced post-hoc instead. Exhaustion is a recorded stop reason. Components never grant themselves additional work.

docs.title: Money
docs.text:
Resources.spend_micros, recorded in Usage, reports charged monetary spend in integer micro-USD (1 unit = one millionth of a US dollar). A wrapper reports the amount its provider actually billed; estimates keep their status and price basis in evidence instead of appearing as exact bills. Core never infers money from tokens and never converts currencies.

Report spend_micros=None when billed spend is unavailable. A successful result can still carry its measured tokens and score. Aggregating any unknown amount produces an unknown total; known individual charges remain in history. The default 0 means known free work, including ordinary local callables. Neither missing telemetry nor the choice of subscription or API-key login establishes a bill or its absence. SDK-calculated prices remain estimates.

With no monetary ceiling, token and trial limits continue to work normally. With a run, task, or trial monetary ceiling, an unknown charge makes that ceiling unverifiable. The completed result is retained, further work is refused, and built-in policies report accounting_unavailable when this causes their stop. An unknown proposal's candidate is saved but its evaluation is skipped. Budget.allows returns false for unknown spend under a monetary ceiling; remaining_after rejects that subtraction. Inspection shows spend=unknown.

Budget(spend_micros=...) sets a ceiling with post-hoc enforcement: spend is known only after a call returns, so the first action that crosses the ceiling is billed, recorded as a typed ResourceExhausted failure, and halts the run. There is no hard cap — reservation-based preflight is future work. A ceiling of 0 means free work only: unpaid components run normally, and the first paid action fails typed and stops the run.

A ceiling can also sit on an individual trial. When a trial spends past its own spend_micros, the run halts — including for subsequent free work, since a breached ceiling is a property of the run's history, not of the next action. A trial with no ceiling anywhere, neither aggregate nor per-trial, stays unbounded, exactly as trials=None means unlimited trials.

spend_micros is wrapper-self-reported and not independently verified by the framework: a wrapper that omits or understates its provider's charge understates trusted accounting, and the round-up conversion convention is advisory. The framework guarantees exact aggregation of known reports and propagates unknown totals. User-owned cost reporters can price tokens or look up a receipt. Estimates remain evidence and do not satisfy or consume a billed-spend budget; use token/trial bounds when a bill is unavailable.

Enforcement bounds the framework's paid actions, not a provider's billing. Under durable execution a crash between a paid call and its commit leaves the charge real but unrecorded, and recovery re-executes the call; bounding that requires provider-side idempotency, which is future work.

docs.title: Evidence and uncertainty
docs.text: An evaluation can return scalar or objective-keyed metrics, uncertainty, immutable evidence, and action usage. Evidence records what was observed; it is not a candidate-controlled score. External evaluators also record environment and bounded process evidence where available.

docs.title: Typed failures
docs.text:
Invalid candidate shape, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure retain their distinct types and details. A trial with no valid evaluation is non-rankable. It never becomes zero, negative infinity, or a fabricated metric.

Run-level capability and durability errors use the shipped error hierarchy, including CapabilityError, BudgetUnavailable, and InvalidDecision.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text: The candidate may propose artifact content and declare causal observations. The task/evaluator owns hidden data, environment, metrics, and failure translation; the coordinator owns effective budgets and commitment; governance owns permissions and promotion.

docs.title: Define what better means
docs.text:
A parser that gets "30s" right can still get "2h" wrong. Before improving it, you need a way to measure its answers and decide which revision to keep. An evaluator computes measurements; an objective says which measurement to improve and whether higher or lower is better. The measurements come from the evaluator, independently of a proposer's claims; see evaluation authority.

You want to… Use Grade answers An evaluator returning a score Track several measurements A dictionary of metrics Choose what determines the winner Maximize or Minimize

The revisions are handwritten. Python executes and grades them; no model, SDK, or credentials are needed.

Open in Colab · Download the notebook

To run this page: expand the required setup and run its cells from top to bottom, then run the examples below in order. Every definition is here; no other page needs to be executed. Rerunning the cells repeats the same results.

Required setup for a fresh notebook

Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

Starting source. SEED reads a duration's number but ignores its unit. CONTRACT tells the proposer what the parser should do.

import meta_evolve as meta

CONTRACT = """Implement parse_seconds(text) for whole-number durations.
Inputs contain a number followed by s, m, or h, such as '30s' or '2h'.
Return the duration in seconds as an integer. Return only Python source.
"""

SEED = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    return int(text[:-1])
'''

Revisions. MINUTES adds minutes support; COMPLETE adds hours as well.

MINUTES = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    return quantity * 60 if text[-1] == "m" else quantity
'''

COMPLETE = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    seconds_per_unit = {"s": 1, "m": 60, "h": 3600}
    return quantity * seconds_per_unit[text[-1]]
'''

Proposer. propose sends the contract and source to a simulated agent. Given SEED, it returns MINUTES; given MINUTES, it returns COMPLETE. Its choice depends on the source, without a hidden response counter.

def agent(message):
    """Simulate source revisions, without a model or a call counter."""
    source = message.rsplit("Current source:\n", 1)[1]
    if source == SEED:
        return MINUTES
    if source in (MINUTES, COMPLETE):
        return COMPLETE
    raise ValueError("This simulation only recognizes the tutorial sources.")


def propose(source):
    message = f"{CONTRACT}\nCurrent source:\n{source}"
    return agent(message)

The Start here walkthrough introduces the starting parser. You can close this section once its cells have run.

docs.title: 1. Choose the answers that matter
docs.text:
An evaluator can be an ordinary Python function. Ours loads the parser, checks six expected answers, and returns the fraction correct. A score of 1.0 means all six checks pass. load_parser executes the source to obtain the function; this small evaluator is for the reviewed, handwritten code shown here.

CASES = (
    ("30s", 30),
    ("90s", 90),
    ("2m", 120),
    ("3m", 180),
    ("1h", 3600),
    ("2h", 7200),
)


def load_parser(source):
    namespace = {}
    exec(source, namespace)
    return namespace["parse_seconds"]


def evaluate(source):
    parse = load_parser(source)
    passed = 0
    for text, expected in CASES:
        actual = parse(text)
        if type(actual) is int and actual == expected:
            passed += 1
    return passed / len(CASES)


print(f"Starting score: {evaluate(SEED):.0%}")
# Output:
# Starting score: 33%

Only the two seconds checks pass. These expected answers belong to the evaluator: a proposed parser revision cannot change them. Choose cases that represent the behavior you need; this six-case demonstration measures only the cases shown.

docs.title: 2. Select the best score
docs.text:
meta.improve() evaluates the seed, proposes revisions from the best version so far, and evaluates each valid revision. With a scalar evaluator, the measurement is named score and larger values win by default. trials=2 allows two proposal attempts after the seed evaluation.

result = meta.improve(
    seed=SEED,
    proposer=propose,
    evaluator=evaluate,
    trials=2,
)

The returned run keeps each attempt and its measurements. trials() lists the seed followed by the revisions; best_trial() gives the selected attempt.

for number, attempt in enumerate(result.trials()):
    print(f"Version {number}: {attempt.metrics['score']:.0%}")
print(f"Selected score: {result.best_trial().metrics['score']:.0%}")
# Output:
# Version 0: 33%
# Version 1: 67%
# Version 2: 100%
# Selected score: 100%

The proposer supplies source, and the evaluator independently measures it. The 100% score comes from running the checks on COMPLETE.

docs.title: 3. Report named measurements
docs.text:
An overall score can hide a weak category. Return a dictionary to record named metrics from the same six checks. We will retain overall score, accuracy on hours, and the number of wrong_answers.

def evaluate_metrics(source):
    parse = load_parser(source)
    passed = 0
    hours_passed = 0
    hours_count = 0
    for text, expected in CASES:
        actual = parse(text)
        correct = type(actual) is int and actual == expected
        passed += correct
        if text.endswith("h"):
            hours_count += 1
            hours_passed += correct
    return {
        "score": passed / len(CASES),
        "hours": hours_passed / hours_count,
        "wrong_answers": len(CASES) - passed,
    }

for source in (SEED, MINUTES, COMPLETE):
    metrics = evaluate_metrics(source)
    print(f"Overall: {metrics['score']:.0%}; hours: {metrics['hours']:.0%}; "
          f"wrong answers: {metrics['wrong_answers']}")
# Output:
# Overall: 33%; hours: 0%; wrong answers: 4
# Overall: 67%; hours: 0%; wrong answers: 2
# Overall: 100%; hours: 100%; wrong answers: 0

The minutes revision improves the overall score while still failing both hours checks. Recording hours makes that gap visible. It does not automatically make hours accuracy a selection objective.

docs.title: 4. Declare which metric determines better
docs.text:
Pass one objective to meta.improve(). meta.Maximize selects higher values of a named metric; meta.Minimize selects lower values.

Use one proposal attempt here so the hours gap remains visible. Greedy search builds on the best measured version, just as improve() does by default.

metrics_result = meta.improve(
    seed=SEED, proposer=propose, evaluator=evaluate_metrics, trials=1,
    objective=meta.Maximize("score"),
)
selected = metrics_result.best_trial().metrics
print(f"Overall: {selected['score']:.0%}; hours: {selected['hours']:.0%}")
# Output:
# Overall: 67%; hours: 0%

The selected parser is MINUTES, because score is the objective. Every metric remains available for inspection, including the hours result that did not improve. If your evaluator uses a name other than score, declare the matching objective. A scalar evaluator measures the declared objective directly; a mapping must include its exact name. See the scalar minimization example.

For reusable declarations or several ordered objectives, use meta.Task and meta.Experiment. This expanded declaration executes the same search:

metrics_experiment = meta.Experiment(
    seed=SEED,
    proposer=propose,
    task=meta.Task(
        evaluator=evaluate_metrics,
        objectives=(meta.Maximize("score"),),
    ),
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=1),
)

expanded_metrics = meta.run(metrics_experiment)

For a measurement where less is better, change the objective to Minimize:

errors_result = meta.improve(
    seed=SEED, proposer=propose, evaluator=evaluate_metrics, trials=1,
    objective=meta.Minimize("wrong_answers"),
)
print("Selected wrong answers:", errors_result.best_trial().metrics["wrong_answers"])
# Output:
# Selected wrong answers: 2

With these fixed six cases, fewer wrong answers and a higher overall score select the same revision. Other measurements, such as runtime, may reward different candidates; choose an objective that matches your actual goal.

An exception while executing or grading source produces a failed evaluation with no score. A measured wrong answer contributes to the score above. Inspect results and failures explains how to tell those outcomes apart.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
In the objective declaration, change meta.Maximize("score") to meta.Maximize("hours"), keeping the one-attempt limit. Predict the selected score, then rerun that declaration and its result cell.

The printed result becomes Overall: 33%; hours: 0%. The seed and minutes revision both score zero on hours, so the revision does not beat the seed on the declared objective. The seed stays selected even though the revision has a higher overall score. This shows why the objective matters separately from the list of measurements you record.

docs.title: Why didn't my new metric change the winner?
docs.text:
Returning a metric records it. The objective decides whether it influences selection; adding hours to the dictionary alone leaves score in charge. Use the metric's exact name in the objective, and choose its direction.

For your own task, replace CASES and the evaluator with independent checks that represent your goal. Replace the source and proposer with your starting value and revision function. Keep grading outside the proposer, and try the evaluator on a known good and a known bad value before starting a search.

Next, give the proposer feedback: record which checks failed so the next revision can address them. See the evaluation reference for additional result forms and ordered objectives. To understand the observations behind a score, read Evidence.

docs.title: Learning from experience
docs.text:
Recorded candidates, outcomes, and evaluation evidence can help later proposals investigate a failure, preserve a successful change, or compare approaches before trying another revision.

Experience is explicit and off by default. Recording outcomes for search and inspection does not automatically provide feedback to the proposer.

docs.title: Why experience matters
docs.text:
Search uses evaluation results to decide which candidates deserve more work. Experience gives the proposer information that can help it decide what to change. A score can tell search which prompt performed better; the recorded responses can help a proposer understand what the weaker prompt missed.

The same distinction applies beyond prompts. A code proposer might inspect a prior implementation and its test evidence. A harness proposer might compare recorded execution traces to understand a successful revision. These observations can suggest a change, but the next candidate still needs independent evaluation.

docs.title: What counts as experience?
docs.text:
Feedback is one useful selection from a broader history:

Prior information A question it can help answer Candidates and source revisions What was tried, and what changed? Measurements and recorded evaluation evidence Where did an approach succeed or fall short? Failed attempts and their recorded outcomes What prevented an attempt from producing a valid result? Lineage and comparisons between attempts Which alternatives are worth investigating together?

Only recorded information can be retrieved. An infrastructure failure remains a typed outcome, not evidence of a low-quality candidate or an invented low score.

Here, learning means using observations to inform a proposal. The experience mechanism does not itself train model weights or guarantee that a revision will improve. The parser feedback lesson demonstrates one narrow case: using recorded development checks to choose handwritten fixes.

docs.title: How experience reaches a proposer
docs.text:
Recording history does not automatically expose it to a proposer. An experiment can select context before each proposal, authorize the proposer to inspect prior records during its work, or combine both approaches. Selected context is useful when the relevant evidence is predictable; inspection lets a proposer investigate questions as they arise. Both are bounded and recorded.

The experience concept distinguishes recorded history, disclosed observations, and the proposer's declared use. Access or a citation alone does not establish an improvement.

docs.title: Does it help?
docs.text:
Compare runs with and without experience while holding the task, seed, proposer, and search settings fixed under comparable budgets. Inspect outcomes and experience usage as well as the best score: retrieving more history has a cost and need not produce better proposals. Keep final evaluation separate from the development evidence that guides revisions.

The parser guide makes this comparison in a fresh notebook. Its proposer uses the latest failed checks to choose a minutes fix, then an hours fix. With feedback it reaches 100%; without feedback it keeps the seed at 33%, using the same three evaluations. This demonstrates the handwritten rule's use of observations, not model performance or accuracy on unseen inputs.

docs.title: Supported scope
docs.text: The mechanisms below are Shipped. Access is limited to authorized prior records within the same task and run. Cross-run knowledge reuse and semantic retrieval are Design—not shipped. Experience changes what a proposer may observe, never its evaluator, budget, permissions, or promotion authority.

docs.title: No memory
docs.text: With no context= or experience= declaration, a proposer receives no prior records. NoMemory states that policy explicitly when a named declaration is useful.

docs.title: Pushed context
docs.text:
A plain callback reads this feedback through keyword-only context: def propose(parent, *, context): .... This opt-in supplies the authorized context object; the experiment still decides which observations it may contain. See callback migration for older signatures.

A ContextPolicy selects a bounded bundle before each proposal. RecentAncestors favors the newest records in the current parent's lineage; AncestorsOnly retains the oldest records. BestSibling exposes a bounded sibling view. The selected structured records, rendered text, reason, logical time, and usage are committed before the proposer runs.

import meta_evolve as meta

experiment = meta.Experiment(
    task=task,
    seed=seed,
    proposer=proposer,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=3),
    context=meta.RecentAncestors(max_records=20, max_chars=4000),
)
result = meta.run(experiment)

Read context.evidence.latest("your-evidence-kind") inside the proposer. It returns an immutable item with .data and exact .ref provenance, or None when the declared policy selected no match. Latest means last in selected order, including ties within a step. It may refer to an older ancestor or sibling. The accessor recognizes evidence labels from both proposers and evaluators; reserve your feedback label for its intended producer.

Calling it with context disabled raises meta_evolve.errors.ContextDisabled, a CapabilityError, at the call site. Use context.evidence.enabled to make feedback optional in deliberate off comparisons. A declared empty policy is enabled even when no evidence matches; pull access alone does not enable it. context.evidence.truncated reflects omitted records or clipped rendering, without identifying the cause. Structured evidence remains readable with max_chars=0, while a small max_records can omit evidence entirely. Neither lookup nor status inspection performs a query or changes usage.

docs.title: Upgrading bounded feedback
docs.text:
Existing context.bundle consumers keep working. Replace evidence filtering and max(logical_step) with context.evidence.latest(kind) when selected order is the intended rule; multiple same-step matches now resolve to the last item. Use .data instead of .value.data. Explicitly choose RecentAncestors for recency; AncestorsOnly@1 does not silently change retention. Manual context construction for tests or custom runners supplies context_policy to enable lookup. Workspace context replacement retains this declaration.

This source change adds automatic proposer manifest dependencies for evidence lookup, disabled-context errors, and actual context construction. The shared context-policy source module also changes the hashes for AncestorsOnly and BestSibling, although their selection semantics remain the same. Historical stores remain readable; incompatible resumes refuse before new work. Continue old runs in their matching environment, or explicitly version changed author components and start a new run. Do not rewrite manifests or stored selections. The verification record records the old-store capture and exact digest changes. This follow-up does not change the selected #313/#319 release scope.

docs.title: Audited pull
docs.text:
PullAccess grants bounded operations, result counts, records, and characters. The proposer uses an ExperienceReader only inside that grant. Each request, result, denial, and usage charge is retained; hidden or future records fail closed through typed access errors.

For a SourceTree task, the same reader can inspect an exact prior artifact occurrence without receiving a whole repository implicitly:

artifacts = context.experience.search(record_kinds=("artifact",), limit=1)
artifact_ref = artifacts.references[0]

listing = context.experience.list_source_paths(artifact_ref, limit=20)
read = context.experience.read_source(
    artifact_ref,
    paths=("solver.py",),
)
return meta.ProposalResult(
    candidate=revise(parent, read.files[0].source),
    derived_from=(read.artifact_ref,),
)

Listings are lexicographic; reads preserve requested order. Both retain only a prefix of complete entries that fits the grant and charge the exact rendered characters. A missing path atomically denies the read. Canonical diff_source(older_ref, newer_ref) is also shipped: it verifies both prior occurrences, returns a bounded path-ordered unified diff, and charges two results. A source patch callback may instead request a bounded disposable Git presentation:

from meta_evolve.adapters import GitHistoryView

proposer = meta.PatchProposer(
    edit,
    history=GitHistoryView(
        max_ancestors=4,
        max_archive_members=2,
        max_chars=128_000,
    ),
)

The edit callback runs ordinary git log, git show, and git diff commands with cwd=context.workspace.root and env=context.workspace.environment. The selected parent remains HEAD; the manifest is available as context.workspace.history. Git metadata is external and disposable, and direct workspace mutation is rejected before the returned exact-file patch is applied. Whole-tree reader operations, semantic retrieval, and cross-run access are not shipped.

docs.title: Source-inspection contract
docs.text:
Each target is an exact ExperienceRef(kind="artifact") occurrence for a SourceTree / utf8-tree-v1 value, in the same task/run and strictly before the effective observation boundary. The storage edge revalidates the digest before decoding. Equal bytes do not collapse distinct occurrences.

ExperienceRequest.paths is an ordered tuple of strings; its empty default is omitted canonically from schema-v3 records. Wrong Python shapes fail before auditing. Empty reads, duplicate/non-normalized paths, wrong reference kinds, invalid logical time, and missing, hidden, future, retracted or cross-run targets enter the normal audit lifecycle and share an opaque denial. One missing path denies the whole read. Durable corruption and infrastructure failures stay typed.

Authorization and existence checks precede capacity resolution. Listing/reading reserve one result; diff reserves two, after verifying older then newer operands. Operation/result exhaustion is recorded cumulatively. Record/character bounds retain the largest deterministic prefix of complete entries, charging one record per entry and exactly len(rendered) characters, including separators. An oversized first entry gives a successful truncated zero-record result after its result charge; an empty canonical diff is not truncated.

Listings render lexicographically sorted normalized paths as compact JSON-string lines. Reads preserve requested order as compact JSON Lines with exactly path and source, stable keys, Unicode preserved, and no trailing newline. Diff uses meta-evolve-unified-diff/v1: sorted changed paths, optional filtering that keeps that order, LF-normalized lines with final-terminator state, deterministic Myers diff with deletion-before-insertion ties, three context lines, and changes merged across at most six unchanged lines. JSON file operands, uniform hunk ranges, missing-final-newline markers and complete per-path hunks are platform-independent.

Source results in meta_evolve.domain retain occurrence refs, verified digests, complete entries, rendering, truncation and cumulative ExperienceUsage. Replay returns committed outcomes without live reads; durable loading independently reconstructs them from stored artifacts. Only successful observations authorize derived_from; diff admits its two operands in order.

docs.title: Git-history contract
docs.text:
source-history-manifest/v1 is Git-neutral. Selection is parent first, then breadth-first causal ancestors, then archive order, deduplicated by occurrence. The head is the first entry; refs have one run and declared kinds, and parents stay within the authorized manifest. Equal digests may occur more than once. Each entry retains its digest, logical step, proposal/evaluation refs and selection rationale. Source bytes, Git IDs, environment values and repository layout are excluded from the manifest.

The adapter uses the outer pull grant for a complete selected-parent listing, metadata search, ancestor traversal and complete additional-tree reads. It commits one SourceHistoryMounted before the callback. That fact records the manifest without new usage, operation category or derivation authority. Replay reproduces the audited prefix; durable loading revalidates observations and the manifest.

Git objects, refs, configuration, index, attributes, hooks and home live in an external disposable sidecar. Selected-parent HEAD, causal commits and ephemeral archive refs present the authorized history. Direct workspace mutation remains a PolicyViolation; the sidecar is disposed before capture. Version/bounds changes alter configured proposer identity. This adapter adds no persistent Git identity, root export, experiment field or independent agent runtime.

docs.title: Declared derivation
docs.text: A rich proposal may declare which authorized observations influenced it. Those references are validated against the experience it actually received. Empty derivation remains compatible with ordinary callables.

docs.title: Causal provenance
docs.text:
Everyday users can rely on Run.lineage(), Run.trials(), and RunExperienceUsage. Strict ledger ordering, logical-time validation, and replay are isolated in the advanced provenance reference. RunExperienceUsage.by_operation provides canonically ordered non-zero operation totals through meta_evolve.views.ExperienceOperationUsage; they sum exactly to the aggregate pull usage, in this order: search, open, ancestors, siblings, compare, list_source_paths, read_source, diff_source. History mounting reuses audited operations; it adds no category or duplicate charge.

See authority and promotion for the roles that remain outside candidate control and their relationship to execution isolation.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text: Add replaceable components at declared seams; never branch the coordinator on a concrete domain, provider, evaluator, policy, or backend.

docs.title: Artifact domains
docs.text:
An artifact codec declares a stable kind, representation, interfaces, canonical encode/decode behavior, and rejection boundary. Register it with Registry. The same codec encodes the seed and every successor; rejected values become typed invalid-output trials.

The complete artifact-domain tutorial is extracted, executed in a clean interpreter, and checked against the published codec conformance suite.

docs.title: Components and identity
docs.text: Local callables are convenient but not cold-resumable. Registered durable-local proposers, evaluators, search policies, and context policies use explicit component references plus behavior-affecting configuration. Resume rebuilds the recorded implementation from that registry and refuses mismatches.

docs.title: Published conformance
docs.text:
Install the reusable test suites with uv sync --extra conformance. Run your Test... subclass with uv run pytest path/to/test_codec.py; a passing run reports passed laws, while undeclared optional cases appear as skips.

Every extension component family has a published reusable suite: codecs, repository-editing proposers, evaluators, search programs, context policies, workspaces, sandboxes, and typed mutation surfaces. Subclass one, name the subclass Test..., and override its fixtures and hooks. Each runs unchanged here against the built-in implementations (or, for the proposer suites, reference callables) plus at least one written the way an outside author would write it — MutationSurfaceTests against TextParam, PolicyParam, ParentSelection, and TrialLimit; SearchProgramTests against Greedy, BestOfN, BestOfK, Population, CandidatePolicy, and a next-only custom program.

A program with a next_cohort method also runs the suite's cohort laws: every member of a generation is reconstructed from its recorded base, the answer is repeatable and at width one equals next, and every interleaving of a generation's completions (up to width three) leaves the policy seeing the same state, next cohort and ranking. A wide program cannot drive the synchronous path the other laws use, so hand it to the cohort_searches fixture.

The two proposer suites are exercised by in-repository reference callables (tests/test_proposer_conformance.py); no first-party provider adapter ships, so those callables are the reference subjects.

SandboxProviderTests checks the declared cwd and exact environment, verbatim argv, separated output streams, ordinary nonzero exits, enforced timeout, independent stdout/stderr byte ceilings, bounded partial output, and wall-only usage. Its timeout and probe-sleep fixtures are overridable for container and remote startup costs. Passing it does not prove filesystem isolation or that a provider executed rather than simulated every probe; CPU, memory, network, syscall, and broader execution isolation remain outside the suite.

ContextPolicy.select receives a typed, read-only ExperienceGraph. Import ExperienceGraph and ExperienceQuery from meta_evolve; the returned ExperienceNode, ExperienceRecord, and ExperienceState values are root exports too. Replay construction remains an application service, so helpers such as replay_experience_graph stay under meta_evolve.application.

State the limits rather than implying coverage that does not exist. A suite checks the laws it names and no others, and it makes an unexercised law visible: EvaluatorTests skips its typed-failure check when a subclass declares no rejected_candidates and its semantic oracle when it declares no scored_candidates, ArtifactCodecTests skips its aliasing law when mutable_values is () and its decode-validation law when rejected_payloads is (), and ContextPolicyTests makes a policy that selects nothing say so through expects_records. NoMemory is outside that suite, since meta.run normalizes it away before any policy runs.

The subclass contract follows one rule set, stated in the package docstring: required hooks raise NotImplementedError; optional laws skip visibly or cross-check a declaration; a law needing an uncontaminated second subject asks for a factory (make_evaluator, search_factory) and refuses the same object twice; laws observe subjects through kernel records or author-supplied projections, never the subject's own equality or self-report.

One trap is worth knowing when you write a codec: decode returning an equal value is not the same as returning an independent one. A codec that hands back the instance it was given lets an evaluator reach and edit the caller's own object. ArtifactCodecTests.mutable_values has no default for that reason — declaring () is a positive claim that your values are immutable, not a way to skip the question. Every value law observes through value_state, an observation the codec has no hand in — never through the value type's __eq__ (which usually ships with the codec and could certify a collapse) and never through the codec's own encode (which could special-case the watched objects); the default projection knows exact canonical and kernel types and refuses anything else. Mutable values additionally require mutate, the edit the aliasing law watches. rejected_payloads is the mirror of rejected_values on the decode side — decode is validation, and () is a positive claim that every payload decodes. EvaluatorTests.scored_candidates is the analogous semantic oracle: every other evaluator law holds for lambda c: 0.0, so state expected metrics wherever your scores are predictable. EvaluatorTests keeps a matching candidate-mutation law, so the failure is caught where it starts and where it does damage.

Component family Reusable coverage today Artifact codecs Published ArtifactCodecTests Repository-editing proposers Published RepositoryProposerTests and PullRepositoryProposerTests; exercised by in-repo reference callables Evaluators Published EvaluatorTests Search programs Published SearchProgramTests; Greedy, BestOfN, BestOfK, Population, CandidatePolicy, and a next-only custom program Context policies Published ContextPolicyTests Workspaces Published WorkspaceProviderTests Sandboxes Published SandboxProviderTests; cwd/environment/argv/streams, timeout, independent byte bounds, partial output, and wall-only usage Typed mutation surfaces Published MutationSurfaceTests; four built-in implementations

Store adapters keep an internal tests/store_contract.py. It is not one of those extension families and is not published from meta_evolve.conformance.

Published means an extension author can subclass the suite from an installed package. Internal means repository tests reuse assertions that are not part of the installed extension surface. Every published suite is subclassed inside tests/ — the built-ins where they exist, and in-repository reference callables for the two proposer suites, whose first-party provider adapters were replaced by the user-owned SDK boundary (no provider adapter ships). The published-conformance section of the extensions guide owns suite contents and limitations. Its migration section shows the required pre-1.0 codec and mutation-surface fixture updates.

docs.title: Migrating pre-1.0 conformance subclasses
docs.text:
The strengthened codec and mutation-surface laws intentionally changed their subclass fixtures. There are no compatibility aliases: update subclasses so the new laws run instead of silently retaining the weaker contract.

For codecs, rejected_payloads and mutable_values are now required. value_state must project custom values the default inert projection cannot read, and mutate is required only when mutable_values is non-empty.

Before:

class TestRecipeCodec(ArtifactCodecTests):
    @pytest.fixture
    def codec(self): return RecipeCodec()

    @pytest.fixture
    def values(self): return (Recipe(["mix"]),)

    @pytest.fixture
    def rejected_values(self): return (7,)

After:

class TestRecipeCodec(ArtifactCodecTests):
    # codec, values, and rejected_values stay as above
    @pytest.fixture
    def rejected_payloads(self): return (7, None)

    @pytest.fixture
    def mutable_values(self): return (Recipe(["mix"]),)

    def value_state(self, value): return tuple(value.steps)

    def mutate(self, value): value.steps.append("bake")

Return () from mutable_values for an immutable value type and omit mutate. Return () from rejected_payloads only when every canonical payload is valid input to decode; both empty tuples are positive claims.

For mutation surfaces, replace the singular mutation plus expected_surface fixtures with plural (mutation, expected_successor) pairs, and replace invalid_mutation with invalid_mutations.

Before:

@pytest.fixture
def mutation(self): return Rename("new")

@pytest.fixture
def expected_surface(self): return NameParam("new")

@pytest.fixture
def invalid_mutation(self): return Rename(7)

After:

@pytest.fixture
def mutations(self):
    return ((Rename("first"), NameParam("first")),
            (Rename("second"), NameParam("second")))

@pytest.fixture
def invalid_mutations(self):
    return (Rename(7),)

Keep surface, no_op_mutation, and foreign_mutation unchanged. Supply more than one valid pair wherever the domain allows, so an implementation that accepts one fixture value but substitutes its own value for others cannot pass.

docs.title: Design rule
docs.text:
Introduce a protocol only when a current acceptance test needs an independently testable second implementation. Keep the public call smaller than the internal port, preserve immutable inputs and typed failures, and make authority and accounting explicit.

The generated API reference lists every shipped root name and the namespaced harness and policy families. See the harness evolution and policy evolution guides.

docs.title: Improve an agent's harness
docs.text:
Our help assistant answers “reset password” but misses “please reset password.” We'll improve the instruction it follows, then test the answers it produces. A harness is the instructions and settings around an agent; here it holds one matching instruction.

Change the instruction → run the same assistant → test its answers → keep the best measured settings.

This five-cell lesson is self-contained. The assistant and proposer are handwritten Python simulations, with no model, API key, or earlier notebook required. The assistant recognizes exactly two instructions; it does not understand arbitrary prompts.

Open in Colab · Download the notebook · Download the complete Python example

Or copy the five Python blocks into a fresh Jupyter notebook.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

docs.title: 2. Start with one instruction and three questions
docs.text:
HARNESS_SEED is the starting configuration. Its planner instruction requires an exact question match. The assistant's HELP_NOTES stay fixed: it can answer password and invoice questions if its matching rule finds the topic.

answer receives a question and the configuration. HELP_CASES contains the questions and expected answers used to measure it. These checks stay outside the configuration being revised.

The fixed-evaluation notebook extends this story with a typed mutation boundary: a permitted mistake is graded, while a change to a protected declaration is refused before evaluation. That additional validation does not apply to the plain dictionary used here.

import meta_evolve as meta

HARNESS_SEED = {"planner": "Match exact questions."}
HELP_NOTES = (
    ("reset password", "Open Settings > Password."),
    ("download invoice", "Open Billing > Invoices."),
)


def answer(question, configuration):
    instruction = configuration["planner"]
    if instruction not in ("Match exact questions.", "Match topic words."):
        raise ValueError("Unsupported matching instruction")
    question = question.lower()
    for topic, reply in HELP_NOTES:
        if instruction == "Match exact questions.":
            matches = question == topic
        else:
            matches = set(topic.split()) <= set(question.split())
        if matches:
            return reply
    return "I don't have a matching help note."


# These expected answers stay fixed while the instruction changes.
HELP_CASES = (
    ("reset password", "Open Settings > Password."),
    ("please reset password", "Open Settings > Password."),
    ("download invoice", "Open Billing > Invoices."),
)

docs.title: 3. Test answers and retain the checks
docs.text:
evaluate_harness asks the assistant each question and compares the actual answer with the expected answer. The score is the fraction of checks that pass. The retained evidence contains each question, both answers, and the result.

def evaluate_harness(configuration):
    checks = []
    for question, expected in HELP_CASES:
        actual = answer(question, configuration)
        checks.append({"question": question, "expected": expected,
                       "actual": actual, "passed": actual == expected})
    return meta.EvaluationResult(
        metrics={"score": sum(check["passed"] for check in checks) / len(checks)},
        evidence=(meta.EvidenceDraft(kind="help-checks", data={"checks": checks}),),
    )

A missing help note is an ordinary answer that can fail a check. An unsupported instruction raises an execution error; Meta-Evolve records an evaluation failure with no score.

docs.title: 4. Propose a broader matching instruction
docs.text:
Our handwritten proposer changes planner to Match topic words.. With this instruction, the assistant accepts extra words around a topic, so “please reset password” can match “reset password.” It returns a new dictionary without changing the parent. The notes, questions, and expected answers stay the same.

def propose_harness(parent):
    # Change the instruction, preserving the previous configuration.
    return {**parent, "planner": "Match topic words."}

docs.title: 5. Run, inspect, and use the settings
docs.text:
improve evaluates the starting settings, tries the proposed revision, and keeps the version with the better score. trials=1 stops this run after one proposal attempt. Testing the starting settings and the revision uses two evaluations; each evaluation checks all three questions.

The output below comes from the recorded checks. The starting version can still win when a proposed change does not improve its score.

harness_result = meta.improve(
    seed=HARNESS_SEED,
    proposer=propose_harness,
    evaluator=evaluate_harness,
    trials=1,
)
for label, version in (("Starting", harness_result.trials()[0]),
                       ("Selected", harness_result.best_trial())):
    checks = version.evidence[0].data["checks"]
    print(f"{label}: {sum(check['passed'] for check in checks)}/{len(checks)} checks")
    for check in checks:
        print(check["question"], "->", check["actual"])

selected_harness = harness_result.best().value
print("Selected configuration:", dict(selected_harness))
print("Attempts:", harness_result.usage().trials)
print("Evaluations:", harness_result.usage().evaluations)
print("Reuse:", answer("please download my invoice", selected_harness))
# Output:
# Starting: 2/3 checks
# reset password -> Open Settings > Password.
# please reset password -> I don't have a matching help note.
# download invoice -> Open Billing > Invoices.
# Selected: 3/3 checks
# reset password -> Open Settings > Password.
# please reset password -> Open Settings > Password.
# download invoice -> Open Billing > Invoices.
# Selected configuration: {'planner': 'Match topic words.'}
# Attempts: 1
# Evaluations: 2
# Reuse: Open Billing > Invoices.

Only the matching instruction changed. The polite password answer now passes, while the two previously correct answers still pass: 2/3 → 3/3. selected_harness holds the settings you can pass back to the assistant. HARNESS_SEED remains unchanged.

The last call uses the selected settings for another question. This is a reuse demonstration, not a held-out quality measurement. It happens outside the run's two accounted evaluations. These results describe our three questions and handwritten simulation; they do not establish real-model or general quality.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change trials=1 to trials=0 and rerun the last cell. The starting settings remain selected at 2/3. “Please reset password” still has no matching note, and the reuse question also fails to match. There are zero attempts and one evaluation.

Restore trials=1, then add ("recover my credentials", "Open Settings > Password.") to HELP_CASES and rerun cells 2–5. Neither matching instruction understands that phrasing: the selected settings pass 3/4 checks. Changing an expected answer also changes the measurement; the evaluator checks returned answers, not the name of the instruction.

To adapt the example, replace answer with your agent, HELP_CASES with your fixed checks, and propose_harness with your revision function. Use your model SDK shows how to connect actual model calls.

docs.title: Go further
docs.text: A plain dictionary is enough for this instruction experiment. The separate Meta-Harness repair study changes a worker's instructions, runs repository repairs, and independently tests the produced code. Its typed harness declaration also validates which components and interfaces may change. Those structured mutation guarantees do not apply to the plain dictionary used here.

docs.title: Check fresh work after selection
docs.text: Search results measure the cases used during search. The repair study adds private selection and a controlled held-out comparison with fixed evaluation rules and budgets. Follow that path when you need an independent check before adopting selected settings.

docs.title: Export and reuse a structured harness
docs.text:
Here, reuse means passing selected_harness to answer. The repair study demonstrates eligible export of a typed harness and leaves adoption to the caller. Its specialized comparison and export APIs operate on structured harnesses. To retain this simple run's history, follow Save and reopen a run; saving local history does not make its callables resumable.

Improve a search policy · Choose an example

docs.title: Set limits and stopping conditions
docs.text:
Limit how many revisions a run tries, stop when its score is good enough, or cap its evaluation work. Start with trials for proposal attempts; use a Task when you need an objective target or an evaluation ceiling.

You want to… Setting Limit proposal attempts trials / max_trials Stop at a target score satisfy Cap evaluations, including the seed evaluations in Budget Narrow one execution budget in run()

The examples keep the same duration parser, proposer, and evaluator, so you can see exactly what each control changes. The handwritten revisions score 33%, 67%, and 100% on six fixed checks. No model, SDK, or credentials are needed.

Install.
