docs.title: Choose what to try next
docs.text:
A small Python loop can propose a revision, test it, and keep the better version. That is often enough. Meta-Evolve becomes useful when you want to compare search choices, inspect every attempt, or keep the history.

Start with a version → revise it → test it → inspect what happened.

A search policy chooses which version to revise next. Here, following the best version gets stuck at score 5; exploring another branch reaches 10 with the same seven evaluations. We'll run both and see why.

This is a deliberately constructed search demonstration with named versions and assigned scores, not an empirical optimizer benchmark. It needs no model, API key, checkout, or earlier lesson.

Open in Colab · Download the notebook

Or copy the first five Python blocks into a fresh Jupyter notebook. Three more cells show a tie, a failure, and saved history.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

docs.title: 2. Start with versions and scores
docs.text:
Think of each name as a possible version of your prompt, skill, or program. These numbers make the choice easy to see:

seed (0)
├─ attractive (5) → plateau versions (5)
├─ delayed (1)    → winner (10)
└─ weak versions (0)

The evaluator measures a version. Here, evaluate simply looks up its score; in your task it would run your checks. Task groups that evaluator and the work allowance: six proposed revisions, plus one evaluation of the starting version. Higher scores win.

import meta_evolve as meta


MAX_TRIALS = 6
ROOT_SEED = 11
RUN_BUDGET = meta.Budget(evaluations=MAX_TRIALS + 1, trials=MAX_TRIALS)
SCORES = {
    "seed": 0,
    "attractive": 5,
    "delayed": 1,
    "weak": 0,
    "weak-2": 0,
    "weak-3": 0,
    "weak-4": 0,
    "plateau-1": 5,
    "plateau-2": 5,
    "plateau-3": 5,
    "plateau-4": 5,
    "plateau-5": 5,
    "winner": 10,
}


def evaluate(candidate):
    return SCORES[candidate]


TASK = meta.Task(
    evaluator=evaluate,
    objectives=(meta.Maximize("score"),),
    budget=RUN_BUDGET,
)

docs.title: 3. Define how revisions are proposed
docs.text:
The parent is the version we are revising. This simulated proposer tries attractive the first time it receives seed, then delayed, then the weak versions. Revising attractive only produces more versions scoring 5. Revising delayed produces winner.

proposer() creates a fresh function with its own attempt counts. Call it once per run so earlier attempts cannot affect a later comparison. Its context argument is unused; this example needs no feedback.

def proposer():
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}

    def propose(parent, *, context):
        index = counts.get(parent, 0)
        counts[parent] = index + 1
        if parent == "seed":
            return (
                "attractive",
                "delayed",
                "weak",
                "weak-2",
                "weak-3",
                "weak-4",
            )[index]
        if parent == "delayed":
            return "winner"
        if parent == "attractive":
            return f"plateau-{index + 1}"
        return parent

    return propose

docs.title: 4. Try a handwritten loop
docs.text:
Evaluate the starting version, try six revisions, and keep a revision only when its score is strictly better. This is Greedy's basic parent-selection rule.

manual_propose = proposer()
manual_best = "seed"
manual_score = evaluate(manual_best)
manual_evaluations = 1
for _ in range(MAX_TRIALS):
    candidate = manual_propose(manual_best, context=None)
    score = evaluate(candidate)
    manual_evaluations += 1
    if score > manual_score:
        manual_best, manual_score = candidate, score
print(f"Handwritten: {manual_best}, score={manual_score}, evaluations={manual_evaluations}")
# Output:
# Handwritten: attractive, score=5, evaluations=7

This loop is reasonable for a disposable experiment. You can also write different search rules yourself. The next cell adds recorded attempts and lets us swap the search policy while keeping the rest of the experiment fixed.

docs.title: 5. Compare Greedy and TreeSearch
docs.text:
improve() uses Greedy. To choose another policy, declare an Experiment and pass it to run(). Greedy revises the best version so far. TreeSearch also explores other branches. Both inherit the allowance in TASK; the starting version, evaluator, proposal rules, and random seed stay the same, with fresh proposer state for each run.

The output reads parent → revision: score. inspect().decisions connects each recorded parent choice to its attempt. trials() includes the starting evaluation; best() returns the selected version and usage() reports the work.

search_runs = {}
for name, policy in (
    ("Greedy", meta.Greedy()), ("TreeSearch", meta.policies.TreeSearch()),
):
    run = meta.run(meta.Experiment(
        task=TASK, seed="seed", proposer=proposer(),
        search=policy, random_seed=ROOT_SEED,
    ))
    search_runs[name] = run
    print(f"{name}: seed score={run.trials()[0].metrics['score']}")
    for choice in run.inspect().decisions:
        if choice.kind == "trial":
            attempt = choice.trial
            print(f"  {choice.parents[0].value} → "
                  f"{attempt.artifact.value}: {attempt.metrics['score']}")
    summary = run.summary()
    print(f"  Selected: {run.best().value}, score={summary.primary_score}, "
          f"evaluations={summary.evaluation_count}, proposals={run.usage().trials}")
# Output:
# Greedy: seed score=0
#   seed → attractive: 5
#   attractive → plateau-1: 5
#   attractive → plateau-2: 5
#   attractive → plateau-3: 5
#   attractive → plateau-4: 5
#   attractive → plateau-5: 5
#   Selected: attractive, score=5, evaluations=7, proposals=6
# TreeSearch: seed score=0
#   seed → attractive: 5
#   seed → delayed: 1
#   attractive → plateau-1: 5
#   attractive → plateau-2: 5
#   seed → weak: 0
#   delayed → winner: 10
#   Selected: winner, score=10, evaluations=7, proposals=6

Greedy keeps revising attractive and gets no further improvement. TreeSearch tries delayed, then later revises it into winner. A weaker version can therefore be worth revisiting. This example illustrates that possibility; which search works well depends on your task and allowance.

Each run used six proposals and seven evaluations. The handwritten loop's seven evaluations are separate work. These first runs keep history in memory.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
In cell 2, change MAX_TRIALS = 6 to MAX_TRIALS = 5, then run cells 2–5. Both searches now select attractive at 5, using six evaluations each. TreeSearch needs its sixth proposal to reach winner here.

Set MAX_TRIALS = 0 to measure only seed: score 0, one evaluation. Restore 6 and rerun cells 2–5 before continuing.

For your own task, replace the starting value, evaluate, and proposer. Hold those pieces and the allowance fixed while comparing search choices.

docs.title: 6. Inspect a tie and a failed attempt
docs.text:
The run records unsuccessful attempts too. Start at attractive: its revision plateau-1 scores the same 5, so the starting version remains selected.

Then simulate an evaluator error. The attempted version is still recorded, with a failure message and no measurements. The successful starting evaluation remains selected. These are two separate, one-proposal runs.

search_tie = meta.improve(
    seed="attractive", proposer=proposer(), evaluator=evaluate, trials=1,
)
print("Tie scores:", [attempt.metrics["score"] for attempt in search_tie.trials()])
print("Still selected:", search_tie.best().value)
print("Tie work:", search_tie.usage().trials, "proposal,",
      search_tie.usage().evaluations, "evaluations")

def broken_evaluation(candidate):
    if candidate != "seed":
        raise RuntimeError("Example evaluator could not run.")
    return evaluate(candidate)

search_failure = meta.improve(
    seed="seed", proposer=proposer(), evaluator=broken_evaluation, trials=1,
)
search_failed_attempt = search_failure.trials()[1]
print("Failed version:", search_failed_attempt.artifact.value)
print("Failure state:", search_failed_attempt.state)
print("Failure:", search_failed_attempt.failure.kind, search_failed_attempt.failure.message)
print("Measurements:", dict(search_failed_attempt.metrics))
print("Still selected:", search_failure.best().value)
print("Work:", search_failure.usage().trials, "proposal,",
      search_failure.usage().evaluations, "evaluations")
# Output:
# Tie scores: [5, 5]
# Still selected: attractive
# Tie work: 1 proposal, 2 evaluations
# Failed version: attractive
# Failure state: evaluation_failed
# Failure: evaluator_failure Example evaluator could not run.
# Measurements: {}
# Still selected: seed
# Work: 1 proposal, 2 evaluations

An incorrect answer can receive a low score. An evaluator that could not run has no score to compare. Here the failed evaluation still counts as work: one proposal and two evaluations, including the starting version.

docs.title: 7. Save a new run
docs.text:
To keep history, open Storage.durable() and pass it as storage=. This executes a fresh TreeSearch run on disk; it does not save the earlier in-memory runs.

A new folder preserves previous saves when you rerun the cell. last-search-run.txt records that folder's path so we can find it after a kernel restart. Capture the summary while storage is open.

from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

search_directory = Path("runs") / f"search-{uuid4().hex[:12]}"
search_directory.mkdir(parents=True)
with meta.Storage.durable(search_directory / "history") as search_storage:
    saved_search = meta.run(meta.Experiment(
        task=TASK, seed="seed", proposer=proposer(),
        search=meta.policies.TreeSearch(), random_seed=ROOT_SEED,
    ), storage=search_storage)
    saved_search_summary = saved_search.summary()

Path("last-search-run.txt").write_text(str(search_directory), encoding="utf-8")
print("Saved score:", saved_search_summary.primary_score)
print("Saved evaluations:", saved_search_summary.evaluation_count)
# Output:
# Saved score: 10
# Saved evaluations: 7

docs.title: 8. Restart the kernel and reopen
docs.text:
Restart the kernel, then run this cell alone in the same working directory. It needs only Meta-Evolve and the saved files, including the path note. No proposer, evaluator, or earlier Python variables are needed.

from pathlib import Path
import meta_evolve as meta

search_directory = Path(Path("last-search-run.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
with meta.open_run(search_directory / "history") as reopened_search:
    for search_attempt in reopened_search.trials():
        print(search_attempt.artifact.value, search_attempt.metrics["score"])
    reopened_summary = reopened_search.summary()
    search_selected = reopened_search.best().value
    print("Selected path:", " → ".join(reopened_summary.winning_lineage))
    print("Retained evaluations:", reopened_summary.evaluation_count)
# Output:
# seed 0
# attractive 5
# delayed 1
# plateau-1 5
# plateau-2 5
# weak 0
# winner 10
# Selected path: seed → delayed → winner
# Retained evaluations: 7

The seven measurements are still there. Reopening reads history; it does not propose revisions or spend more evaluations. Continuing unfinished work is a separate capability called resuming. Saving these local functions does not make them resumable.

Read results inside the with block while the history is open. search_selected is an ordinary string you can keep after it closes. The durability reference covers continuation.

Keep the saved folder and path note on persistent disk if your notebook service discards local files when its runtime is deleted. Save and reopen a run covers choosing an older run and exporting a selected program you can use elsewhere.

docs.title: Inspect results and failures
docs.text:
The last proposed revision may be worse than an earlier one, or may fail to execute. The selected artifact answers “what should I keep?” The run's history answers “what happened along the way?” This guide shows how to read both, using a run with an improvement, a regression, and a failed evaluation. An unsuccessful measurement has no score; a measured wrong answer can have a low score. Failures explains that distinction.

You want to… Use Read a compact outcome summary() Read the selected source and score best() and best_trial() See every attempt or the winning path trials() and lineage() Understand a failed measurement failure and inspect() Count work usage()

The setup creates inspection_result: a parser run with scores of 33%, 67%, 33%, then a failed evaluation. The revisions are handwritten; Python executes and grades them. No model, SDK, or credentials are needed.

Open in Colab · Download the notebook

To run this page: expand the required setup, copy its Python blocks into notebook cells, and run them from top to bottom. Then run the examples below in order. Every definition is here; no other page needs to be executed. Rerunning the cells repeats the same results.

Required setup for a fresh notebook

Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

Starting source and instructions. SEED reads a duration's number but ignores its unit. CONTRACT tells the proposer what the parser should do.

import meta_evolve as meta

CONTRACT = """Implement parse_seconds(text) for whole-number durations.
Inputs contain a number followed by s, m, or h, such as '30s' or '2h'.
Return the duration in seconds as an integer. Return only Python source.
"""

SEED = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    return int(text[:-1])
'''

Evaluation. evaluate returns the fraction of six checks answered correctly. load_parser executes the source locally; use this evaluator with the reviewed, handwritten code shown here.

CASES = (
    ("30s", 30),
    ("90s", 90),
    ("2m", 120),
    ("3m", 180),
    ("1h", 3600),
    ("2h", 7200),
)


def load_parser(source):
    namespace = {}
    exec(source, namespace)
    return namespace["parse_seconds"]


def evaluate(source):
    parse = load_parser(source)
    passed = 0
    for text, expected in CASES:
        actual = parse(text)
        if type(actual) is int and actual == expected:
            passed += 1
    return passed / len(CASES)


print(f"Starting score: {evaluate(SEED):.0%}")
# Output:
# Starting score: 33%

Revisions. MINUTES adds minutes support. COMPLETE also handles hours; keep it for the exercise at the end.

MINUTES = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    return quantity * 60 if text[-1] == "m" else quantity
'''

COMPLETE = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    seconds_per_unit = {"s": 1, "m": 60, "h": 3600}
    return quantity * seconds_per_unit[text[-1]]
'''

Create a history to inspect.

A proposer receives the current source and returns a proposed replacement. Its optional second argument, context, includes step: the proposal number, starting at 1 in this greedy run. Use it to return three fixed revisions in order: the minutes fix, the original parser, then syntactically broken source. This deliberately scripted proposer ignores its parent so the history is easy to reproduce and inspect.

BROKEN = "def broken("
INSPECTION_REVISIONS = (MINUTES, SEED, BROKEN)


def propose_mixed_history(source, *, context):
    return INSPECTION_REVISIONS[context.step - 1]

meta.improve() evaluates the seed, proposes from the best version so far, and evaluates each valid revision. Higher scalar scores win by default. trials=3 allows three proposal attempts after the seed. It returns a run containing the outcomes and selected version.

inspection_result = meta.improve(
    seed=SEED,
    proposer=propose_mixed_history,
    evaluator=evaluate,
    trials=3,
)

Rerunning this setup produces the same history; context.step starts again for each run. The Start here walkthrough explains the shared parser. Close this section once its cells have run.

After running the setup, capture a compact report:

inspection_snapshot = inspection_result.summary()
inspection_snapshot

The notebook shows a completed run, a baseline score of 33% and selected score of 67% (as numeric fractions), three proposals, four evaluations including the baseline, and one failed attempt. History is not saved durably in this example. Completion, measurement, and improvement are separate facts. A selected seed or a tie is not an improvement; a failed evaluation has no score.

Use print(inspection_snapshot) for plain text. Capture while storage is open; the report remains displayable after storage closes. Detailed source, evidence, and failure information remain in the explicit queries below.

docs.title: 1. Read the selected source and score
docs.text:
best() returns the selected artifact; its .value is the source string. best_trial() returns the selected attempt with its measurement and evidence. Printing the source does not execute it.

selected = inspection_result.best()
print(f"Selected score: {inspection_result.best_trial().metrics['score']:.0%}")
print(selected.value, end="")
# Output:
# Selected score: 67%
# def parse_seconds(text):
#     quantity = int(text[:-1])
#     return quantity * 60 if text[-1] == "m" else quantity

The minutes revision stays selected, even though it was followed by two more attempts. Selection is based on measured quality, not recency.

docs.title: 2. Read every attempt and the winning lineage
docs.text:
trials() includes the seed and every attempted revision, including failures. Check failure before reading a score: a failed evaluation has no measurement.

for number, attempt in enumerate(inspection_result.trials()):
    label = "Seed" if number == 0 else f"Revision {number}"
    if attempt.failure is not None:
        print(f"{label}: {attempt.failure.kind} (no score)")
    else:
        print(f"{label}: {attempt.metrics['score']:.0%}")
# Output:
# Seed: 33%
# Revision 1: 67%
# Revision 2: 33%
# Revision 3: evaluator_failure (no score)

Revision 2 executes successfully but gives wrong answers. Its 33% score is a valid measurement, so it stays in history as a regression from the 67% parent. Revision 3 cannot execute, so there is no score to compare.

lineage() returns the attempts along the selected artifact's parent chain. Here it contains just the seed and the minutes revision:

print("Attempts in history:", len(inspection_result.trials()))
print("Versions in winning lineage:", len(inspection_result.lineage()))
# Output:
# Attempts in history: 4
# Versions in winning lineage: 2

The later revisions were proposed from the minutes revision. Neither belongs to the winning lineage, but both remain available through trials(). An attempt's evidence holds any observations attached by the evaluator or proposer; this scalar evaluator attaches none. The feedback guide shows how to record failed checks there.

docs.title: 3. Understand a failed evaluation
docs.text:
The malformed source reached the evaluator, where loading it raised a SyntaxError. The callable boundary recorded an evaluator_failure with exception details and empty metrics:

failed_attempt = inspection_result.trials()[-1]
print("Failure:", failed_attempt.failure.kind)
print("Exception:", failed_attempt.failure.details["exception_type"])
print("Metrics:", dict(failed_attempt.metrics))
# Output:
# Failure: evaluator_failure
# Exception: SyntaxError
# Metrics: {}

A failed measurement is not a zero score. A source version that runs and fails every check would score zero under our evaluator. More detailed evaluators can report typed failures for invalid output, timeouts, or infrastructure problems. A proposal failure can occur before any artifact is produced.

If every evaluation fails, there is no winner. inspect() gives a summary without requiring one. Try a separate seed-only run:

failed_run = meta.improve(
    seed=BROKEN,
    proposer=propose_mixed_history,
    evaluator=evaluate,
    trials=0,
)
overview = failed_run.inspect().overview
print("Rankability:", overview.rankability)
print("Selected attempt:", overview.best_trial)
print("Evaluations:", failed_run.usage().evaluations)
# Output:
# Rankability: unrankable
# Selected attempt: None
# Evaluations: 1

trials(), inspect(), and usage() still work. Calling best() or best_trial() on that run raises meta.NoSuccessfulEvaluation.

docs.title: 4. Count the work
docs.text:
usage() totals the work charged to a run. The main run made three proposals and evaluated four source versions, counting the seed and the failed evaluation.

usage = inspection_result.usage()
print("Proposal attempts:", usage.trials)
print("Evaluations:", usage.evaluations)
# Output:
# Proposal attempts: 3
# Evaluations: 4

The manual evaluate(SEED) preview and the separate seed-only run are outside this run's accounting.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
In the required setup, change the meta.improve() call from seed=SEED to seed=COMPLETE, leaving the proposer and three-attempt limit unchanged. Predict the winner, then rerun that call and the inspection cells.

The seed now scores 100% and stays selected. The three proposals still produce 67%, 33%, and a failed evaluation. History still contains four attempts, but the winning lineage contains only the seed. There are still four evaluations.

docs.title: Why isn't the last attempt the selected result?
docs.text:
Selection follows the objective, so a later regression or failed measurement does not replace a better measured version. Use trials() for all attempts and lineage() for the selected version's parent chain.

For your own run, use these same queries on the result of improve() or run(). Check for failures before indexing metrics; if nothing was measured successfully, start with inspect() instead of asking for a winner.

Next, set limits and stopping conditions to control how much work the experiment can do. The result reference covers aggregate inspection, comparisons, and additional queries.

docs.title: Improve source against an independent grader
docs.text:
Start with handwritten repairs and real subprocess graders, with no model calls or credentials. Then replace the booking-range fixture with your model wrapper through the same proposer boundary.

A source file can be the candidate too. This complete example repairs a small clamp() function against three independent checks. Copy it into a Python file with meta_evolve installed; the candidate and grader are both inline.

docs.title: Propose a patch and measure it
docs.text:
SourceTree stores immutable source. PatchProposer applies a TextPatch in a private mutable workspace and captures an immutable successor. The patch names one file, its exact expected bytes, and the replacement. CommandEvaluator independently materializes each candidate and runs the evaluator-owned grader.

The fixed repair is handwritten. The example demonstrates the API and evaluation boundary, not a model discovering a repair.

import sys
import meta_evolve as meta

BAD = "def clamp(value, low, high):\n    return value\n"
FIXED = "def clamp(value, low, high):\n    return max(low, min(value, high))\n"
seed = meta.SourceTree({"clamp.py": BAD})


def repair(tree, context):
    return meta.TextPatch(path="clamp.py", expected=tree["clamp.py"], replacement=FIXED)


# The grader belongs to the evaluator, outside the candidate's source tree.
GRADER = """
import runpy
try:
    clamp = runpy.run_path("clamp.py")["clamp"]
    passed = all(clamp(value, 0, 10) == expected
                 for value, expected in ((-5, 0), (5, 5), (15, 10)))
except Exception:
    passed = False
raise SystemExit(0 if passed else 1)
"""
evaluator = meta.CommandEvaluator(
    command=meta.ProcessSpec(argv=(sys.executable, "-c", GRADER)),
    environment=meta.EvaluationEnvironment(name="clamp-checks", version="1"),
)
result = meta.run(meta.Experiment(
    seed=seed,
    task=meta.Task(artifact=meta.SourceTree, evaluator=evaluator),
    proposer=meta.PatchProposer(repair),
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=1),
))
print("Scores:", [t.metrics["score"] for t in result.trials()])
print("Parent unchanged:", seed["clamp.py"] == BAD)
print("Selected source:")
print(result.best().value["clamp.py"], end="")
print("Usage:", result.usage().trials, result.usage().evaluations)
# Output:
# Scores: [0.0, 1.0]
# Parent unchanged: True
# Selected source:
# def clamp(value, low, high):
#     return max(low, min(value, high))
# Usage: 1 2

The grader checks all three inputs. Exit 0 passes the suite; exit 1 is a valid failing measurement. The poor candidate remains a measured result with score 0.0. Candidate load or execution errors also fail this particular grader's suite.

The evaluator records process evidence alongside each measurement. trials() retains both candidates, and lineage() follows the selected source's parents. A patch whose expected bytes do not match produces InvalidOutput; an evaluator infrastructure failure produces EvaluatorFailure. Neither becomes a low score.

The proposer edits source, not the grader, budget, or promotion rules. The local subprocess is a development execution boundary, not a sandbox for hostile code. These three selection checks are not an untouched final test split, and passing them establishes nothing about other functions.

docs.title: Repair booking ranges
docs.text: A booking tool should merge touching ranges: (9, 10) and (10, 11) must become (9, 11). The maintained agent_test_repair application starts with source that merges overlaps but leaves touching bookings separate. Its fixture replaces start < merged[-1][1] with start <= merged[-1][1].

cd meta-evolve
uv sync --locked

Run from the repository root. These first output lines are checked against the actual command; it also prints the selected source, its diff, and evaluations: 2.

Output

docs.title: The actual declaration
docs.text:
This function comes from the maintained application:

main.py · repair_intervals
def repair_intervals(
    build_agent: Callable[[str], Proposer],
    *,
    grader: Path = GRADER,
    random_seed: int = 0,
) -> meta.Run:
    """Run the repair loop with one agent factory and one grader.

    Both are injectable so the same loop serves every caller: ``main`` passes
    the committed fixture, a live run passes a factory that wraps a real model
    SDK, and the test suite passes counting fixtures and a deliberately broken
    grader. Nothing else about the task, seed, search, or budget changes.
    """

    experiment = meta.Experiment(
        task=grading_task(grader),
        seed=meta.load_source_tree(CANDIDATE),
        proposer=build_agent(INSTRUCTIONS),
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=MAX_TRIALS),
        random_seed=random_seed,
    )
    return meta.run(experiment)

CANDIDATE names the directory containing only intervals.py. INSTRUCTIONS describes the failing case; build_agent returns a source-tree proposer. The fixture already knows the fix. grading_task owns the external runner, grader, score threshold of 1.0, and budget of at most two revisions and three evaluations. Greedy stops after the first passing revision. No context policy is configured. The candidate cannot edit the grader or expand these limits.

The independent grader covers overlapping, disjoint, touching, contained, and unsorted ranges. Its runner interprets exit 0 as score 1.0, exit 1 as score 0.0, and a missing/crashing grader as EvaluatorFailure with no score. A candidate that cannot import fails its tests; it is distinct from a broken grader.

These cases guide selection and are not an untouched final split. The local process boundary is not hostile-code isolation. Passing tests here demonstrates this repair, not model ability or correctness for an arbitrary repository.

main.py · print_diff
def print_diff(result: meta.Run) -> None:
    """Show the selected repair against its direct parent."""

    lineage = result.lineage()
    if len(lineage) < 2:
        print("No revision selected; the seed remains best.")
        return
    diff = meta.diff_artifacts(lineage[-2].artifact, result.best())
    for file in diff.files:
        print(f"Diff: {file.path} ({file.status})")
        for line in file.lines:
            if line.kind in {"added", "removed"}:
                prefix = "+" if line.kind == "added" else "-"
                print(f"{prefix} {line.text}", end="" if line.text.endswith("\n") else "\n")

In a scratch checkout, make the replacement string in fixture_agent identical to its original start < merged[-1][1]. Rerun: predict scores: [0.0], grader passed: False, and evaluations: 3. Both allowed revisions are tried, but the printed scores follow only the selected artifact's lineage: the seed remains selected because neither revision improves it. All three evaluations remain in result.trials(). Restore the fixture afterward.

For your own task, replace the candidate files, instruction brief, and independent grader. Supply an SDK-backed callable factory to repair_intervals to replace the fixture; keep evaluation and permissions outside candidate authority.

docs.title: Use your model wrapper
docs.text:
repair_intervals already accepts your agent factory. The adapter below asks for the complete contents of intervals.py, then builds a new source tree with that one file replaced. Your model never needs to match a patch hunk's whitespace. The original tree and every other file stay intact.

main.py · sdk_agent
def sdk_agent(client, instructions: str) -> Proposer:
    """Wrap a text-generating client as a source-tree proposer.

    ``generate`` returns a ProposalResult with replacement text or a failure.
    Keep its usage, evidence, and metadata with the candidate.
    """

    def repair(tree: meta.SourceTree, *, context) -> meta.ProposalResult:
        reply = client.generate(
            instructions=(instructions + " Return the complete intervals.py source "
                          "only, without Markdown fences or commentary."),
            input=tree["intervals.py"],
        )
        if reply.failure is not None:
            return reply
        return replace(reply, candidate=meta.SourceTree(
            {**tree, "intervals.py": reply.candidate},
        ))

    return repair

client.generate(instructions=..., input=...) returns a ProposalResult containing source text or a typed failure. The adapter preserves its usage, evidence, metadata, and derivation references. Replace generate with your own agent call while keeping that contract; the grader, search, and budget continue to work as before. This example supplies the failing case in INSTRUCTIONS and declares no feedback policy.

Run with the live parser's OpenAI wrapper

From the same checkout, set OPENAI_API_KEY in your environment and run the command below. It reuses the live parser's request and accounting wrapper, including its 120-second request timeout and disabled retries. OPENAI_MODEL can select another compatible model. This command makes at most two model requests; the independent grader can stop search after the first successful repair.

uv run --with openai==2.54.0 python - <<'PY'
from functools import partial
from examples.agents.agent_test_repair.main import (
    print_diff, repair_intervals, sdk_agent,
)
from examples.learn.llm.openai_client import OpenAIClient

with OpenAIClient.from_environment() as client:
    print("Wrapper:", client.configuration)
    result = repair_intervals(partial(sdk_agent, client))
print(result.summary())
print_diff(result)
print("Model tokens:", result.usage().tokens)
PY

The command makes live requests and may incur cost. The diff above comes from the fixture; this page makes no claim about a live model's repair. The wrapper retains token counts and response evidence; billed spend stays unknown unless you configure a cost reporter. The live path has the same local subprocess boundary described above.

docs.title: Complete booking-range source
docs.text:
candidate/intervals.py 
"""Collapse booking ranges into the blocks an operator actually sees.

A range is an inclusive ``(start, end)`` pair. Two ranges belong to the same
block when they overlap *or* touch: ``(9, 10)`` and ``(10, 11)`` describe one
uninterrupted block from 9 to 11 and must come back as ``(9, 11)``.
"""


def merge_intervals(intervals):
    """Return the fewest non-touching blocks covering ``intervals``, in order."""

    merged = []
    for start, end in sorted(intervals):
        if merged and start < merged[-1][1]:
            last_start, last_end = merged[-1]
            merged[-1] = (last_start, max(last_end, end))
        else:
            merged.append((start, end))
    return merged
grader.py 
"""Evaluator-owned checks for the materialized interval candidate."""

from __future__ import annotations

import importlib.util
import traceback
from pathlib import Path


# Overlapping and disjoint ranges are the cases anyone writes first, and the
# shipped code gets both right. Only the touching ones — where a block ends
# exactly where the next begins — catch the defect.
CASES: tuple[tuple[list[tuple[int, int]], list[tuple[int, int]]], ...] = (
    ([], []),
    ([(1, 4)], [(1, 4)]),
    ([(1, 3), (2, 4)], [(1, 4)]),
    ([(1, 5), (2, 3)], [(1, 5)]),
    ([(1, 2), (4, 5)], [(1, 2), (4, 5)]),
    ([(5, 6), (1, 2)], [(1, 2), (5, 6)]),
    ([(1, 2), (2, 3)], [(1, 3)]),
    ([(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (6, 7)], [(1, 4), (6, 7)]),
)


def _mismatch(merge, intervals, expected) -> str | None:
    actual = merge(list(intervals))
    # The block type is the candidate's call; the block contents are not.
    if [tuple(block) for block in actual] == expected:
        return None
    return f"merge_intervals({intervals!r}) returned {actual!r}, expected {expected!r}"


def grade(workspace: Path) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Anything the candidate causes — wrong answers, code that fails to
    load or run — is an ordinary failure. Only a grader-internal fault may
    escape as an exception, which the runner reports outside the pass/fail
    protocol.
    """

    try:
        candidate = workspace / "intervals.py"
        spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("candidate_intervals", candidate)
        if spec is None or spec.loader is None:
            raise ImportError(f"cannot load candidate module: {candidate}")
        module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
        spec.loader.exec_module(module)
        merge = module.merge_intervals
        failures = [
            message
            for intervals, expected in CASES
            if (message := _mismatch(merge, intervals, expected)) is not None
        ]
    except Exception:
        return False, f"candidate failed to load or run:\n{traceback.format_exc()}"
    if failures:
        return False, "\n".join(failures)
    return True, f"all {len(CASES)} merge_intervals cases passed"
main.py 
"""An injected proposer repairs a real bug; a grader subprocess decides.

The seed is a ``SourceTree`` holding a function whose documented contract and
shipped behaviour disagree on one character. The proposer is supplied by the
caller through the user-owned callable boundary: the committed script injects
a deterministic fixture, and a real SDK wrapper plugs into the same seam. The
evaluator is a *separate process* running an evaluator-owned grader the
proposer never sees, so the score is a verdict about the code rather than a
report from the thing being scored.

The grader obeys the fixed exit protocol: ``0`` passes, ``1`` is a rankable
failure with a failing score, and anything else is an ``EvaluatorFailure``.
That third code is the load-bearing one here. With an agent in the loop, a
grader that is itself broken must not quietly rank every attempt as bad work;
it must stop the run and say so.

Every piece is importable and injectable: ``repair_intervals`` takes the agent
factory and the grader path, so a deterministic test drives this same logic
through counting fixture proposers and a deliberately broken grader.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path

import meta_evolve as meta
from meta_evolve.ports import Proposer


HERE = Path(__file__).parent
CANDIDATE = HERE / "candidate"
RUNNER = HERE / "run_grader.py"
GRADER = HERE / "grader.py"

AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 120.0
# One proposal per trial, and the run stops early the moment the grader
# passes. The wall ceiling is sized for a live SDK wrapper whose sessions each
# stay inside AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, plus the grader subprocesses between
# them; the committed fixture never comes near it.
MAX_TRIALS = 2
BUDGET = meta.Budget(
    evaluations=MAX_TRIALS + 1,
    trials=MAX_TRIALS,
    wall_seconds=AGENT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS * (MAX_TRIALS + 1),
)

# What a developer is handed by CI: the failing case, not the fix. The repo
# states the contract in the module docstring; finding the one character that
# disagrees with it is the agent's job.
INSTRUCTIONS = (
    "The test suite for intervals.py fails one case: "
    "merge_intervals([(1, 2), (2, 3)]) returned [(1, 2), (2, 3)] where "
    "[(1, 3)] was expected. Read intervals.py, find why it disagrees with "
    "the contract it documents, and fix it. Change only intervals.py, and "
    "keep merge_intervals' name and signature."
)


def grading_task(grader: Path = GRADER) -> meta.Task:
    """Score candidates by running the grader in its own process.

    ``CommandEvaluator`` materializes each candidate tree into a fresh
    workspace and runs the fixed runner there. The grader lives outside
    ``candidate/``, so it is never part of any ``SourceTree`` a proposal
    could read or edit, and its exit code — not anything the candidate
    prints about itself — is what becomes the score.
    """

    return meta.Task(
        evaluator=meta.CommandEvaluator(
            command=meta.ProcessSpec(
                argv=(sys.executable, str(RUNNER), str(grader)),
                environment={"PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE": "1"},
            ),
            environment=meta.EvaluationEnvironment(
                name="python-intervals-tests",
                version="1",
            ),
        ),
        artifact=meta.SourceTree,
        # Stop as soon as the grader passes: further attempts cost money and
        # cannot improve on a passing suite.
        objectives=(meta.Maximize("score", satisfy=1.0),),
        budget=BUDGET,
    )


def repair_intervals(
    build_agent: Callable[[str], Proposer],
    *,
    grader: Path = GRADER,
    random_seed: int = 0,
) -> meta.Run:
    """Run the repair loop with one agent factory and one grader.

    Both are injectable so the same loop serves every caller: ``main`` passes
    the committed fixture, a live run passes a factory that wraps a real model
    SDK, and the test suite passes counting fixtures and a deliberately broken
    grader. Nothing else about the task, seed, search, or budget changes.
    """

    experiment = meta.Experiment(
        task=grading_task(grader),
        seed=meta.load_source_tree(CANDIDATE),
        proposer=build_agent(INSTRUCTIONS),
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=MAX_TRIALS),
        random_seed=random_seed,
    )
    return meta.run(experiment)


def fixture_agent(_instructions: str) -> Proposer:
    """The committed proposer: a deterministic stand-in for an SDK wrapper.

    It occupies exactly the seat a user-owned SDK wrapper occupies — a factory
    that takes the instructions and returns an ordinary proposer callable —
    but it already knows the one-character repair, so the committed script
    runs offline, credential-free, and for free. It takes no shortcut past the
    evaluator: its candidate is scored by the same grader subprocess a live
    wrapper's would be, and the instructions it ignores are the ones a live
    wrapper would forward to its model.
    """

    def repair(tree: meta.SourceTree, *, context) -> meta.SourceTree:
        return meta.SourceTree(
            {
                **tree,
                "intervals.py": tree["intervals.py"].replace(
                    "start < merged[-1][1]", "start <= merged[-1][1]"
                ),
            }
        )

    return repair


def sdk_agent(client, instructions: str) -> Proposer:
    """Wrap a text-generating client as a source-tree proposer.

    ``generate`` returns a ProposalResult with replacement text or a failure.
    Keep its usage, evidence, and metadata with the candidate.
    """

    def repair(tree: meta.SourceTree, *, context) -> meta.ProposalResult:
        reply = client.generate(
            instructions=(instructions + " Return the complete intervals.py source "
                          "only, without Markdown fences or commentary."),
            input=tree["intervals.py"],
        )
        if reply.failure is not None:
            return reply
        return replace(reply, candidate=meta.SourceTree(
            {**tree, "intervals.py": reply.candidate},
        ))

    return repair


def print_diff(result: meta.Run) -> None:
    """Show the selected repair against its direct parent."""

    lineage = result.lineage()
    if len(lineage) < 2:
        print("No revision selected; the seed remains best.")
        return
    diff = meta.diff_artifacts(lineage[-2].artifact, result.best())
    for file in diff.files:
        print(f"Diff: {file.path} ({file.status})")
        for line in file.lines:
            if line.kind in {"added", "removed"}:
                prefix = "+" if line.kind == "added" else "-"
                print(f"{prefix} {line.text}", end="" if line.text.endswith("\n") else "\n")


def main() -> None:
    """Run the loop with the fixture and print what the grader decided.

    Swap ``fixture_agent`` for your own factory to put a real agent in the
    loop; the printing below distinguishes "the best candidate scored X" from
    "nothing was scored at all", which is the difference the exit protocol
    exists to preserve.
    """

    result = repair_intervals(fixture_agent)
    try:
        trial = result.best_trial()
    except meta.NoSuccessfulEvaluation:
        # Not "every candidate is bad": no candidate was scored at all. Every
        # evaluation recorded a typed failure carrying no metric, so there is
        # nothing to rank -- a grader fault (exit 2) is the one this example
        # exists to show.
        print("no candidate scored: every evaluation failed before producing one")
        print(f"run {result.id.value} recorded why; the seed source is unchanged")
        raise SystemExit(1)
    print(f"scores: {[step.metrics['score'] for step in result.lineage()]}")
    print(f"grader passed: {trial.metrics['score'] == 1.0}")
    print(f"best source:\n{result.best().value['intervals.py']}")
    print_diff(result)
    print(f"evaluations: {result.summary().evaluation_count}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
run_grader.py 
"""Fixed grader runner: exit 0 pass, 1 rankable failure, other grader fault.

The runner loads the evaluator-owned grader named by ``argv[1]`` and grades
the current working directory — the materialized candidate workspace.
Anything the candidate causes is an ordinary exit ``1``; a missing, crashing,
or malformed grader exits ``2`` so it surfaces as an ``EvaluatorFailure``
instead of ranking every candidate as failing.
"""

import importlib.util
import sys
import traceback
from pathlib import Path

exit_code = 2
try:
    grader_path = Path(sys.argv[1])
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("external_grader", grader_path)
    if spec is None or spec.loader is None:
        raise ImportError(f"cannot load external grader: {grader_path}")
    grader = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(grader)
    result = grader.grade(Path.cwd())
    if (
        not isinstance(result, tuple)
        or len(result) != 2
        or type(result[0]) is not bool
        or not isinstance(result[1], str)
    ):
        raise TypeError("grader must return tuple[bool, str]")
    print(result[1])
    exit_code = 0 if result[0] else 1
except BaseException:
    traceback.print_exc()
raise SystemExit(exit_code)

docs.title: Give the proposer feedback
docs.text:
A score tells you how well a revision performed. Evidence such as failed checks tells you what needs fixing. This guide records those checks, supplies them to a proposer, and uses them to choose the next revision. Then you will turn feedback off and compare the results.

You want to… Use Record failed checks EvaluationResult with evidence Use checks in a revision The proposer's context argument Supply prior observations RecentAncestors Compare with feedback off context=None

The proposer chooses handwritten revisions; Python executes and grades them. No model, SDK, or credentials are needed.

Here, feedback means evaluator observations supplied to the proposer. The API's broader experience vocabulary also covers other authorized history and explicit pull access.

Open in Colab · Download the notebook

To run this page: expand the required setup, copy its Python blocks into notebook cells, and run them from top to bottom. Then run the examples below in order. Every definition is here; no other page needs to be executed. Rerunning the cells repeats the same results.

Required setup for a fresh notebook

Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

Starting source and instructions. SEED reads a duration's number but ignores its unit. CONTRACT tells the proposer what the parser should do.

import meta_evolve as meta

CONTRACT = """Implement parse_seconds(text) for whole-number durations.
Inputs contain a number followed by s, m, or h, such as '30s' or '2h'.
Return the duration in seconds as an integer. Return only Python source.
"""

SEED = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    return int(text[:-1])
'''

Checks. CASES holds six fixed expected answers. load_parser executes the source locally; use these checks with the reviewed, handwritten code here.

CASES = (
    ("30s", 30),
    ("90s", 90),
    ("2m", 120),
    ("3m", 180),
    ("1h", 3600),
    ("2h", 7200),
)


def load_parser(source):
    namespace = {}
    exec(source, namespace)
    return namespace["parse_seconds"]

Revisions. MINUTES fixes minutes; COMPLETE adds hours as well.

MINUTES = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    return quantity * 60 if text[-1] == "m" else quantity
'''

COMPLETE = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    seconds_per_unit = {"s": 1, "m": 60, "h": 3600}
    return quantity * seconds_per_unit[text[-1]]
'''

The Start here walkthrough introduces the starting parser. You can close this section once its cells have run.

docs.title: 1. Record useful feedback
docs.text:
A scalar evaluator can return just a score. meta.EvaluationResult can also attach evidence: observations that explain a measurement. meta.EvidenceDraft describes one observation to record. We will store each wrong answer's input, expected value, and actual value.

def evaluate_with_feedback(source):
    parse = load_parser(source)
    failures = []
    for text, expected in CASES:
        actual = parse(text)
        if type(actual) is not int or actual != expected:
            failures.append({
                "input": text, "expected": expected, "actual": actual,
            })

    return meta.EvaluationResult(
        metrics={"score": (len(CASES) - len(failures)) / len(CASES)},
        evidence=(meta.EvidenceDraft(
            kind="failed-cases", data={"failures": failures},
        ),),
    )

score is the fraction of checks passed; 1.0 means all six pass. "failed-cases" is our label for this evidence, and data holds its contents. An exception while loading or running the parser still produces a failed evaluation with no score.

docs.title: 2. Use the failed checks to choose a revision
docs.text:
A proposer requests keyword-only context. context.evidence.latest("failed-cases") returns the last matching evidence in the selected bundle, with its contents in .data. Older ancestors may still have failures we have already fixed.

This proposer fixes minutes if any minute checks failed, then hours if any hour checks failed. If there is no feedback, or nothing failed, it returns the source unchanged. That rule makes the effect of feedback visible.

def propose_with_feedback(source, *, context):
    if not context.evidence.enabled:
        return source
    latest = context.evidence.latest("failed-cases")
    if latest is None:
        return source

    failed_inputs = [case["input"] for case in latest.data["failures"]]
    if any(text.endswith("m") for text in failed_inputs):
        return MINUTES
    if any(text.endswith("h") for text in failed_inputs):
        return COMPLETE
    return source

This is a small rule-based demonstration, with two known fixes. The proposer uses the recorded checks; it does not call the evaluator itself. With a model, you would put relevant observations into your SDK request. The bundle also provides context.bundle.rendered when you want its text rendering. The enabled check deliberately makes feedback optional for the comparison below. Calling latest() with feedback disabled instead raises meta_evolve.errors.ContextDisabled. A declared policy with no matching selected evidence returns None. Both proposers and evaluators can record evidence; this example reserves "failed-cases" for its evaluator.

docs.title: 3. Supply feedback and run
docs.text:
Recording evidence does not automatically send it to the proposer. meta.RecentAncestors selects recent prior records from the current parent's lineage. Rejected siblings are outside that ancestry. max_records limits the structured records; max_chars limits their text rendering. Selected records retain canonical order. A small record limit can still omit evidence; latest means latest in this bundle, not necessarily the current parent's feedback. AncestorsOnly remains available when you want oldest-record retention instead.

For one bounded run, pass an objective and the policy directly to improve():

simple_feedback = meta.improve(
    seed=SEED, proposer=propose_with_feedback, evaluator=evaluate_with_feedback,
    objective=meta.Maximize("score", satisfy=1.0),
    trials=2, context=meta.RecentAncestors(max_records=40, max_chars=16_000),
)

Run the equivalent expanded declaration below; we will reuse it to compare feedback on and off.

feedback_experiment = meta.Experiment(
    seed=SEED,
    proposer=propose_with_feedback,
    task=meta.Task(evaluator=evaluate_with_feedback,
                   objectives=(meta.Maximize("score", satisfy=1.0),)),
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=2),
    context=meta.RecentAncestors(max_records=40, max_chars=16_000),
)
feedback_result = meta.run(feedback_experiment)

docs.title: 4. Read the checks and the result
docs.text:
trials() lists the seed followed by each attempted revision. Each entry's evidence contains its recorded observations. The proposal count in usage().trials excludes the seed; usage().evaluations includes its evaluation. These runs make two proposals and three evaluations.

first_attempt = feedback_result.trials()[0]
for case in first_attempt.evidence[0].data["failures"]:
    print(f"{case['input']!r}: expected {case['expected']}, got {case['actual']}")
# Output:
# '2m': expected 120, got 2
# '3m': expected 180, got 3
# '1h': expected 3600, got 1
# '2h': expected 7200, got 2

The seed's minute failures lead to MINUTES. Its remaining hour failures lead to COMPLETE. best_trial() returns the selected attempt and its measurements.

for number, attempt in enumerate(feedback_result.trials()):
    failures = attempt.evidence[0].data["failures"]
    print(f"Version {number}: {attempt.metrics['score']:.0%}; "
          f"failed checks: {len(failures)}")
print(f"Selected score: {feedback_result.best_trial().metrics['score']:.0%}")
# Output:
# Version 0: 33%; failed checks: 4
# Version 1: 67%; failed checks: 2
# Version 2: 100%; failed checks: 0
# Selected score: 100%

The evaluator and cases stayed fixed. The proposer used observations to choose source, and independent evaluation determined whether that choice helped.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Turn feedback off while keeping the same task, seed, proposer, and search. Python's replace copies a declaration with only the named field changed. Predict the score before running:

from dataclasses import replace

without_feedback = meta.run(replace(feedback_experiment, context=None))
print(f"With feedback: {feedback_result.best_trial().metrics['score']:.0%}")
print(f"Without feedback: {without_feedback.best_trial().metrics['score']:.0%}")
print("Evaluations in each run:", feedback_result.usage().evaluations,
      without_feedback.usage().evaluations)
# Output:
# With feedback: 100%
# Without feedback: 33%
# Evaluations in each run: 3 3

Without supplied observations, this proposer returns the seed unchanged twice. The evaluator still records failed checks, but the proposer does not receive them. Both runs evaluate the seed and two proposals. The score difference comes from the explicit rule above; it is not a prediction of model performance or accuracy beyond these six development checks.

docs.title: Why isn't my proposer receiving feedback?
docs.text:
Recording evidence and supplying it are separate steps. Declare a context policy, then read context.evidence.latest(kind) in the proposer. Check .enabled for disabled context and the exact evidence label for an enabled lookup with no match. RecentAncestors favors newer ancestor records; rejected siblings remain outside that ancestry. In this example the bounds retain the full selected history, so the latest failed checks reflect the current parent.

For missing or truncated observations, see the context bounds reference.

For your own task, record actionable observations in the evaluator and adapt the proposer to use them. A model proposer must put the selected observations into its SDK request. Keep the evaluator and budget fixed while comparing feedback on and off. The experience concepts explain what is shared and who controls access.

Next, inspect results and failures to trace what the proposer tried and why a version stayed selected. The experience reference covers other context policies and explicit history inspection; the live parser example shows an SDK request containing development observations.

docs.title: Save and reopen a run
docs.text:
An improvement run contains more than its selected source: it also has earlier versions, measurements, and work counts. Save that history to disk so you can close your notebook, reopen the result, and decide what to reuse. Reopening reads recorded facts; resuming performs compatible unfinished work. Runs and history explains that distinction.

Here, we'll also export the selected parser and use it after the history is closed. The next guide applies the same save/reopen calls to a search comparison.

You want to… Use Save a run as it executes storage= with Storage.durable() Read it after restarting open_run() Reuse the selected source Export best().value

The revisions are handwritten; Python executes and grades them. No model, SDK, or credentials are needed.

Open in Colab · Download the notebook

To run this page: expand the required setup and run its cells in order, then save the run in section 1. Stop and restart the kernel at section 2; continue with only the reopening cell and export cells. Every definition is here; no other page needs to be executed.

Required setup for a fresh notebook

Use a fresh notebook environment running Python 3.12 or newer. Install directly from the published documentation:

%pip install https://sentient-xyz.github.io/meta-evolve-docs/downloads/meta-evolve.zip

If you already imported Meta-Evolve, restart the kernel after installing. Then run the remaining cells in order.

Archived or offline docs: use the ZIP included with that build. Put meta-evolve.zip in the notebook's working folder (%pwd shows it; hosted notebooks let you upload files), then run %pip install ./meta-evolve.zip instead. Installing from source may still download build tools.

Starting source and instructions. SEED reads a duration's number but ignores its unit. CONTRACT tells the proposer what the parser should do.

import meta_evolve as meta

CONTRACT = """Implement parse_seconds(text) for whole-number durations.
Inputs contain a number followed by s, m, or h, such as '30s' or '2h'.
Return the duration in seconds as an integer. Return only Python source.
"""

SEED = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    return int(text[:-1])
'''

Evaluation. evaluate returns the fraction of six checks answered correctly. load_parser executes the source locally; use this evaluator with the reviewed, handwritten code shown here.

CASES = (
    ("30s", 30),
    ("90s", 90),
    ("2m", 120),
    ("3m", 180),
    ("1h", 3600),
    ("2h", 7200),
)


def load_parser(source):
    namespace = {}
    exec(source, namespace)
    return namespace["parse_seconds"]


def evaluate(source):
    parse = load_parser(source)
    passed = 0
    for text, expected in CASES:
        actual = parse(text)
        if type(actual) is int and actual == expected:
            passed += 1
    return passed / len(CASES)


print(f"Starting score: {evaluate(SEED):.0%}")
# Output:
# Starting score: 33%

Revisions. The simulated agent adds minutes support, then hours support.

MINUTES = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    return quantity * 60 if text[-1] == "m" else quantity
'''

COMPLETE = '''def parse_seconds(text):
    quantity = int(text[:-1])
    seconds_per_unit = {"s": 1, "m": 60, "h": 3600}
    return quantity * seconds_per_unit[text[-1]]
'''

Proposer. propose supplies the instructions and current source to the simulated agent. Its response depends on the source, so reruns repeat the same revisions without a hidden response counter.

def agent(message):
    """Simulate source revisions, without a model or a call counter."""
    source = message.rsplit("Current source:\n", 1)[1]
    if source == SEED:
        return MINUTES
    if source in (MINUTES, COMPLETE):
        return COMPLETE
    raise ValueError("This simulation only recognizes the tutorial sources.")


def propose(source):
    message = f"{CONTRACT}\nCurrent source:\n{source}"
    return agent(message)

The Start here walkthrough introduces the starting parser. You can close this section once its cells have run.

docs.title: 1. Run with storage on disk
docs.text:
meta.improve() evaluates the seed, proposes revisions from the best version so far, and evaluates each returned source. Higher scalar scores win by default. trials=2 allows two proposals after the seed evaluation.

By default, the run's history lives in memory. meta.Storage.durable() opens storage on disk. Passing it as storage= records the run there as it executes. The with block keeps storage open for the run and closes it on exit.

Each execution below creates a new folder under runs/. The random suffix keeps earlier runs separate; it does not affect the proposer's choices.

from pathlib import Path
from uuid import uuid4

run_directory = Path("runs") / f"duration-{uuid4().hex[:12]}"
run_directory.mkdir(parents=True)

with meta.Storage.durable(run_directory / "history") as storage:
    saved = meta.improve(
        seed=SEED,
        proposer=propose,
        evaluator=evaluate,
        trials=2,
        storage=storage,
    )
    saved_usage = saved.usage()
    saved_snapshot = saved.summary()

Path("last-duration-run.txt").write_text(str(run_directory), encoding="utf-8")
print("Saved proposal attempts:", saved_usage.trials)
print("Saved evaluations:", saved_usage.evaluations)
saved_snapshot
# Output:
# Saved proposal attempts: 2
# Saved evaluations: 3

The final expression displays the captured report in a notebook, after the storage block has closed. Use print(saved_snapshot) for plain text. Its location describes where history was saved at capture; it does not check that those files still exist. This local callable run is saved but does not declare resume support. A fresh saved.summary() is a storage query and requires an open handle; the next section shows how to reopen history.

usage().trials counts two proposal attempts after the seed; usage().evaluations counts three evaluations, including the seed. The earlier manual evaluate(SEED) preview is outside these counts.

last-duration-run.txt is a small note containing the latest run folder's path. It lets the next cell find that folder after Python variables disappear. Rerunning the saving cell updates the note and keeps earlier run folders. The history holds the recorded artifacts and outcomes, not your notebook's Python variables. Keep these files on persistent disk if your notebook service discards local files when its runtime is deleted.

docs.title: 2. Restart the kernel and reopen
docs.text:
Restart your notebook kernel now, then run the next cell by itself in the same working directory. Meta-Evolve must still be installed. This cell includes all its imports and needs no SEED, proposer, or evaluator definitions.

meta.open_run() opens the only run in this folder for inspection, without proposing or evaluating source. It validates the history before entering the block and closes storage on exit, including on error. An empty store raises RunNotFound; multiple runs raise RunSelectionRequired with available IDs. Pass run_id=... to choose explicitly: content-derived ID order does not tell you which run is newest.

trials() lists the seed and attempted revisions. best_trial() returns the selected attempt and its measurements; best().value gives the selected source string. Read these while the storage handle is open:

from pathlib import Path
import meta_evolve as meta

run_directory = Path(Path("last-duration-run.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
with meta.open_run(run_directory / "history") as reopened:
    for number, attempt in enumerate(reopened.trials()):
        print(f"Version {number}: {attempt.metrics['score']:.0%}")
    selected_source = reopened.best().value
    print(f"Retained score: {reopened.best_trial().metrics['score']:.0%}")
    print("Retained evaluations:", reopened.usage().evaluations)
# Output:
# Version 0: 33%
# Version 1: 67%
# Version 2: 100%
# Retained score: 100%
# Retained evaluations: 3

The same three measurements are still available after the original process exits. Reopening reads recorded results; it does not spend more evaluations or rerun a model. The selected source is now an ordinary string you can use after storage closes. To inspect again, reopen the storage handle as above.

If last-duration-run.txt is missing, check that section 1 completed and that you are in the same working directory. To open an older run, replace the line that reads the note with run_directory = Path("runs/duration-YOUR-SAVED-SUFFIX"), using its actual folder. Its original run ID is still in storage.runs(); reopening does not create one.

Saving local functions does not make the run resumable. Reopen means reading past results; resume means continuing unfinished work and requires reconstructible components. See the durability reference when you need that separate capability.

docs.title: 3. Export and use the selected source
docs.text:
Write the retained source to a normal Python file, then print it for review. Neither writing nor printing source executes it.

export_path = run_directory / "selected.py"
export_path.write_text(selected_source, encoding="utf-8")
print(export_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")
# Output:
# def parse_seconds(text):
#     quantity = int(text[:-1])
#     seconds_per_unit = {"s": 1, "m": 60, "h": 3600}
#     return quantity * seconds_per_unit[text[-1]]

The source is the handwritten COMPLETE revision from the required setup. Load that reviewed file and call its parser. This cell executes the exported code. It needs no live run or open storage handle.

namespace = {}
exec(export_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), namespace)
parse_seconds = namespace["parse_seconds"]
print("4m:", parse_seconds("4m"))
print("2h:", parse_seconds("2h"))
# Output:
# 4m: 240
# 2h: 7200

Keep these pieces according to what you need:

File or folder What it preserves runs/duration-…/history/ The full recorded run: source versions, measurements, lineage, work counts, and any evidence or failures runs/duration-…/selected.py Just the selected source, ready to copy into another project last-duration-run.txt The path used to find the most recently saved run folder

An export does not contain the evaluation history. Keep the whole history/ directory when you want to reopen the run. You can regenerate selected.py from that history by rerunning sections 2 and 3.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
After the restart, rerun the setup definition cells (the installation need not repeat). Keep a note of the earlier run_directory. Change trials=2 to trials=1 in section 1 and predict the retained score and work count. Save another run, restart again, then reopen and export using sections 2 and 3.

The reopened history now has two versions, scoring 33% and 67%, and two evaluations. The exported parser still returns 240 for "4m", but returns 2 for "2h": one proposal added minutes support only. The earlier 100% run remains in its own folder. Reopen that earlier folder using its saved path: its three versions and 100% result are unchanged. A successful example input is not a substitute for the full set of checks.

docs.title: Do I need my original functions to reopen?
docs.text:
No. The reopening cell reads recorded artifacts, measurements, and usage; it needs only the installed package and saved history. It makes no model requests. Continuing unfinished work is a separate operation: local notebook functions are not automatically reconstructible for resume.

For your own experiment, pass durable storage to improve() or run() and keep both its location and run ID. After reopening, use the selected value in the way its type requires; this example exports Python because its artifact is source. Custom artifact values additionally need their codec registry via registry=.

docs.title: Choose a run in a shared store
docs.text:
This optional example saves two small experiments in a separate shared store. Keep the first run's ID as well as its directory so that reopening selects the intended experiment. The parser history and its export remain in their folders.

from pathlib import Path
import meta_evolve as meta

run_directory = Path(Path("last-duration-run.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
with meta.Storage.durable(run_directory / "shared-history") as storage:
    chosen = meta.improve(
        seed=0, proposer=lambda value: value + 1, evaluator=float,
        trials=1, storage=storage,
    )
    meta.improve(
        seed=10, proposer=lambda value: value + 1, evaluator=float,
        trials=1, storage=storage,
    )
(run_directory / "chosen-run.txt").write_text(chosen.id.value, encoding="utf-8")

Restart the kernel again, then run this cell. It reads the ID from the file; neither list position nor score decides which experiment to open.

from pathlib import Path
import meta_evolve as meta

run_directory = Path(Path("last-duration-run.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
chosen_id = (run_directory / "chosen-run.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
with meta.open_run(run_directory / "shared-history", run_id=chosen_id) as reopened:
    chosen_value = reopened.best().value
print("Explicitly selected:", chosen_value)
# Output:
# Explicitly selected: 1

Next, choose what to try next. With evaluation, feedback, and saved history in place, use a small branching example to see when another search strategy helps. The durability reference covers recovery and resume.

docs.title: Build an autoresearch loop with Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
What it does. This autoresearch example improves a recipe for conducting small searches, judging a recipe by the solutions those searches find.

How it works. An outer loop revises the allowed moves for inner number searches. Public results guide revisions, private aggregate scores select a recipe, and held-out tasks check the selection. Tasks and limits stay fixed.

Status: Shipped. Offline; optional next step after your first run.

docs.title: Component worksheet
docs.text:
Question This method What changes? A Text JSON recipe declaring the moves an inner researcher can try. What generates the change? A deterministic proposer follows declared recipe successors using public feedback; each recipe configures the inner number proposer. What judges it? Fixed inner tasks produce private aggregate quality; outer Greedy selects on that metric. What is retained? An outer Run with recipes, public reports, private metrics, derivation, and outer usage. The final held-out report is produced separately.

Inspired by AIDE², this is no reproduction or evidence of recursive self-improvement; promotion is external.

docs.title: The result first
docs.text:
After checkout setup, run this from the repository root:

uv run python examples/research/autoresearch/main.py
Output
autoresearch teaching run: outer=(evaluations=3,trials=2) inner=(evaluations=5,trials=4)
recipe=(1,) public={'public-large': 0.14285714285714285, 'public-small': 0.3333333333333333} private_quality=0.180556
recipe=(1, 2) public={'public-large': 0.2, 'public-small': 1.0} private_quality=0.321429
recipe=(1, 2, 4) public={'public-large': 0.3333333333333333, 'public-small': 0.5} private_quality=0.600000
selected=(1, 2, 4)
held_out_baseline={'held-out-small': 0.16666666666666666, 'held-out-large': 0.09090909090909091}
held_out_selected={'held-out-small': 0.5, 'held-out-large': 0.14285714285714285}
promotion=none

The same results, rounded for comparison:

Moves Public small Public large Private aggregate (1,) 0.333333 0.142857 0.180556 (1, 2) 1.000000 0.200000 0.321429 (1, 2, 4) 0.500000 0.333333 0.600000

The selected recipe regresses on the small public task while improving the private aggregate. Public observations inform proposals; the declared private metric decides selection. These authored cases demonstrate that distinction.

The inspection cells below use lab and result from the optional notebook. The outer evidence contains public per-task reports:

[
    (str(trial.artifact.value), tuple(item.kind for item in trial.evidence))
    for trial in result.trials()
    if trial.artifact is not None
]
Output
[('{"moves":[1]}', ('autoresearch-public-report',)),
 ('{"moves":[1,2]}', ('autoresearch-public-report',)),
 ('{"moves":[1,2,4]}', ('autoresearch-public-report',))]

docs.title: The two levels
docs.text:
“Inner” and “outer” describe which thing is being improved:

outer Meta-Evolve run
│
├─ artifact: a recipe for conducting inner research
├─ proposer: one declared recipe revision
├─ evaluator: fixed tasks and budget ceilings
└─ search: select using private aggregate quality
       │
       ├─ inner run on public task A
       ├─ inner run on public task B
       ├─ inner run on private task A
       └─ inner run on private task B

report(result), after outer selection
├─ seed researcher on held-out tasks
├─ selected researcher on the same held-out tasks
└─ report the comparison; promote nothing

An inner run searches for an integer near a target. The recipe determines its move sequence: (1,) takes single steps; (1, 2, 4) tries larger jumps within the same four-proposal ceiling. All outer attempts remain recorded.

In meta-evolution notation, the recipe is θ, the bounded researcher is Iθ, and private aggregation is E_outer. Replace the integer task with your domain and its independent checks.

docs.title: The five Meta-Evolve declarations
docs.text:
The canonical module's run_outer uses the ordinary public API:

main.py · run_outer
def run_outer() -> meta.Run:
    """Optimize the inner researcher under evaluator-owned selection."""

    experiment = meta.Experiment(
        task=meta.Task(
            evaluator=evaluate_researcher,
            artifact=meta.Text,
            objectives=(meta.Maximize("private_quality"),),
            budget=OUTER_BUDGET,
        ),
        seed=SEED,
        proposer=propose_researcher,
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=OUTER_TRIALS),
        context=meta.AncestorsOnly(max_records=CONTEXT_RECORDS),
        random_seed=0,
    )
    return meta.run(experiment)

Read it as a sentence: Task fixes evaluation and limits; SEED is the starting recipe; propose_researcher proposes a successor; Greedy selects by private quality; and AncestorsOnly supplies authorized parent-lineage records.

The outer run records candidates, metrics, hypotheses, evidence, derivation references, and outer usage. Its proposer filters the supplied records for public reports; the raw trusted context also contains private aggregate metrics.

docs.title: The candidate-controlled surface
docs.text:
The complete mutable artifact is tiny JSON:

{"moves":[1,2,4]}

decode permits only the moves key, one to four integer moves, and values between 1 and 8. An invalid recipe produces a typed InvalidOutput with no metric, so malformed output can never outrank a valid researcher.

import meta_evolve as meta

outcome = lab["evaluate_researcher"](meta.Text('{"moves":[0]}'))
print("failure:", type(outcome.failure).__name__)
print("metrics:", dict(outcome.metrics))
Output
failure: InvalidOutput
metrics: {}

The declared owners are:

Control Owner Move recipe Candidate Public, private, and held-out tasks Evaluator Inner and outer budgets Experiment private_quality calculation Evaluator Greedy admission Search policy Whether a winner is deployed Governance / user

These are in-process Python fixtures. Candidate data is validated; actual execution isolation is a separate authority boundary.

docs.title: One candidate evaluation
docs.text:
evaluate_researcher first validates the recipe. It then performs four inner runs under the same protocol and budget ceilings. Each task has its own target, and the recipe changes proposal behavior. The source is extracted here:

main.py · evaluate_researcher
def evaluate_researcher(candidate: meta.Text) -> EvaluationResult:
    """Select on private quality while exposing only public task traces."""

    try:
        researcher = decode(candidate)
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError) as error:
        return EvaluationResult(failure=InvalidOutput(message=str(error)))
    public = score(researcher, PUBLIC_TASKS)
    private = score(researcher, PRIVATE_TASKS)
    return EvaluationResult(
        metrics={"private_quality": fmean(private.values())},
        evidence=(
            EvidenceDraft(
                kind=PUBLIC_REPORT,
                data={"scores": public, "inner_trials_per_task": INNER_TRIALS},
            ),
        ),
    )

Public per-task outcomes become inspectable evidence. Private task names, targets, and per-task outcomes are not placed in evidence. The outer search policy uses their aggregate metric for selection.

The deterministic proposer extracts only autoresearch-public-report records. Its ProposalResult.derived_from points to the report it used. That records the declared basis of the revision; a citation alone does not prove benefit.

score() reduces each in-memory inner run to a quality value. The outer report does not retain reopenable inner IDs, full inner histories, or captured partial episode outcomes. The policy example shows those additional retention choices.

docs.title: Exact budget arithmetic
docs.text:
The seed and two successors give the outer run:

3 outer evaluations = 1 seed + 2 proposals
2 outer trials      = 2 proposals

Each outer evaluation runs four tasks. Each permits the seed plus four inner proposals, but stops early if it reaches the target:

5 inner evaluations per task
× 4 tasks per outer evaluation
× 3 outer evaluations
= 60 inner evaluations used for selection at most

After selection, the seed and winner each run on two held-out tasks:

5 × 2 recipes × 2 held-out tasks = 20 post-selection evaluations at most

These are ceilings, not equal consumed work. The outer budget counts outer evaluations; this evaluator does not forward inner usage in EvaluationResult. Outer usage therefore does not measure total nested cost. An adaptation that needs physical cost comparisons must explicitly report that usage.

report(result) performs the held-out executions and formats their scores. They are not attached to the original outer Run; calling report() again executes them again. Keep a final comparison separate from further search.

docs.title: Why three task splits?
docs.text:
The public tasks provide feedback for proposing the next researcher. The private aggregate decides which recipe is selected. Held-out tasks are touched only after the search has selected a winner.

Split Candidate model may see details? Affects selection? Public Yes Indirectly, through proposals Private No Yes, through aggregate quality Held-out No during search No

If the outer model sees private targets or per-task results, “private” is only a label. If held-out results influence another proposal, those tasks have become part of development and a new untouched suite is required.

docs.title: Replacing the deterministic proposer with an agent
docs.text:
The deterministic proposer keeps CI credential-free. A model-backed wrapper should preserve this boundary:

ProposerContext → allowlisted public evidence → private workspace
  → one bounded agent session → validated ProposalResult
  → derived_from references and usage

Do not give the model raw outer context because it contains the aggregate private metric needed by trusted search. Build an allowlisted workspace. The prompt-optimization example shows how a callable outer proposer can run a bounded source-tree agent one level down and lift the result back into meta.Text.

For a source-code researcher, change the artifact to meta.SourceTree, use an exact mutation allowlist, and evaluate each candidate in a fresh workspace. Keep benchmark source, credentials, permissions, and promotion controls outside that tree.

docs.title: What the comparison may claim
docs.text:
Under these toy tasks and equal inner budget ceilings, the selected recipe has higher private and held-out quality than the seed.
