def sweep(shape, make_components, adir):
    """Crash after EVERY committed boundary K; resume each; return (#boundaries,
    all-equivalent?, best, #mid-attempt-rollforwards)."""
    ref_components = make_components()
    ref = shape(meta.Storage.durable(adir / 'ref'), ref_components)
    rid, best = ref.id, ref.best().value
    ev = meta.Storage.durable(adir / 'ref').events.read(rid)
    total = n_batches(shape, make_components)
    all_ok, rollfwd = True, 0
    for k in range(1, total):
        p = adir / f'k{k}'
        # Install and run on one handle; resume from a freshly opened handle.
        s = meta.Storage.durable(p)
        install_crash(s, n=k)
        try:
            shape(s, make_components())
        except CRASH:
            pass
        crashed = meta.Storage.durable(p).events.read(rid)
        if crashed and isinstance(crashed[-1].body, ExperienceOperationAttempted):
            if replay_run_projection(rid, crashed).resolution_for(crashed[-1].body.operation_id) is None:
                rollfwd += 1
        registry = make_components().registry
        r = meta.resume(rid, storage=meta.Storage.durable(p), registry=registry)
        if not (r.best().value == best and meta.Storage.durable(p).events.read(rid) == ev):
            all_ok = False
    return rid, ev, total - 1, all_ok, best, rollfwd

docs.title: Crash recovery for durable runs (meta.resume)¶
docs.text:
The central promise of a durable Meta-Evolve run: a process that dies partway through loses no committed work, and once resume-d reaches the exact result an uninterrupted run would have reached.

Interrupted is logically equivalent to uninterrupted.

This notebook walks the lifecycle end to end:

  1. Run a durable-local run to completion, uninterrupted, on path A — its best() is the reference.
  2. Start the same run on path B, but simulate a process crash after a few committed batches.
  3. Reopen path B and resume the run.
  4. Assert the resumed best() equals the uninterrupted reference.

Key concepts: atomic batch commits (a crash leaves only whole batches, never a half-written one), the recovery frontier (resume replays the committed prefix and continues deterministically from the last decided step), and deterministic run identity (the run id is derived from the inputs, so the run on path B shares path A's id and resume can address it).

docs.title: Components — imported from the example module¶
docs.text: durable-local mode requires registered, source-digestible, module-level functions so resume can verify the components it replays are byte-for-byte the ones recorded. Functions defined inside a notebook cell have no resolvable source file, so durable-local would reject them (CapabilityError). We therefore import the real components from examples/operations/crash_recovery/main.py (an importable module) and show their source below — the notebook orchestrates the lifecycle with the example's own building blocks.

docs.title: Simulating a crash — you never write this¶
docs.text:
A real crash (power loss, kill -9, OOM) needs no code; the OS/hardware supplies it. CrashAfter exists only so a deterministic notebook can stand in for one — in production you never author it or touch storage._commit_strategy.

A faithful crash never truncates the append-only store: it just stops committing after some whole batch n, so the n committed batches on disk are exactly what an uninterrupted run would have written, with no partial batch.

docs.title: (1) Uninterrupted reference run on path A¶
docs.text: A counting wrapper with an unreachable threshold rides along to tally path A's own committed batches.

docs.title: (2) Start the same run on path B — then crash mid-way¶
docs.text: The run id matches path A's by construction, so we can resume it by id.

docs.title: (3) Reopen path B and resume(run_id, ...)¶
docs.text: No crash wrapper this time — a fresh durable handle on the same path, exactly as a restarted process would.

docs.title: Advanced examples¶
docs.text: The basic lifecycle resumed from a single mid-run crash. These show the guarantee is total — resume works from every committed boundary — and extends to M3 policy-pushed context and pull experience. All components come from main.py / advanced.py (importable + source-digestible, as durable-local requires).

docs.title: A. Fault matrix — resume from every committed boundary¶
docs.text: Crash after each batch K in turn; each resume reaches the identical best() and a byte-identical final stream.

docs.title: B. The recovery frontier¶
docs.text: resume classifies where the crash left the run (via classify_frontier) before continuing deterministically. The phases seen across boundaries:

docs.title: C. Cold rebuild from empty tables¶
docs.text: A fresh process reopens the durable store; the read model is rebuilt purely from the committed event log — no in-memory state carried over.

docs.title: D. Resumable with M3 policy-pushed context (AncestorsOnly)¶
docs.text: The run records a context-policy manifest, its declaration, and each per-trial selection. resume rebuilds the context policy from the registry and reuses the committed selections — equivalent at every boundary.

docs.title: E. Resumable with M3 pull experience (PullAccess)¶
docs.text: Here the proposer reads experience each step, audited as an attempt then a resolution (two atomic batches). A crash between them leaves a trailing unresolved attempt; resume rolls it forward — recomputing the resolution and reusing the committed operation id — to a byte-identical stream.

docs.title: F. Resume is safe to re-run¶
docs.text: Resuming an already-complete run is a no-op returning the same result. (Two processes racing to resume one crashed run is also safe: exactly one commits and the other gets EventStreamConflict — never a double-commit or partial write. See tests/test_resume_faults.py.)

docs.title: Milestone 5 tour: immutable source, external evidence¶
docs.text: This tour follows the canonical clamp repair in six small steps. The declaration path stays at source, patch, evaluator, budget, and search vocabulary. Returned lineage entries provide optional inspection after the run.

docs.title: 1. Load immutable source¶
docs.text: The source tree contains exact UTF-8 text. The tour stages only the declared tracked candidate/clamp.py bytes into its temporary evidence directory before loading. This isolates the tour from checkout-generated __pycache__ without adding ignore rules: production load_source_tree still rejects every undeclared file.

docs.title: 2. Declare the exact-file repair¶
docs.text: The patch names one file, commits the parent text it expects, and supplies its replacement. A conflict, invalid path, or unchanged replacement is a typed proposal outcome.

docs.title: 3. Declare the independent evaluator¶
docs.text: The grader remains outside the candidate tree, and the fixed run_grader.py owns the exit protocol: exit 0 passes, exit 1 is a rankable task failure, and any other exit is a typed evaluator failure.

docs.title: 4. Declare one budget¶
docs.text: Two evaluations cover the broken seed and one successor. The same budget is passed to the task and run.

docs.title: 5. Run one local Greedy step¶
docs.text: Proposal and evaluation each receive a fresh workspace. Durable storage retains the committed history, while the live local callbacks remain non-portable.

docs.title: 6. Inspect the result and durable boundary¶
docs.text: The public lineage query is progressive disclosure: it returns immutable lineage entries for inspection without putting kernel construction types into the declaration story. Content digests and semantic outcomes are deterministic; observed process wall time is intentionally omitted.

docs.title: Failure boundary: a broken grader is not a low score¶
docs.text: Candidate-caused breakage remains the rankable score 0 seen above. This separate probe removes the grader itself: runner exit 2 becomes EvaluatorFailure, with no metric to rank.

docs.text: SealQA question: Who holds the all-time record at the Grammys for the most wins in the album of the year category?

docs.title: What changes¶
docs.text: Only the solver prompt changes. The frozen question and documents, hidden exact answer, declarations, and evaluator remain outside candidate authority. The path is two initial solves, one structured comparison, one feedback-derived edit, and one edited-prompt solve: 5 live sessions.

docs.title: Live declaration¶
docs.text: Bring your own user-owned SDK wrapper and identify its behavior-affecting declaration. Set META_EVOLVE_LIVE_SDK=1 only after authenticating it and reviewing its session, tool, permission, and spending limits. Every inner run declares INNER_BUDGET.wall_seconds = 1860; the wrapper must honor that bound or refuse preflight. These calls may incur cost.

docs.title: Visible record¶
docs.text: The next cell exposes prompt artifacts, the preferred candidate, textual feedback, edit lineage, typed failures, exact-answer measurements, and aggregate usage. Malformed comparison output, a missing edit, timeout, or provider failure has no metric.

docs.title: Live observation¶
docs.text: No official provider capture is pending. A user may perform one authorized run with a declared wrapper. Any published capture must keep the single outcome—including a tie, regression, or typed failure—and sanitize credentials without rerunning for improvement.

docs.title: Audit and exercise¶
docs.text:
• Did the editor see only the preferred prompt and textual feedback?
  • Did the evaluator-only answer enter any solver or editor request?
  • Is one edited evaluation enough to claim a robust improvement?

docs.title: Autoresearch, in miniature¶
docs.text: Can an outer Meta-Evolve run improve the recipe used by an inner researcher while private tasks, budgets, and promotion remain outside candidate authority? This notebook executes the deterministic teaching example. The standalone chapter contains the complete explanation.

docs.title: Run the outer loop¶
docs.text: The seed and two successors each receive the same four inner benchmark tasks and the same five-evaluation inner budget. Public task scores are evidence; private quality is the selection metric.

docs.title: Read the evidence boundary¶
docs.text: The proposer derives each edit from a public-report evidence record. Private task details never enter that evidence. Held-out scores are calculated only after result.best() has fixed the selected recipe, and promotion=none is explicit.

docs.title: Change and predict¶
docs.text: Reduce INNER_TRIALS from four to two and update INNER_BUDGET. Predict the selected recipe first. If it changes, did the researcher become worse, or did the evaluation choose a different researcher for a different resource regime?

docs.title: ACE: improve an agent's playbook¶
docs.text:
What it does. ACE improves reusable instructions one rule at a time, preserving useful entries while correcting, retiring, or adding others.

How it works. A Generator attempts a task, a Reflector extracts lessons, and a Curator edits the playbook. Later attempts use the revised rules.

In this example. A financial-tagging agent starts with the wrong interest convention and no lease convention. Follow two revisions, inspect the changed rules, and check the final playbook on fresh disclosures.

The saved outputs come from deterministic Python agents. No credentials or model calls are needed. This is a mechanism demonstration inspired by ACE, with authored lessons and curation.

docs.title: Components of the loop¶
docs.text:
Role Here Artifact A JSON playbook with an identity, section, rule, and status for each entry Proposer revise(lessons) amends and retires entries, then adds a missing rule Evaluator playbook_suite(agent) checks answers against fixed company conventions Search Greedy evaluates the seed and tries two revisions on the private split Result Selected rules, revision history, consolidation checks, and held-out answers

Attempt → lesson → edit a rule → check a fresh task.

Download notebook · Complete source · Display helpers

Seven cells take you through the study and a small exercise. The page and notebook share the same cells and recorded outputs. Setup downloads the library and a checksum-verified example archive; subsequent cells run locally.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the example¶
docs.text: Use a Python 3.12+ Jupyter kernel on macOS or Linux. Run these cells in order, or copy them into an empty notebook. Setup needs internet access; a checkout and companion-file uploads are unnecessary.

docs.title: 2. Read the starting playbook¶
docs.text: Northwind uses its own taxonomy elements for cash interest and operating leases. The starting manual names the generic interest element and an unsupported scaling rule. It says nothing about leases. These are the instructions we will improve; the agent and the grading rules stay fixed.

docs.title: 3. Learn from the missed answers¶
docs.text:
study_playbook runs development → private search → consolidation → held out once, in that order. Its search declaration uses an ordinary meta.Experiment with a bounded Greedy policy. The remaining displays read this study; they do not rerun phases.

First, inspect the seed's two development answers. The fixture follows the conventions it is given. Python publishes the authored lesson for each completed wrong answer; only these development lessons reach the curator.

docs.title: 4. Follow the two revisions¶
docs.text:
The first proposal amends the interest rule and retires the unsupported scale entry. The next adds the lease rule. Each version answers two differently worded private disclosures; Greedy keeps the best measured playbook and stops at 100%. Private answers and held-out tasks never enter the published development lessons.

The table reports those private scores. The diffs below it show the actual rule text, keyed by the same entry identities throughout the run.

docs.title: 5. Keep a smaller playbook¶
docs.text: Retirement stops an entry being included in the agent's instructions while keeping it in the candidate's record. After selection, consolidation proposes removing retired entries and independently checks both versions on the private split. Here the checks are neutral, so the pruned playbook is accepted. Earlier versions still contain the retired entry.

docs.title: 6. Check fresh disclosures¶
docs.text: The accepted playbook now tags the held-out borrowings and right-of-use notes. These tasks were evaluated only after selection and consolidation. This reports final behavior on two authored cases; it is not a held-out before/after comparison or a claim about benchmark gains.

docs.title: 7. Change a lesson and predict the edit¶
docs.text: Give the curator a different interest convention. Before running the cell, predict whether it amends the existing entry or appends a conflicting one. This is a local proposal exercise: it shows the edit without evaluating or replacing the study's selected playbook.

docs.title: Reading the evidence¶
docs.text:
The saved private scores progress from 0% → 50% → 100%. The corrected interest entry keeps its identity, the scale entry is retired before being pruned, and a new lease entry supplies the missing convention.

The paper's Generator / Reflector / Curator system uses learned reflection and incremental context updates. Here Python supplies the lessons and edits. Learned reflection, semantic retrieval/deduplication, helpful/harmful counters, and online adaptation are outside this demonstration.

Identity, authority, and saved runs

Entries retain their logical identities across amendments and retirement. Canonical JSON gives equal playbooks equal bytes. The curator declares its development lessons; the evaluator declares its fixed agent, split membership, and budgets. Candidates control only playbook content.

The notebook uses in-memory storage. Passing storage=meta.Storage.durable(path) to study_playbook saves the outer search for reopening. Development, consolidation, and held-out outcomes remain on the returned study; they are not persisted or resumable phases. See the storage contract.

Failures remain different from wrong answers Outcome Meaning invalid The candidate is not a valid playbook or transition wrapper-failed The agent did not produce a usable answer unverifiable The target needed for checking is absent infrastructure-failed A timeout or infrastructure fault prevented measurement

A completed wrong answer scores zero. These failures carry no rankable score. An incomplete split refuses an aggregate rather than averaging its successful rollouts. All phases retain their failures and reported usage; focused failure tests exercise these boundaries.

For the script, run uv run python examples/research/context_evolution/main.py --sibling ace from a checkout. The example README covers the source layout, fixture command, and InnerAgent boundary for your own SDK. Browse the source to inspect each stage.

For a smaller introduction, improve a support agent's playbook with six tickets and one revision per recorded mistake.

EvoSkill notebook · Feedback Descent · Explore examples

docs.title: EvoSkill: teach an agent a reusable skill
EvoSkill: teach an agent a reusable skill¶
docs.text:
What it does. EvoSkill discovers reusable skills from an agent's failures, keeping the underlying model fixed.

How it works. An executor attempts tasks; a proposer diagnoses failures and suggests skills; a generator writes the skill folders. New folders are evaluated before selection. The paper retains a Pareto frontier using validation performance.

In this example. Watch three Claude agents answer OfficeQA questions, propose and build a native SKILL.md, then retry a missed question. This small adaptation uses Population(size=3) and a final held-out comparison; it does not reproduce the paper's search or benchmark results.

Experimental/live-only.

Role Here Artifact A folder of reusable skill files Proposer revise: diagnose failures, propose a skill, then build its files Evaluator evaluate: run the executor and apply the independent OfficeQA scorer Search Population chooses which folder to revise next Result Selected skills, candidate history, SDK receipts, and held-out comparison

Run one cell at a time. The first six code cells show the agent workflow; the last two run the longer search and held-out check. Setup fetches two readable Python helpers and pinned data automatically. Use a Python 3.12+ kernel with pip on macOS or Linux, authenticated with claude auth login or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Run All makes at most 25 paid SDK calls and can take tens of minutes.

Download notebook · SDK options and callable · Grading and folder helpers

For the script, install examples/research/evoskill/requirements.txt and run uv run --no-sync python examples/research/evoskill/main.py.

Saved live run: 2026-09-21, Claude SDK 0.2.156. Outputs below are captured agent responses; rerunning makes new paid calls. The capture used 25 SDK calls over 35 minutes, with an SDK cost estimate of $3.19. The final notebook was verified by replaying these same responses: all prompts, scores and selected skill bytes matched.

docs.title: Components: three callable agents¶
docs.text:
executor(task) returns an Answer; proposer(feedback) returns a SkillProposal. Both use the Claude SDK's native JSON-schema outputs. The generator loads the fixed skill-builder skill and writes a real SKILL.md.

The options include setting_sources=["project"] and add_dirs=[skill_repo, ...]: the added repository contains .claude/skills/. Each call starts a fresh session so the next executor discovers newly written skills.

docs.title: 1. Ask Haiku and inspect the answers¶
docs.text:
All three questions ask for millions of nominal dollars:

  • UID0003 — Monthly sum: total national-defense expenditures across the twelve months of 1953.
  • UID0012 — Department total: spending by the highest-spending federal department in fiscal 1955.
  • UID0045 — Country lookup: total U.S. claims in 1997 on the country formerly called Zaire.

The table shows each answer beside OfficeQA's ground truth; expand a trace to inspect the actual tool calls. Only final_answer reaches the official scorer. Its explanation stays separate.

One explicit task clarification: UID0003 names Table 2 of the February 1954 Treasury Bulletin. Tables 2 and 3 print conflicting monthly values; the official answer matches Table 2. The original question and this addition are recorded. The gold answer and official scorer are unchanged.

docs.title: 2. Propose a skill from the failed traces¶
docs.text: Sonnet receives the missed answers and their observable traces, without the gold answers. Its structured output is just a name and a high-level description. If every answer passes, the next three cells skip the unnecessary revision.

docs.title: 3. Build the proposed skill¶
docs.text: The generator invokes its initialized skill-builder, then writes the proposed folder. Inspect the rendered skill below. The expandable trace shows that the builder was actually invoked; generated_skills validates what changed.

docs.title: Treasury Bulletin table lookup¶
docs.text: Use with Read, Glob and Grep only. Do the arithmetic by hand and show it briefly.

docs.title: 1. Parse the question first¶
docs.text:
Write down, before searching:

  • Entity (agency, department, fund, security type, account).
  • Measure (receipts, outlays, debt, holdings, yield, and so on).
  • Period: year, month, quarter, and whether it is fiscal or calendar.
  • Requested units (millions, billions, percent) and any calculation (sum, difference, change, percent change, average).

docs.title: 2. Find the table and edition¶
docs.text:
1. Grep for the table title or distinctive row labels, such as the entity name, "Table OFS-1", "FFO-", or "Budget Receipts and Outlays". Use several synonyms. OCR often breaks words or case.
  2. List the candidate files with Glob. Identify each file's edition (month and year) from its header or filename.
  3. Pick the edition by these rules:
    • Data for a period normally appears in the edition published shortly after it. Fiscal year-end data usually appears in the September or December edition, or a later edition that carries annual tables.
    • If several editions report the same figure, prefer the most recent edition. It has revisions. Use an earlier edition only if the question names it, or if it is the only one that shows the figure.
    • For a historical annual series, check the table that lists that year as a column or row. Do not assume the edition year equals the data year.
  4. Read the table's title, subtitle, units line ("In millions of dollars") and footnotes. Do this before reading any numbers.

docs.title: 3. Read the right cell¶
docs.text:
• Wide tables are often split into blocks (part 1 with columns A–F, part 2 with columns G–L), or the header line is shifted from the data lines. Count the columns.
    • Count the number of values in the row. Compare that with the number of header names. Align from the right edge for totals and from the left edge for labels.
    • If a header cell is empty or unnamed, check whether it belongs to a spanning header, such as a department that has sub-columns. Check the neighbouring rows and the total column. Sub-columns plus the remainder should sum to the total.
    • Verify the alignment with a check. Pick a row whose total is known and confirm that the parts add up to it. If they do not, shift the alignment by one and retest.
  • Department subtotals: a department may appear as a total row followed by indented component rows, or as a group of columns. Take the row or column the question names. Do not double-count the subtotal and its components when summing.
  • Footnote markers (1/, (a), *, r, p, e) that are attached to numbers are not digits. "r" means revised and "p" means preliminary. Strip the marker, but note it.
  • Read negatives written as parentheses or minus signs, and dashes or "*" for zero or less than 0.5 unit. Watch for OCR errors: "O" and "0", "l" and "1", a missing decimal point, or commas replaced by periods. Flag a value that breaks the pattern of its row or column.
  • Confirm that the period label matches (for example the "Fiscal year" versus the "Calendar year" columns, or the month columns at the right of the table).

docs.title: 4. Units and periods¶
docs.text:
• Convert only when the question asks for different units. Millions to billions: divide by 1,000. Say which conversion you applied.
  • Fiscal year (US federal): October to September. Calendar year: January to December. If the table gives a fiscal-year figure and the question asks for calendar year (or the reverse), find a table that gives the correct basis. Otherwise state the assumption.
  • Percent versus percentage points. Rounding: report to the precision the question asks for. If none is stated, use the table's precision, or two decimals for a computed ratio.

docs.title: 5. Cross-check (do at least one)¶
docs.text:
• Find the same figure in a second table in the same edition (for example a summary table versus a detail table), or in the next edition, and compare. Explain any difference by revision, or by a definitional difference.
  • Check that components add to the reported total.
  • Sanity-check the magnitude against neighbouring years or rows.

docs.title: 6. Compute¶
docs.text: Show the formula with the numbers you read, and do the arithmetic step by step. Re-add or re-divide once to check it.

docs.title: 7. Final answer¶
docs.text:
Give:

  • The plain number in the requested units, with no footnote markers, and with commas only if they are natural. Include the unit (for example "$12,345 million") when it is unambiguous.
  • One line naming the entity, the table (title and number), the edition (month and year), and the row and column used. Add a note if you made an assumption or the editions differ.

Stop when the answer has been read from the right cell, cross-checked, and stated. If the data truly are absent from every edition you can find, say so and give the closest available figure, labelled as such. Do not guess.

docs.title: 4. Retry a missed question¶
docs.text: This is another ordinary executor call. It discovers the new skill from disk. Compare the answers and inspect whether the skill was used. A retry can still miss: creating a skill does not establish that it helps.

docs.title: 5. Continue with a population of three¶
docs.text:
Longer step. seed is the folder just generated, captured as a path-to-text dictionary. No SkillSet is needed; snapshots are validated with SourceTree. Two small callbacks repeat the calls above for whichever parent the search selects.

Here proposer names the inner agent that proposes a skill plan. The outer revise function combines that call with generator, which builds the files. Meta-Evolve receives the complete workflow as proposer=revise; search chooses the parent folder, and revise decides how to change it.

The search grades that seed on all three development questions and tries up to two further revisions. Population(size=3) retains up to three folders, selecting parents through tournaments of two. A perfect score stops early. The final table shows each candidate's parent, score and frontier membership, including regressions. Wrong answers score zero; failed SDK calls or grading remain unrankable failures.

docs.title: 6. Check three held-out questions¶
docs.text: Compare the original empty folder and the selected folder on UID0001 (1940 defense spending), UID0002 (1934 Veterans Administration spending), and UID0006 (largest country's claims in 1995). Their answers never go to the proposer. Both versions search the same nine Treasury documents with the same Haiku agent and scorer. The tables show exactly which questions each version solved.

This is a bounded live adaptation of Meta-Harness, Algorithm 1: agent diagnosis uses prior harness behavior, followed by independent evaluation. The paper searches executable harness programs and returns a Pareto frontier. This lesson changes planner/context settings under Greedy search and adds private selection.

The deterministic reference retains the full M8 audit, confinement, source-citation and replay study. The introductory help assistant is a credential-free first step. See the harness contract and Claude SDK reference.

docs.title: Meta-Harness: teach an agent to repair better¶
docs.text:
What it does. Meta-Harness improves the program around a fixed model: the harness that controls its work and context.

How it works. A proposer inspects previous harness code, scores and execution traces, writes a revised harness, and evaluates it on tasks. The paper searches executable harness programs and returns a Pareto frontier.

In this example. A Claude repair worker edits Python. A separate agent reads development evidence and revises only its planner instructions or access to the repository contract. Greedy search, private selection and a held-out comparison measure those changes through fresh repairs and independent checks.

Experimental/live-only. Offline rehearsals verify execution and accounting; saved live model outputs are still pending. See the verification record.

Role Here Artifact The worker's planner text and context setting Proposer revise: diagnose development evidence and return a typed harness edit Evaluator evaluate: run the worker, then independently check its repaired code Search Greedy tries two revisions; private checks select the final harness Result Harness and repair diffs, phase histories, receipts, and held-out comparison

The harness is the candidate. A repair is the worker's output used to judge that candidate. The worker model, tests and budgets remain fixed.

Repair → test → revise the harness → repair again.

Seven cells take you from a starting harness to an independently checked selection. Both agents use the Claude Agent SDK. This small study uses four authored repository contracts; its results demonstrate the mechanism, not benchmark gains.

Download notebook · Complete source · SDK helper

docs.title: 1. Prepare a fresh workspace¶
docs.text:
Use a local Jupyter kernel with Python 3.12+ on macOS or Linux. Authenticate with claude auth login in a terminal, or supply ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to the kernel's environment. Run the cells below in order; the same cells can be copied from this page into an empty notebook. No checkout, earlier lesson, or companion-file upload is needed. Setup downloads the matching library and verifies the support archive.

The launch check must pass before any agent call. It needs working sandbox-exec on macOS or Landlock ABI 3+ on Linux; hosted notebook environments are unverified. If an enclosing sandbox prevents launch, use a supported local terminal/kernel.

docs.title: 2. Components of the harness¶
docs.text:
The starting worker sees the issue and solution.py. Setting include_spec=True also gives it the repository's contract.md. Planner text changes how it approaches the repair. Both are typed mutation surfaces; model, tools, tests and budgets stay outside the candidate. Each worker gets a fresh SDK session with Read, Edit and Write restricted to its files. The proposer can read its supplied evidence only.

The development issues concern ledger amounts and customer labels. For example, the ledger contract defines parentheses as a negative amount and an em dash as zero. A context change makes that contract available; the worker must still write working code, which the independent checks measure.

docs.title: 3. Measure the worker's actual repairs¶
docs.text:
repair asks the SDK worker to edit a real file, captures it, and runs it in a confined Python process. The evaluator compares its answers with fixed expectations in the parent process. Each task has four checks; quality is the fraction passed. The table appears as each harness is evaluated in cell 5.

The worker receives neither the hidden expected answers nor later tasks. A completed wrong answer or task exception fails a check. Invalid Python, timeouts, SDK errors and infrastructure failures are retained as unrankable outcomes. Unknown SDK usage stops the run and keeps its receipt.

docs.title: 4. Let an agent diagnose one change¶
docs.text: The selected development evidence contains the parent harness, its repaired source, pass/fail checks, and observable SDK traces. The proposer reads those files through the SDK and returns a structured HarnessEdit. The helper validates the declared surface, preserves the diagnosis and prediction, and cites the supplied evidence. Private and held-out observations never enter this workspace.

docs.title: 5. Try two revisions¶
docs.text:
This cell evaluates the seed and makes at most two proposed revisions. Greedy selection retains the highest development score, favoring the earlier occurrence on a tie. Both attempts stay visible even when they fail or do not improve quality.

Live calls begin here. Run All makes at most 13 SDK calls across all phases. Each session allows eight turns and $0.35 of SDK-estimated cost. Allow several minutes; progress and check tables appear as calls finish. Billed spend is unknown.

docs.title: 6. Follow the evidence¶
docs.text: Read the harness change, then expand a repair to see the actual code diff and its checks. Worker traces are available beneath each repair. This cell reads retained results and makes no model calls; it is safe to rerun.

docs.title: 7. Check fresh tasks and keep the result¶
docs.text:
Every rankable development occurrence receives the same private warehouse counts task. The highest score wins; ties favor the earliest occurrence. This can overturn the development winner. The selection is written to disk before the untouched shipping priorities task runs once for the original seed and once for the selected harness, with identical model and limits.

Only a strict held-out improvement exports selected-harness. Ties, regressions, failures, and a selection that keeps the seed are valid results. The report includes usage from every phase and reconciles tokens against the saved SDK receipts.

"""Compare two workers and take the less loaded one.

Two probes per task instead of one per worker. Most of the balance for a small

def choose(cluster, size):
    first = cluster.pick()
    second = cluster.pick()
    if second == first:
        second = (first + 1) % cluster.size
    return first if cluster.load(first) <= cluster.load(second) else second

docs.title: Improve a scheduler¶
docs.text:
Jobs of different sizes arrive at a group of workers. Where should each job go? Our starting program takes turns: worker 0, worker 1, and so on. That is cheap, but when large jobs arrive at regular intervals, the same workers get overloaded.

Try a small change: look at two workers and choose the less busy one. Here, load() asks for a worker's current load: one probe.

def choose(cluster, size):
    first = cluster.pick()
    second = cluster.pick()
    if second == first:
        second = (first + 1) % cluster.size
    return first if cluster.load(first) <= cluster.load(second) else second

The fixed simulator runs this Python code on development workloads:

Program Load imbalance ↓ Probes per job ↓ Quality ↑ Starting round-robin 0.2071 0 0.7929 Inspect every worker 0.0381 7 0.8219 Inspect two workers 0.0464 2 0.9136

Two probes buy much better balance than the starting program. Inspecting every worker balances jobs a little better, but takes seven probes per job here. The two-worker program offers the better tradeoff under the fixed score: quality = max(0, 1 - imbalance - 0.02 * probes_per_job). Imbalance is zero for an even distribution and one when a single worker gets everything. These measurements describe this simulator, not hardware speed.

The proposer tries handwritten revisions, including mistakes; the simulator measures them.

docs.title: Run it in Jupyter¶
docs.text:
Use a fresh Jupyter kernel with Python 3.12 or newer, on macOS with usable sandbox-exec, or Linux with usable Landlock ABI 3+. The runtime must allow confined child processes. The third cell checks that they really work before the study starts. Hosted notebooks, including Colab, are not verified here.

Save the notebook in an ordinary project folder, outside your Python installation and, on Linux, outside /tmp, /var/tmp, /usr, and other system directories. Its downloaded code needs a protected location; temporary execution workspaces are created separately. No model key, GPU, or repository checkout is needed.

Run these four cells in order. Installation and download use the same published documentation build. An archived copy also works: put its meta-evolve.zip and systems-example.zip beside the notebook; the cells find them automatically. Installation may download build tools. Restart the kernel first if you have already imported Meta-Evolve or this example.

docs.title: 3. Check this runtime¶
docs.text: This probe starts a confined Python process and checks that it cannot read the downloaded workload file. It is setup, outside the study's measured work. If it fails, the following cells leave the study stopped and explain the remedy.

docs.title: 4. Run and compare¶
docs.text: The study evaluates the seed and eight revisions, then selects and checks a program on separate workloads. Below are its development measurements.

docs.title: Check the selected program¶
docs.text: Development feedback helps propose changes. Selection tests eligible programs on a different, published workload after proposing ends. Final checking tests only the starting and selected programs after selection. Keeping those phases separate prevents treating a development score as a result on new jobs.

docs.title: Change one line¶
docs.text: What if the comparison used >= instead of <=, choosing the busier worker? Change the selected source and run it through the same fixed development evaluator. This optional check runs separately from the recorded study above.

docs.title: Research question: ADRS¶
docs.text: Can verifier-guided revisions improve a systems algorithm? This shipped, fixture-only study is inspired by ADRS. It is not a reproduction of ADRS, its ten case studies, or live-model gains. Use the paper-reading worksheet to map the research mechanism onto the components below.

docs.title: Component mapping¶
docs.text:
Role Maintained study Artifact / seed SourceTree containing the round-robin scheduler.py Proposer Eight authored revisions, produced in confined child processes Evaluator / objective Fixed simulator; maximize quality from imbalance and probes Search Greedy with eight proposal attempts after the seed Feedback Development observations and verifier failures External controls Workload splits, confinement, budgets, selection, final checking Retained results Durable development history plus later measurements and decision record

Scope and acceptance remain in #195 B2 and the milestone record. Source checked on 2026-09-15: primary report.

docs.title: API decision evidence: issue #314
docs.text: Recorded September 18, 2026. This verifies the foundation and comparison decisions, not a released 0.2 package. The programming model continues to own the current executable contract.

docs.title: Exact baselines
docs.text:
Baseline Identification Purpose Main before #297 c04ec6b4b949b8a2702779107e25acd24feb8020, package 0.1.0 Historical manifests, stores, and matching-runtime continuation #297 source reference Same commit plus retained source patch, SHA-256 b88e5c438e4ca2b4cf0d5bffffb9a8e40a945f1500df269c25476364f6527d51 Separate source/docstring changes from invocation changes Study Retained .py and example source hashes in the comparison receipt Explicit lowering alternatives, never installed package features

Both baselines were archived separately and built as wheels and source archives with uv build --offline. Each wheel was installed non-editably into its own Python 3.12.13 environment. The wheel source inventories matched every captured source-file hash. The recorder rejects imports outside the selected interpreter's installation. Both report version 0.1.0; version equality is not source equality.

The lock SHA-256 is 2d246d5312b6c1eb68ee9dd851ac0be39f31ff7ac0e86fe73f6748a42c02aea1. The complete baseline manifest records wheel/archive hashes, source hashes, pyproject hash, source patch, schema versions, and inventory. The reference patch changed twelve source files' docstrings only; ASTs with docstrings removed matched main. It excludes concurrent #315 behavior work. #297 was still open/uncommitted at capture; its separate verification retains its own checks and publication limits.

GitHub returned no releases. The paginated tag inventory contained archive tags, not a release reservation. PyPI's meta-evolve project endpoint returned 404. These observations support 0.2.0 as a working target, not a claim of registry ownership or permission to publish. #319 must recheck at release time.

docs.title: Six journeys and observed tradeoffs
docs.text:
Journey Observation Authoring / authority consequence Duration parser Both forms reached 100%; two proposals, three evaluations. Reuse across two tasks/seeds agreed. improve() keeps direct imports/callables; Improver adds a constructor without removing task/seed choices. SDK callback Explicit context preserved normal defaults; 14 tokens and unknown spend retained; billed failures retained cost. One keyword opt-in replaces positional inference. Resources removes engine-count fields; SDK requests and feedback grants stay explicit. Search comparison Equal explicit allowances agreed; bare Greedy at budget 25 changed from 20 to 25 attempts. Remove duplicate ordinary limit. Preserve evaluator, seed, budget, and proposer controls; intentional default changes remain visible. Failed/incomplete reporting All four lifecycle/rankability states observed; current summary raised on both unrankable states. Report costs before requesting a winner; no numeric sentinel or new result-wrapper class. Reopen/resume Seven frozen stores read unchanged; source changes refused before work. Registration/source/environment decisions remain necessary; a shorter author declaration cannot remove verification. Composition AutoResearch, policy evolution, and ACE agreed under procedure lowering. Improver removed no recipe/suite/stage orchestration. Candidate configuration cannot acquire evaluation or access authority.

Quality/cost objectives, scalar evaluation, missing metrics, thresholds, and Specialists also matched under both objective declarations. All five inheriting presets exercised zero/two/unbounded task allowances. Failed-proposal termination, custom search, BestOfK, and synchronous wide-cohort refusal were checked. The distributed capture is serial execution, not concurrency evidence.

AutoResearch exercised 15 ordinary runs per side; policy evolution 13 with ten retained inner stores; ACE 15 with 14 wrapper sessions, six during search. The comparison retained different method-specific results and normalized storage locators explicitly. These are deterministic fixture traces, not independent reader studies, live-model findings, speedup measurements, or evidence of RSI.

docs.text: Status: Shipped. This records the source implementation of #316, under the Author API revision gate. The programming model owns behavior; the migration guide owns author actions. This record does not claim a package release, merged PR, hosted CI result, or meta-evolve-docs deployment.

docs.title: Historical capture
docs.text:
Before changing argument binding or registry manifests, an isolated wheel was built from c04ec6b4b949b8a2702779107e25acd24feb8020 plus the local #297 and #315 source changes. A separate Python 3.12.13 environment installed that wheel; the capture executed its installed package rather than checkout imports.

tests/fixtures/pre_316_invocation/capture.json records package location, wheel hash, all Python source hashes, component-source hash, captured store hashes, manifests, event digests, usage, and matching-runtime continuation. Its source-tree SHA256 is 5367ba3044c27308f93a097063ecbd6cd8105ae617fd5a60a44097176b54f44b. The hashed source remains distinct from the ongoing #314 broader captures. The generated pre-cutover-source.patch reconstructs that package from the base commit; reconstruction was checked against all 198 recorded Python hashes.

The committed optional/variadic cases use the unchanged frozen functions in tests/fixtures/api_v01/components.py. Both legally stop after one decision, retain best value 1, and continue under their matching old runtime to the same events and usage as uninterrupted execution. Their final best values are 6 and 3. Under new invocation, fresh runs of those exact functions would instead select 300 and 0; the proposer manifest mismatch prevents that behavior from being mistaken for continuation.

The history test requires every non-proposer manifest to remain equal, including the policy and optional context selector. It checks the unchanged user-function digest, automatic dependency difference, no callback/preflight activity, and unchanged events/usage after refused resume. Source and fixture bytes are never rewritten to make verification pass.

The pre-315 budget fixture also remains unchanged. Its earlier successful cross-resolver continuation is historical evidence for the budget slice. With

docs.title: 316 integrated, it now correctly refuses unverified old invocation; current
docs.text: partial/full budget runs still agree exactly. Historical readability is independent of continuation permission.

docs.title: Implementation checks
docs.text:
Focused tests cover ordinary defaults, explicit keyword context, positional-only parents, aliases, variadics, partials, bound/decorated/local objects, route precedence, preparation-time refusals, exact context, and single invocation. They also exercise user and framework source sensitivity, fresh imports, every committed recovery frontier, and admitted serial distributed execution.

The migrated examples keep their explicit structural and patch interfaces. Ordinary callbacks and their direct Python callers use keyword context; deterministic notebook outputs were re-executed and compared. EvoSkill's closing exercise changes its seeded proposal order because its wrapper source is part of the declared factory identity; its partial-competence outcome is unchanged. Live drivers were exercised with deterministic substitutes, without paid calls.

docs.title: Capability-lesson newcomer walkthrough
docs.text:
This is the revised task handoff from #281 to #275. Use #277's exploratory findings and reusable regression checklist to record each scenario's cells or commands, expected and actual result, environment, tested commit, assistance needed, outcome, and linked defects.

This page is a facilitator's handoff. Give participants the prompts below one at a time, without the expected results in the observer checklist. The walkthrough checks whether someone can find, explain, and adapt an experiment, as well as execute its cells.

docs.title: Run a session
docs.text:
1. Start with a reader who can use Python functions and notebooks but has not used Meta-Evolve. Record their relevant experience and any prior exposure to these docs. Use an empty notebook and working folder, without a checkout.
  2. Record the documentation source/build revision, package version, installation URL or archive hash, and imported package location, then open the homepage. Let the reader choose links; do not supply a direct guide link unless help is needed.
  3. Ask them to think aloud. Record the first point where they hesitate, their interpretation, and the page, heading, or cell involved. Ask neutral questions such as “What do you expect this to do?” Avoid explaining the API for them.
  4. If they ask for help, record their attempted approach before helping. Mark that task as assisted even if it succeeds afterward. Stop at a blocker when continuing would only repeat the same problem.
  5. Use a new notebook for the chosen task guide. Observe whether the reader finds and executes required setup, including any folded cells, without prompting. Record time to find the guide, first successful task result, and independent adaptation; separate installation delays from reading and coding time. Complete further guides in later sessions; preserve code and outputs for every attempted task.
  6. For their own evaluator, measure time to a completed bounded experiment and an inspected result. The seed may remain selected; a positive score delta is not required. Observe feedback problems before asking the diagnostic questions below, and distinguish an unprompted discovery from a prompted task.

docs.title: Participant prompts
docs.text:
Give only the current prompt to the participant. The first four form the common entrance walkthrough; the last prompt checks transfer after a task guide.

  1. Find and run: “Starting on the homepage, find a first example you can run without a model account. Set it up in your notebook and run it.”
  2. Explain: “Point to what changes, what proposes a change, and what decides whether it is better. Explain what happened between the printed scores.”
  3. Predict and adapt: “Allow just one revision. Before running, predict the number of evaluations and which inputs will still fail. Run it and use the selected parser on a new input.”
  4. Find a task: “You want to keep the result and inspect it after restarting Python. Find the relevant instructions, then try them in a fresh notebook.”
  5. Transfer: “For a small problem of your own, implement a starting value, revision function, and measurement function. Use the documentation to run a bounded experiment and use its selected result. Explain which rules stay outside the revision.”

For another guide, state the desired outcome in ordinary words before giving its title: for example, “Use failed test cases to guide the next revision.” Then use that page's change-and-predict exercise. Record the prediction before execution, the explanation afterward, and any help required.

After the exercise, ask a question relevant to that guide without naming the answer's location: “Why didn't my new metric change the winner?”, “Why did search revise a weaker version?”, “Why isn't feedback reaching my proposer?”, “Why wasn't the last attempt selected?”, or “Do I need the original functions to reopen?” Record their route, answer, and any assistance. Returning readers should also find the relevant operation with shared setup closed.

docs.title: Read and adapt a flagship
docs.text:
After the common entrance, offer one of these reading tasks. Reading retained outputs requires no model calls; prepare any proposed edit without executing a paid cell. These tasks supplement the existing independent walkthrough gate.

Participant prompt Observer checks "Find an example that improves a drawing. Explain the method without opening its paper, then show why the last drawing was not selected." Reader finds SVG Feedback Descent's summary; separates critique from score; locates revision 5 and the later regression; identifies SCENE and RUBRIC as an adaptation kept fixed within a run "Find an example that teaches a skill. Show what each agent produces and where the framework starts repeating their work." Reader identifies the plan, native skill file, and executor answer; explains revise as the outer proposer; distinguishes the corrected retry from the population outcome and held-out tie "Find an example that changes an agent's setup. What is the candidate, what is tested, and which results were actually recorded?" Reader distinguishes harness from repaired code, fixed independent checks from proposal, and offline rehearsal from pending live capture; finds the deterministic reference and supported runtime requirements

Record the first route, time to find the summary, explanation in the reader's own words, proposed adaptation, and assistance. Do not supply the observer answers before the attempt. A successful reading task is not live validation or a substitute for the three independent participants required by #275.

After the parser walkthrough, ask: “Find how to configure the same example explicitly. Explain what Task, Experiment, Session, and Run each need and do. Show where you would change scoring, generate different revisions, choose a different parent, or pause execution. Predict what has run immediately after constructing an experiment, starting a session, and taking its first step.” Then ask the reader to execute that example and inspect its selected parser. Record their navigation, prediction, explanation, and assistance separately.

docs.title: Tasks for an unfamiliar reader
docs.text:
For the tool-choice page, add these unaided retrieval tasks:

  • Starting at the homepage, decide whether Meta-Evolve fits a small idea of your own. Identify the starting value, revision function, and independent grader; find a guide you could adapt. Explain one reason to choose a bundled optimizer.
  • Find whether closing Python preserves a default run, whether saving makes it resumable, and whether a spending ceiling prevents every overrun.
  • Find what evidence would support a live improvement claim. Separate the handwritten parser's measured scores from model performance.

Record time to find each answer, navigation or search route, interpretation, and assistance. These tasks extend #275/#277; agent checks are not human results.

Observer checklist: use these outcomes to interpret the session, without reading them to the participant. Reproducing output alone does not demonstrate that the reader understands why it occurred.

Task Starting page Expected observable result Follow Start building and run the parser cells First experiment Seed 33%, selected 100%; one proposal, two evaluations; 4m gives 240 seconds Continue to the full parser walkthrough Start here Scores are 33%, 67%, 100%; no SDK request or lesson-file import Identify the artifact, proposer, evaluator, search, feedback, and limits Parser and routing prompt Reader separates simulated responses from actual independent grading Find the callback and result contracts without opening source code Live parser or SVG, then API reference Reader follows the proposer, evaluator, and result links; identifies callback inputs and outputs, EvidenceDraft, the declared context policy, and NoSuccessfulEvaluation; returns to a worked example. Record time, route, and assistance Explain declarations, execution, and inspection Core objects Reader distinguishes the evaluator from Task, reuses the task in Experiment, predicts no execution at declaration, one seed evaluation at local start, and two evaluations after the first parser step; Run queries add no work Inspect results in a fresh notebook Inspection One history keeps the 67% revision after a 33% regression and a failure with no score; four attempts give a two-version winning lineage Define measurements and choose an objective in a fresh notebook Evaluation Reader reports hours separately and predicts how changing the objective changes the winner Change one search declaration Search Reader traces Greedy to 5 and TreeSearch to 10 using six proposals and seven evaluations each; five proposals select 5 for both with six evaluations; the constructed score table is not a benchmark Inspect and retain a search history Search Reader identifies the seed retained on a tie and the failed evaluation with no score, then reopens the saved tree history without callbacks or new evaluations Supply and use feedback in a fresh notebook Feedback Failed checks drive the handwritten fixes to 100%; disabling feedback leaves 33% with the same three evaluations Explain early stopping and exhaustion in a fresh notebook Limits Reader distinguishes attempt limits, score satisfaction, and evaluation ceilings; predicts zero proposals when the seed suffices Save, restart, reopen, and export from a fresh notebook Persistence Fresh kernel reads 33%, 67%, 100% and three evaluations without lesson functions; exported source parses 4m and 2h; an earlier run survives a new save Connect an SDK in a fresh notebook Use your model SDK Reader runs required accounting setup, locates the separate request cell, explains the three-request maximum, and inspects labels and usage without requests; identifies where to replace the SDK and finds the explanation of unknown spend Improve and reuse an agent configuration in a fresh notebook Harness Reader explains 2/3 → 3/3 through the polite password answer, reuses the selected instruction, and predicts that zero proposals retain 2/3; distinguishes this simulation from the linked governed repair study Improve and reuse a search policy in a fresh notebook Policy Reader explains scores 6, 7, 8 through inner traces, distinguishes three outer evaluations from twenty inner evaluations, and predicts why a candidate limit of 99 cannot raise the fixed inner budget Add a value type in a fresh notebook Artifact domain Reader separates valid recipe structure from checklist scores, sees a plain tuple rejected without evaluation, and reopens saved values with a rebuilt registry; reopening does not grant resume capability Transfer the component map Discovery Reader separates an optimized skill artifact from proposer feedback

Reading declarations and running deterministic checks do not require paid calls. Live execution and retained transcripts remain subject to #270's protocol and #271's validation. If live evidence is unavailable, record it as unavailable; test fixtures are not model transcripts and do not fulfill a live validation gate.

docs.title: Evidence and acceptance
docs.text:
Record the exact source commit, OS, Python version, installation method, commands, expected/actual output, and every point requiring maintainer help. Run from an empty working directory so accidental repository imports cannot hide missing definitions. For the live guides, also rehearse extracted downloads. Retain history directories and their original run IDs for fresh-process inspection.

Completing automated example tests does not complete those walkthroughs or the integrated release gate.

docs.title: Practical-journey handoff for #336
docs.text:
The integration verification supplies the exact engineering setup, regression commands, outcomes, and remaining SDK glue. Use the short SDK notebook for three-request wiring and the complete routing journey for development feedback, known failed-work usage, detached snapshots, final separation, and saved history. These live guides remain Experimental/live-only; the engineering rehearsals substitute providers or HTTP responses and authorize no paid calls.

For #275, first give the existing unaided transfer prompt. Start its timer when the task is presented, and stop when the participant has completed a bounded run with their own evaluator and inspected its outcome. Record setup time separately. A seed that remains best counts; a positive score delta is not the success gate. Observe whether feedback is discovered, enabled, and consumed without prompting before asking the following diagnostic prompts, one at a time:

  • “This run has no useful feedback for its revision function. Find why, and explain whether the feedback was disabled or no matching report was selected.”
  • “This run says context was truncated. Determine whether its selected checks are still usable, and explain what the bounds control.”
  • “Compare this failed attempt with a completed wrong answer. Explain the measurements, work counts, and retained usage.”
  • “Keep the result, restart Python, and inspect it without the original functions. Explain which values remain usable after the store closes.”

Facilitator setup uses the credential-free feedback and persistence guides first. context=None exercises deliberate feedback off; RecentAncestors(max_records=0) exercises enabled but empty selection; a large record allowance with max_chars=0 clips only text and leaves structured evidence intact. The optional parser proposer returns its parent without checks. Contrast this with the routing proposer's required-feedback diagnostic using the offline tests below. Do not send a diagnostic SDK request during an unauthorised paid session.

Bhasker and Salah agree session stopping rules and any timing/comparison thresholds before the first scored session. Retain each participant's outcome and assistance, including abandonment. Keep baseline and after conditions explicit; a familiarized retest is not a fresh participant. Three observations do not estimate prevalence. The existing three-user unaided completion and Salah acceptance gates still apply.

For #277, extend the maintained checklist with these scenarios. Each row needs commands/cells, expected and actual results, environment and tested source/package identity, assistance, retained output/history, and linked defects or limitations.

Scenario Expected result and regression owner Improvement, tie, regression, failed seed Correct selected parent, complete or explicitly partial report; test_llm_prompt_lesson.py / test_llm_prompt_feedback.py Disabled, missing, stale, truncated feedback No silent fallback or lookup outside selection; intact report survives text clipping; test_llm_prompt_feedback.py / test_sdk_notebook_feedback.py Missing metric, malformed output, failed rewrite No fabricated score; failed rewrite skips evaluation; known usage remains; routing feedback and SDK failure tests Unknown accounting and final failure Receipts survive; final failure triggers no new search; test_llm_prompt_persistence.py Restart, wrong ID, multiple runs, snapshot lifetime Explicit selection, typed diagnostics, detached display, no SDK calls; routing persistence/reopening tests and #335's contract checks Installed ZIP and copied notebook No checkout imports; real driver or SDK transport, imperfect seed and failure exercised; test_lesson_downloads.py / SDK notebook tests

This is maintained handoff material for #275/#277, not completed independent sessions or a release recommendation. #269 retains independent SDK/accounting review, #274 docs coordination, and #270/#271 live evidence. Participant coordination remains with Salah; no outreach follows from this packet.

docs.title: Regression handoff for #295
docs.text:
Use #277's existing checklist and owner to track these scenarios against the final implementation commit:

  • Copy every core guide from an empty notebook, including folded setup, and compare the visible cells with the rendered output. Also run the whole sequence.
  • Follow each chooser and historical section link; check that task links reach visible instructions and setup links reach the expandable setup control.
  • Rerun and change the objective, search allowance, feedback policy, or seed as instructed. Retain scores, work counts, failures, and winning lineage.
  • Save, exit Python, and reopen using only the reopening cell. Export and use the source. Save with one proposal, then reopen both folders separately; their original run IDs and histories must remain intact.
  • Exercise expansion, copying setup and task cells, keyboard focus, search, and narrow layouts. Record friction separately from execution failures.

Automated checks and agent observations belong in preflight evidence below; independent participant records remain with #275. This handoff supplies updated scenarios and does not close either QA issue.

docs.title: Agent preflight of the rewritten guides
docs.text:
This review identifies documentation defects and checks executable examples. It is not an independent newcomer session; no participant results are recorded here. The three human walkthroughs remain pending.

Reviewed on September 15, 2026, against the uncommitted documentation working tree based on 97ab240, using macOS arm64 and Python 3.12.13.

Finding Change The homepage's Guides card opened the detailed run reference Route it to the task guide index The first lesson used library terminology before explaining the loop Lead with starting values, revision functions, measurement, and history Start here introduced improve(), trials(), and best().value after their first use Explain the calls before their cells Start here printed the selected source without showing how to use it Load the selected parser and call it on 4m A downloaded ZIP may be on the reader's computer rather than in a hosted notebook Explain upload and the notebook's working folder at installation Guide discovery assumed readers knew terms such as candidate and parent Use concrete task descriptions and offer routes for scoring, SDK calls, and saving Three policy-guide calls used the compatibility spelling of run Use Experiment consistently, with execution storage and budget on run

Automated evidence covers displayed cells, exact output, isolated execution, and saved histories. SDK checks use simulated HTTP responses; live model performance and unaided human understanding still need their own evidence.

Validation for this preflight:

  • Start-here, policy, notebook, and curriculum checks: 69 passed; the separate full example-command catalog was excluded.
  • Navigation, ownership, routes, consolidation, notebook, persistence, codec, and capability checks: 102 passed, with one immutable-codec aliasing check inapplicable and skipped. These groups overlap; their counts are not additive.
